statement: Allow pharmacists to treat more sicknesses and conditions
why: This party says that pharmacists have capacity that GPs and other health services may not. Increasing the number of conditions that pharmacists can prescribe or provide care for without needing approval from a doctor or nurse will make it easier for people managing long-term conditions or those with straightforward sicknesses with clear diagnosis. This would reduce wait times for GPs and provide quicker care.
how: This party would list more sicknesses and ailments pharmacists are allowed to treat, including sore throats, tonsillitis, gout and period pain. There would be a protocol for when pharmacists should refer back to a doctor for treatment. Consultation fees would remain capped at $20 for most and $5 for Community Service Card holders.

statement: Remove some rules around pharmacy locations, ownership and licences
why: This party says that removing the rule that prevents a single person or entity from owning more than five pharmacies would make it easier to open new pharmacies. Changing other rules about pharmacy locations, licenses and qualifications for pharmacists would make it easier to open and staff pharmacies anywhere in the country.
how: The party would change regulatory settings to implement the reforms. Online prescription e-lockers can be used to help those in rural areas access medication when pharmacies may have limited opening hours.

statement: Increase the percentage of the health budget spent on Pharmac to over 10 percent by 2033
why: This party says that many medications for conditions like cancer are publicly funded in Australia but not in NZ. The public drug funding system Pharmac, is not receiving enough funding to keep up. Paying for medication can reduce pressure elsewhere in the health system by helping people manage their health conditions effectively.
how: This party would increase funding for Pharmac by 1 percent per year until 2033, from the current base of 4.9 percent of the health budget. More medications on Pharmac's "options for investment" list would become available to New Zealanders. A sustainable funding option would mean Pharmac can spend money on drugs for more health conditions.  This party estimates that this policy would cost over $4bn over 7 years.

statement: Increase the areas of conservation land which can be accessed by helicopter for hunting
why: This party says that in areas of forest and mountains where people want to hunt, there are "no-fly" and "no-landing" areas for helicopters with no clear reasoning. In areas where helicopters are the fastest way in, access restrictions should be justified with obvious safety or conservation reasons.
how: This party would allow the Game Council to designate helicopter landing sites, and restrict commercial venison operators by animal gender when necessary, leaving trophy stags for hunters. DOC would be required to use public tests to designate where aircraft could land, and would not have any say in which types of helicopters were used. The Outdoors Access Commission would be asked to make hunting access a priority in its work programme.

statement: Prevent universities from allocating support of any kind based on ethnicity
why: This party says that previous policy directions have required that public agencies should allocate services based on individual need and value, rather than race. Universities should be included in this directive too, as universities are independent but largely funded by the taxpayer. Grants or donations from private money would be exempt from this requirement.
how: This party would amend the Education and Training Act, adding language preventing benefits or support being offered on the basis of race of ethnicity. This would include scholarships, accommodation support, designated spaces in tertiary institutions and any other types of support. Universities would still be able to confer scholarships based on academic merit, need, geographic location, economic circumstances or disability.

statement: Make the abuse of a companion animal in a family violence situation a crime
why: This party says that pets are being threatened and abused to coerce people in family violence situations and prevent them from leaving. Research shows half of victims delay leaving a violent situation because they are concerned about their pets. Criminalising the abuse of animals in this context will give Police more tools to protect victims. States in Australia and the US have enacted similar laws and New Zealand needs to do the same.
how: This party would amend the Crimes Act to make abusing a pet with the goal of coercion an offence punishable by a maximum seven years in prison. Protection orders would be strengthened to ensure offenders cannot control access to a pet and ensure pets are not left with abusers. Police would be required to record the presence of pets in a family violence situation and receive clear operational guidance around removing pets to a safe place if the animal is at risk of harm.

statement: Ensure agriculture is not part of the emissions trading scheme
why: This party says that New Zealand's dairy industry has a lower emissions footprint than the global average. Adding methane emissions from dairy farming to the Emissions Trading Scheme would make producing dairy more expensive and mean more dairy production happens in other countries. New Zealand should be increasing dairy production instead of reducing it to limit emissions. The Paris Agreement is not fit for purpose.
how: This party would continue to exclude emissions from the agriculture sector from the Emissions Trading Scheme. Agriculture would be permanently excluded. This policy would be part of a changed approach to New Zealand's commitments under the Paris Agreement.

statement: Count carbon dioxide and methane differently under emissions targets
why: This party says that carbon dioxide and methane both contribute to global heating. Carbon dioxide stays in the atmosphere longer than methane, which is largely produced by the dairy and sheep industries.
how: This party would rewrite NZ's Nationally Determined Contributions plan, which is required by the Paris Agreement. It would differentiate between the emissions caused by methane and carbon dioxide so that methane emissions do not have to be reduced by the same degree as carbon emissions. A "split gas approach" would calculate the emissions generated by carbon dioxide and methane differently. Carbon dioxide emissions would be reduced while methane levels could continue at current levels.

statement: Make disrupting lawful hunters with drones or by standing in the line of fire an offence
why: This party says that people can disrupt hunters by stepping into the line of fire, or disturbing game birds with a drone. This should not happen if a hunter is following legal guidelines and safety protocols. While people are free to protest hunting, those protests should not place anyone at risk.  It says that currently there are no laws covering this situation which needs to change.
how: This party would create specific infringement offences for standing in the line of fire of a hunter, and for disturbing game birds with aircraft like drones or helicopters. These infringements would not apply if the hunter was not following the relevant laws and guidelines.

statement: Issue licences for security professionals to have more authority against intrusion or theft
why: This party says that there are twice as many security guards as police officers in New Zealand, but security guards don't have any legal authority. People who do not feel safe in shops buy online instead, impacting small businesses. Licencing trained and vetted security guards to remove people and use proportionate force when necessary would be good for businesses worried about crime. It would accompany current law reforms allowing people to make citizens arrests if no police are present.
how: This party would train vetted security guards; those who complete the training would be issued with a special licence. The licence would allow them to require a person's name an address to enter a premise; issue up to 3-year exclusion notices for a premise or premises; remove people who are threatening or breaching entry conditions; carry out safety searches individuals would have to consent to as a condition of entry; if necessary, use force, until the person complies or the police arrive. Licenced security professionals would have the ability to detain someone while waiting for the police.

statement: Give the Game Council responsibility for game animals on conservation land
why: This party says that legislation currently treats deer as pest animals to be exterminated rather than game animals to be hunted. The Game Council can advise DOC but does not make decisions. Hunters spend time in the area where these animals live and should be making decisions about what happens to game animals on conservation land.
how: This party would transfer responsibility for game animals from DOC to the Game Council. It would also give the Council more funding to recognise its further responsibilities.

statement: Recognise introduced game species in law
why: This party says that game animals on NZ's conservation land are treated as pests which should be killed. However, these animals are valuable to many rural communities and hunters and should be treated as natural resources instead. Hunters can strike a balance between removing game animals to protect the natural environment and ensuring there are enough game for the future.
how: This party would change legislation to designate game animals and birds as natural resources rather than pests. Herds of New Zealand deer, which hunters appreciate, would be designated as specific "Herds of Special Interest" for protection. The whitetail deer on Stewart Island would be given this designation.

statement: Limit the number of branded items in school uniforms to reduce costs
why: This party says that in 2025, 38,000 WINZ hardship loans were issued to help families cover the cost of school uniforms, and in some cases the combined cost for school uniforms is over $1,000. Limiting state schools to just three branded school items will make uniforms more affordable for New Zealanders. Generic items such as socks would be available from low-cost retailers like The Warehouse or KMart. School uniforms can promote school culture but expensive uniforms don't improve educational outcomes, and similar policies in parts of Australia and the UK have been successful.
how: This party would limit state schools to three mandatory branded items as part of a uniform. Alternative, generic options for clothes like skirts, shirts, trousers and socks could be selected from low-cost retail stores. This policy would only apply to everyday items worn to school, not to more special items like branded clothing for sports teams.

statement: Allow children to take any passing school bus, not just buses specifically for one school
why: This party says that school transport rules are based on the nearest school. Parents who choose different schools for reasons like siblings being close together may not be able to use a school bus service. This is particularly difficult for families in rural areas. Allowing children to ride any school bus with space would make it easier for families.
how: This party would introduce a rule where a child living along an existing school bus route could use any available seat. If a bus route became full, another one would be provided by the Ministry of Education. Any extra funding would come from the education budget by cutting other spending.

statement: Give volunteer groups more opportunities and funding for maintenance on conservation land
why: This party says that that DOC has a 30 percent maintenance shortfall and has issued more than 2,300 closure alerts since 2021. Volunteer groups carry out track and hut maintenance, but should receive funding for this over multiple years rather than applying annually. Creating a system for groups to receive biodiversity credits will incentivise further volunteer work in the hills.
how: This party would require DOC to give community groups the first opportunity for funding for maintenance on conservation land. Community groups would be allowed to sign multi-year contracts for work they are able to do. If biodiversity benefits were independently verified, groups including hunters would receive biodiversity credits. The Game Council and Deerstalkers Association would be formally represented when deciding how animals on conservation land were managed.

statement: Return $1 to local authorities for each night an international tourist spends in their area
why: This party says that millions of tourists come to New Zealand, but these visitors can place pressure on local infrastructure. International visitors pay a levy that is collected by central government, but local government needs funding for infrustructure costs like roads and wastewater. Any new taxes or expenses should be very specifically targeted to where they are needed without making things more expensive for residents and ratepayers.
how: This party would use a data programme to determine where international visitors are staying. Each year, the central government would make an automatic annual payment of $1 for each night an international visitor spent in that council area. This dividend could replace some increases to rates which would otherwise pay for infrastructure upgrades. Based on 2026 nights, this would include $8.2m for Auckland, $4.9m for Queenstown and $2m for Rotorua.

statement: Create a regulatory framework for the use of cryptocurrency
why: This party says that it's important to support innovation in the NZ financial system. The party claims that cryptocurrency help businesses engage in the global market. The party argues that the government should regulate digital financial assets to facilitate smoother capital investment while ensuring consumer protection and legality. It wants to ensure legitimate businesses have access to banking and are not turned away due to the novel use of cryptocurrency.
how:
This party would establish clear legal and tax rules for cryptocurrency. Such regulation would define what regulated digital currency is. It would review NZ financial regulations to gauge whether current settings deny legitimate businesses access to banking. The party seeks to scale regulation by firm size. 

The party would allow smaller firms a license to experiment with cryptocurrency. This license would exist under government supervision.

statement: Create tax exemptions for use of cryptocurrency
why: This party says that incentivise and provide stability for those seeking to invest in cryptocurrency for the long term.  The party says it wants to simplify and minimise tax compliance complications for everyday users.
how: This party would introduce exemptions for low-value purchases made using cryptocurrency. This party would apply exemptions for the first twelve months of investments that qualify as personal investments in cryptocurrency. Business investments would remain fully taxable.

statement: Add a physical presence test to permanent residents
why: This party says that people need to be regularly living in NZ to be regarded as a permanent resident. They need to show an ongoing connection to NZ.
how: This party would remove the permanent resident visa category and instead change the resident visa to mandate residents to live 2 out of 5 years in NZ. Exemptions will exist for service members, employees of NZ-owned businesses, and certain family commitments.

statement: Make Student Service Fees voluntary
why: This party says that voluntary student membership of student associations at universities has been undermined by compulsory 'service fees.' The party says these fees add costs for students that should be paid as they use the services. Instead, the party argues that service fees force students to fund union campaigns and media services that not all students support.
how: This party would change regulations so that services are offered as a menu. Students would then select what services they wish to use. This would prohibit compulsory service fees used to fund services traditionally funded by student unions/associations.

statement: Scale back the use and effect of Treaty principles in legislation
why: This party says that, to protect democratic majority rule, judges cannot be allowed to enable Treaty principles to go beyond what Parliament intended. Greater clarity in legislation and removing Treaty considerations would provide greater protection of individual property rights and prevent ethnicity-based equity measures.
how:
This party would add three principles to the Constitution Act. These would be that Parliament is the highest legal authority in NZ; the rule of law is fundamental; and all New Zealanders are equal before the law.  It would also insert property rights into the New Zealand Bill of Rights to ensure homes, farms, businesses and other property are protected.
Tikanga could be used in court only when it was relevant to a case, or where Parliament has expressly provided for it.

statement: Remove ethnicity-based criteria for delivering public services
why: The party says the only criterion for a person receiving publicly funded services should be need, rather than equity across different groups.
how: The party would create a clear statutory duty that public services are delivered based on need, without group-based equity considerations changing the Public Service Act. Agencies would be required to comply with the principle as a matter of law, and decisions that breach it could be subject to judicial review.

statement: Remove group-based equity measures from recruitment in the public sector
why: This party says that that group-based equity measures, such as hiring people of specific ethnic backgrounds, are unneeded. Group-based considerations cannot exist alongside merit-based recruitment.
how: This party would repeal group-based requirements on government departments as employers. It would repeal Section 73 of the Public Service Act, and its equivalent in the Crown Entities Act.

statement: Prevent cultural practices from being used in the public service
why: This party says that taxpayers' time and money should not be spent on cultural practices that some staff may not want to do, like prayers and karakia. The party says that cultural skills should only matter as part of a job if absolutely necessary and should not distract from the primary responsibility employees have. Employees should express cultural or spiritual practices like prayers or karakia outside of the workplace.
how: This party would prohibit cultural or spiritual practices in the workplace of public institutions. It would use a clear letter of expectations to the Public Service Commissioner and Cabinet to enforce the removal of cultural expectations.

statement: Reduce number of ministries into consolidated departments
why: This party says that countries with a similar population to NZ have fewer government ministries.Merging existing ministries can reduce duplication of responsibility. It says that government spending increases are associated with the number of ministers in a government.
how: This party would to reduce the number of ministries by over half with one senior minister responsible for more areas. Other minister positions that are cut will become junior minister roles below the senior minister.

statement: Restrict how many people recieve medical certification for health-related benefits
why: This party says that many people need to get away from sickness benefits and into work. It claims that the country doesn't want to miss out on their potential.
how: This party would make all health and disability benefits subject to approval from an MSD-approved pool of designated doctors. The party would have assessments be made against clear, objective criteria, rather than leaving major long-term benefit decisions to discretion. Reassessment would begin with mental-health-related grants made after the pandemic. Other reassessments would be phased in with the new criteria for existing Jobseeker Support, health conditions or disabilities and Supported Living Payment.

statement: Monitor spending for jobseekers receiving a benefit for more than 4 months
why: This party says that there is a need for greater fairness in the welfare system. Some beneficiaries spend money in ways that do not prepare them for work, such as gambling, alcohol and tobacco. The party argues that taxpayers should not fund the purchasing of products that set people back from potentially finding employment.
how: This party would require that people on a jobseeker benefit for 4 months be automatically shifted onto an electronic money management card system. Such a system would block expenses related to smoking, drinking, and gambling. Carve-outs and modified arrangements where money management would risk safety or block access to necessities.

statement: Create a "Working with Children" card
why: This party says it can take up to 3 years for complaints about worker conduct to reach an employer. The party claims that current checks only capture a snapshot in time and not ongoing accountability.
how: This party would create a Working with Children card. Eligibility for the card would take into account relevant criminal convictions, disciplinary findings and other records relating to children or child-related work. If a cardholder is charged with a disqualifying offence, their card could be suspended or revoked, and their employer notified. This would simplify the system for employers and ensure child safety mechanisms can react in real time.

statement: Establish a public-private partnership to build two independent cancer centres.
why: This party says that cancer is an issue that affects so many families. Cancer is New Zealand’s biggest killer. More than 30,000 New Zealanders are diagnosed each year; by 2044, that number is expected to exceed 45,000.
how: This party would build two centres, built in Christchurch and Auckland. These would be financed through public-private partnerships, charitable donations, existing Crown health investment and other private capital. The investment would be accompanied by a government-run independent philanthropic foundation to help secure additional investment.  This party estimates that this policy would cost 2 billion in baseline capital expenditure.

statement: Allow "innovation trials" for new technology not covered by NZ law
why: This party says that NZ is falling behind because innovative technology like driverless cars and drones available overseas remains illegal. It argues that NZ policy settings are not responsive to change and need greater flexibility. Results from these trials could to help bolster the evidence base for regulatory change.
how: This party would create an application process that would see a singular business be exempt from a particular regulation. The approval would state the safety conditions and how the result will be measured. The Ministry for Regulation would help to run the trials, and companies working in the fields of novel medical technology, drones for agricultural use or driverless cars would be invited to test out this technology.

statement: Establish a $6-a-day infrastructure surcharge to temporary work visas
why: This party says that those on temporary work visas use infrastructure and should help fund its investment. The party claims its tax would raise $80m annually; the NZ temporary work visa would remain cheaper than in both the UK and Australia.
how: This party would add the tax on top of existing taxes. Such a process would be automated through the link between visas and employers.

statement: Deport serious offenders who are not New Zealand citizens
why: This party says it wishes to remove dangerous people from society. In addition, it aims to build greater trust in both law and order and immigration.
how: This party would deport Resident Visa holders convicted of offences carrying sentences of 10 years or more, irrespective of how long they have lived in the country. The party specifies that naturalised citizens would not be deported.

statement: Introduce benefits stand-down for first years of residence visa
why: This party says that that it is unfair for New Zealanders to fund benefits for people who've only recently committed to living and working in NZ. The party claims its change will prevent any encouragement of welfare dependency among new arrivals.
how: The party would have residence-class visa holders made ineligible for all welfare benefits for the first five years. The party claims it would do so by changing the eligibility criteria that presently permit residence-class visa holders to access welfare benefits.

statement: Give teachers legal powers to remove disruptive students from class
why: This party says that disruptive students can be a risk to the safety of other students and teaching staff, distracting others from learning during valuable teaching time.
how: This party would amend legislation so that teachers have an explicit legal power to direct a seriously or persistently disruptive student to leave and go to a staffed, supervised space. A refusal would be escalated to a dean or senior leader. If the student refused again after escalation, staff would be able to use reasonable force to remove them. The current Act would be clarified to allow reasonable and proportionate intervention to prevent harm or the destruction of property. Parents could be fined and authorities involved if they do not attend meetings with their child.

statement: Apply English language requirements for accredited employer work visas
why: This party says that migrants who come to NZ should have a solid base-level understanding of the country's most-used language. By ensuring greater English language proficiency, the party promises to increase public trust in the immigration system.
how: This party would extend existing English language requirements to all Accredited Employer Work Visa candidates. It would  exempt seasonal workers.

statement: Increase support for businesses and households affected by the emissions trading scheme
why: This party says that revenue from the emissions trading scheme is just another means by which the government raises revenue, and damages business competitiveness. The party seeks instead to refund the revenue generated to New Zealanders. The party additionally seeks to support businesses most affected by competitiveness concerns. The party is also concerned with the construction of carbon forests as an inefficient use of land.
how: The party would refund revenue derived from ETS auctions to citizens. Industrial carbon assistance would be raised to 90 percent and 60 percent rates where businesses face carbon-cost disadvantages.  The party would remove mandates for carbon forests, with the intention to use that land for farming instead.

statement: Add annual expiry dates to accredited employer visas
why: This party says that some businesses depend on migrant workers, creating a barrier to employment for New Zealanders. Adding an automatic expiry to accredited employer visas and requiring evidence of sustained need from the employer would ensure businesses hire New Zealanders when possible.
how: This party would add a 12-month expiration date to the accredited employer visa. For a migrant worker to remain eligible, the employer would need to provide up-to-date evidence of demand.

statement: Make Uber and DoorDash-like platform companies provide evidence of work rights
why: This party says that there are as many as 20,980 known overstayers in NZ. Platform apps like Uber and DoorDash do not require evidence of work rights for their drivers, which are needed irrespective of employment status. It is concerned that platform apps can encourage illegal overstaying.
how: This party would establish a dedicated overstayer enforcement unit within Immigration New Zealand. Platform employers such as Uber and DoorDash would be required to verify and report work rights. Employers who facilitate overstaying would lose accreditation.

statement: Expand rural policing
why: This party says that there is a lack of reporting of rural crime in NZ. It attributes this to a lack of trust in whether police will investigate. The prosecution rate is presently at 15%.  The lack of enforcement encourages rural crime.
how: This party would provide additional funding to expand the 111 service and hire more officers for rural areas, with a target of an additional 100,000 extra patrol hours each year. It would establish a dedicated rural crime unit.

statement: Prevent professionals from being disciplined for expressing opinions outside of their practice
why: This party says that treaty and cultural standards as both unnecessary and an improper rationale for disciplinary action. The party is concerned that standards can encroach deeply personal individual views on contentious political matters.
how: This party would ban professional regulators from disciplining members for lawful expression outside their professional practice. It says this would protect free speech and expression. It would require regulators to remain institutionally neutral on political and ideological issues. Mandatory training would be restricted to matters directly connected to professional competence and public safety, and there would be judicial oversight so courts could rein in regulators that went beyond their legal powers.

statement: Require infrastructure projects to consider a cheaper option
why: This party says that potential infrastructure projects, when seeking approval, should be required to publish a lowest-cost safe option alongside the preferred option. Both options should include cost, delivery time, and benefit-cost ratio for each. The party says this is to assess whether the preferred design is taking unnecessary steps or being made with overly conservative assumptions.
how: This party would mandate affordability and efficacy standards, made through the comparison with a cheaper alternative design, be applied to all infrastructure projects seeking government approval.

statement: Require major growth areas to have funded transport-capacity plans
why: This party says that councils are responsible for housing developments, while central government is responsible for state highways. Because of these different priorities, housing projects can occur without central government having to build the road capacity to deal with the increased growth. This worsens traffic, travel times and bus networks.
how: This party would require major growth areas to have funded transport-capacity plans. These plans would guarantee funding mechanisms such as road charges, tolls, developer contributions, council funding and private capital to ensure road capacity keeps up with population growth.

statement: Introduce an affordability test on used-car import regulations
why: This party says that regulations for used cars being imported into NZ can push up costs for people and families needing to buy a car. Import passenger registrations have fallen from around 165,000 in 2017 to 85,000 as people increasingly keep their current car for longer, putting off upgrading to newer, safer models.
how: This party would introduce an affordability test for imported cars. This test would flag a regulation if it is seen to reduce supply, thus increasing the prices of used cars.

statement: Freeze the minimum wage for three years
why: This party says that higher minimum wages can decrease the demand from businesses for workers to employ. The subsequent unemployment disproportionately burdens young people.
how: This party would freeze the minimum wage at its current rate for three years. This would cause the minimum wage to lose value due to inflation,  allowing more headroom in budgets for employers to bring on more staff, including younger people.

statement: Introduce a training wage
why: This party says that the minimum wage can increase wage costs at the expense of employing someone new. Young people are less experienced and more likely to struggle to find a job. Younger workers have less experience, need more training and are more costly to hire.
how: This party would establish a training wage at 60 per cent of the adult minimum wage for workers under 20, available for their first 12 months with an employer. Standard protections would still apply with the new lower wage rate.

statement: Protect employers from personal grievances
why: This party says that employers can worry about discussing the end of an employment relationship. The party also says that once a 90-day period has passed, employers should be able to move on without fear of personal grievances being taken up against them for workers they have stopped employing.
how: This party would allow protected employment exit negotiations. It would limit the time to take a personal grievance to the Employment Relations Authority to 90 days after it is raised, while retaining the existing rules for sexual-harassment grievances.

statement: Make unions collect their own fees
why: This party says that that the relationship between a union and its members is a private association between them and does not concern the employer.  It is unreasonable to expect union fees to be collected through payroll deductions administered by the employer.
how: This party would ensure that employers were not made by law to facilitate the financial relationship between unions and members. Unions would have the ability to set up their own financial capacity through online banking instead.

statement: Reevaluate the tax treatment of software and digital investment
why: This party says that the way Inland Revenue allows the deduction of business costs that come from software platforms varies inconsistently. This disadvantages businesses and technology platforms.
how: This party would review current depreciation and business expense rules to simplify how software and digital investments are treated.

statement: Repeal the Zero Carbon Act and NZ's net zero goal
why: This party says that NZ should play its part to reduce emissions but only in line with what other trading partners do, so that the country is not at a competitive disadvantage. The net zero target is arbitrary, and emissions reductions should be weighted in terms of trade.
how: This party would repeal the current Zero Carbon Act and adopted a trade-weighted approach to emissions reduction instead. The net zero by 2050 goal would be removed, and New Zealand would only do what its trading partners are doing.  This party would also protect NZ workers at risk of losing their jobs in high-emissions industries like steel production, so that these industries face lower carbon prices or none at all and are not at a competitive disadvantage.

statement: Remove the carbon price floor and return ETS profits to households
why: This party says that the Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS) acts as a "carbon tax", with a minimum price for carbon credits set by the government. This means the auctions do not work properly and raises the price of goods and services. The supply of carbon credits should be increased and the profit returned as a refund to New Zealanders.
how: This party would remove the price floor from the Emissions Trading Scheme to place downward pressure on the carbon price. 100 percent of the money from the carbon auction would be returned to New Zealanders as a tax refund. If the amount became so low that the refund was impractical to deliver, it would mean prices had fallen so that people had lower prices for goods and services and would no longer need the tax refund.  Conversions of farmland to permanent forest for creating carbon credits would be discouraged.

statement: Reduce emissions with a focus on new technology
why: This party says that many of the changes required to reduce emissions can be provided by novel technology rather than the emissions trading scheme or similar financial systems. To protect prosperity, it says there should be fewer barriers for people to invest in new technologies, especially those which may reduce emissions.
how: This party would continue to oppose any new financial penalties for carbon emissions. It would remove regulations that it says prevent people from investing in new technology with potential emission-reduction benefits.

statement: Ensure agriculture is not included in emission reduction programmes
why: This party says that emissions-focused regulation worries farmers who are concerned with industry competitiveness in global export markets. The party argues that the government is getting in the way of decisions that should be made by farmers, and that they should be supported in leading environmental protections, since they have a vested interest in the preservation of their land.
how: This party would omit agriculture from climate-related legislation such as the Zero Carbon Act and Emissions Trading Scheme. The party has supported reforms to the Resource Management Act, shifting funding from Te Mana o te Wai to rural catchment groups, increasing funding for rural catchment groups, allowing targeted grazing on suitable DOC land, and continuing the war against wilding pines.

statement: Introduce noise-detecting cameras
why: This party says that neighborhoods are frustrated by loud vehicles late at night. It notes that families are woken up by loud noises and are stressed about how such noise affects their sleep or the sleep of young children.
how: This party would introduce noise-detecting cameras in place of present police officers. These cameras would feature microphones, video and number plate recognition. They would measure the sound generated by passing vehicles, identify which vehicle produced it, and record the evidence needed for enforcement. This change would model similar systems in New York, London, and Taiwan. It would amend existing legislation to introduce the penalty and that the fine for noise charges would be $300. This party estimates that this policy would cost a one-off $2 million.

statement: Create a one-stop consenting body to approve competing supermarkets
why: This party says that NZ has often had political leadership blame companies for their prices. This creates greater bureaucracy in response, such as the recent appointment of a grocery commissioner.
how: This party would establish a one-stop body for consenting new entrants to the supermarket sector. The objective would be to reduce the consenting process from years to months. The party would additionally allow all products approved under the regulations of the United States, United Kingdom, and Australia to be automatically allowed in NZ, so it is easier for grocers to obtain various products.

statement: Remove the "six months" caveat for assisted dying
why: This party says that since 2021, New Zealanders have had the option of assisted dying, and the Ministry of Health's first statutory review recommended 25 changes to the law. The party claims that restrictions such as the six-month-to-live rule place an unnecessary barrier to access for those who remain best placed to make decisions about their own bodies.
how: This party would implement all twenty-five recommendations from the Ministry of Health report. Additionally, the six-month-to-live rule would be replaced by a test based on whether a person's condition is advanced, progressive, and expected to cause death.

statement: Encourage people generating power to sell it to the grid
why: This party says that there's a lack of competition in the energy sector. However, independent analysis commissioned by the government found no material competition problem requiring the break-up of the major generator-retailers. Instead, the party says regulatory barriers are the key driver of the cost of power. Encouraging people to sell excess power would reward people who invest their own money in generation and storage.
how: This party would allow people with excess power, often from solar installed on their house, to sell their excess power. The selling of excess power would be done by businesses and community energy schemes, subject to appropriate metering, network charging and consumer protections.

statement: Open power transmission to private investment
why: This party says that regulatory barriers lift the cost of power for New Zealanders. Allowing private businesses to access the national grid can increase capital investment in energy production, helping to lower costs over time.
how: This party would allow for private firms to finance and build transmission lines connected to the national grid.   To do so, these businesses would have to prove that they meet common technical and reliability standards and have adequate coordination with a system operator.

statement: Establish an accreditation process for contractors to connect households to the power grid
why: This party says that already existing power line companies allow consumers to choose the contractor responsible for connecting their land or property to the power grid. The party says greater consumer choice is preferable to some customers to find themselves locked into a single provider.
how: This party would establish an accreditation process for contractors who wish to enter the market for the connection of land/housing to power lines. The party claims that this process will better allow power line companies to offer more choice in contractors for their consumers.

statement: Mandate consideration of alternatives to power network upgrades
why: This party says that network upgrades for power can be costly for households. Alternative options for consumers should be available as cheaper alternatives to upgrades.
how: This party would require material network reinforcement projects done by power line companies to demonstrate that credible alternatives have been properly considered when tending to customer-funded network upgrades. Such alternatives under consideration would include batteries, demand response, flexible connections, local generation and other technologies competing against conventional poles, wires and substations.

statement: Commission Parliament to explore a deal with Meta for young people on social media
why: This party says that proposals to emulate Australia's social-media ban for under-sixteen-year-olds come with privacy concerns. The party argues that the recent settlement between the United States and Meta (Facebook, Instagram) provides a better framework for dealing with the harm experienced by children due to social media.
how: This party would ask Parliament to investigate forming a similar settlement with Meta which would include changes seen in the United States. Changes would include a default two-hour daily limit for teenagers, locking most teen accounts between midnight and 6 am, switching off push notifications overnight and during school hours, and giving parents greater power to supervise and restrict their children’s accounts. Teenagers would also need parental approval to loosen the main restrictions.

statement: Acquire land for a new school in Epsom
why: This party says that Auckland Grammar does not have the capacity to meet the growing demand across the Epsom area. It cites advocacy from the principals of Auckland Grammar School and Epsom Girls’ Grammar School for a new co-ed school in this area.
how: This party would purchase land from the University of Auckland and its Epsom campus and repurpose the facility into a co-ed high school. Parents would retain eligibility for the grammar school's school zone.

statement: Exclude purely spiritual and religious effects from infrastructure planning law
why: This party says that spiritual beliefs, particularly those that come from Te Ao Māori, should not be used as the basis for assessing an infrastructure project's viability. It says that planning law should regulate effects that can be identified, measured and tested, and protect rights recognised by law. It should not require planners, councils or judges to rule on spiritual or religious beliefs.
how: This party would exclude purely spiritual and religious effects. It would legislate that a religious or spiritual belief, or a claim of spiritual harm, could not on its own be treated as an adverse effect or justify refusing or restricting consent, requesting further information, or imposing a consent condition. The rule would apply equally to all religions and belief systems and use the test already applied under the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act. It would also ban compulsory spiritual observances. No consent or permit could require anyone to perform, take part in, arrange or fu

statement: Remove the use of spiritual practices like karakia during consenting
why: This party says that compulsory karaka and religious prayer required for consenting processes should be removed, as the compulsion element violates the individual right to abstain from cultural practices should they choose. The party says that people should be able to abstain without losing a consent.
how: This party would remove cultural practice requirements from consenting processes. The party says that all protections that exist for heritage sites, urupā, archaeological sites, customary physical uses, water quality, ecosystems and rights in Treaty settlement legislation, outside of consent processes, will remain untouched.

statement: Replace Te Mana o te Wai with measurable freshwater outcomes
why: This party says that the current water standards under the newly introduced government water management entity are too vague its objectives. It says that the standards focus too greatly on 'spiritual' criteria.
how: This party would replace current standards with a sole focus on measurable freshwater outcomes and remove Te Ao Māori-related concerns.

statement: Do not tax KiwiSaver earnings
why: This party says that New Zealanders deserve to keep more of their money for their own retirement. The party argues that the tax made from KiwiSaver is used to top up those with low incomes who have small savings. The party says that people's savings will increase without having to put additional money away for their retirement.
how: This party would remove the government contribution to KiwiSaver to fund the exemption of KiwiSaver from taxation. The party claims they will put rules in place to avoid people using KiwiSaver as a tax shelter.  This party estimates that this policy would cost just under $2.4 billion over four years.

statement: Establish a statutory body to ensure compensation for investors in mineral extraction
why: This party says that New Zealand needs to produce energy through mineral extraction. Extraction takes a long time between the initial investment and the returns, and investors need confidence that consent process will remain in place.
how: This party would establish a statutory body to ensure compensation for investors in mineral extraction. Any future government would be required to pay compensation to investors if permit rights are withdrawn. It would facilitate this by adding property rights into the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act and ensuring that any legal challenge opposing a permit does not suspend that permit.

statement: Create a set of national mineral extractions standards
why: This party says that New Zealand's economy would benefit from more jobs in resource and mineral extraction, and the government would gain from increased royalty payments.
how: This party would guarantee regular updates to the Crown Mineral List, establish national policy direction and standards for mines, quarries and mineral processing under the new planning legislation, retain fast-track access for eligible projects, and have government work alongside industry to build up the workforce in extractive industries.

statement: Expand domestic energy production
why: This party says that global energy markets are becoming more competitive. Expanding domestic energy production could bring commercial and security benefits for New Zealand and allied nations.
how: This party would continue to allow offshore gas exploration. It would encourage businesses to use renewable energy or fossil fuels with no preference for either option. It would revise the Crown Minerals Act to create rules for underground gas storage . It would also provide insurance for LNG (gas) import infrastructure.

statement: Revise legislation for resource extraction
why: This party says that regulatory barriers can create increased costs for investors and firms engaged in mining and gas and oil extraction. Regulations that duplicate criteria that are already met waste time, money and state resources.
how: This party would have separate legislation around mining with the goal of minimising similar regulations. One piece of legislation would focus on the allocation of Crown-owned petroleum and minerals, another on the management of environmental effects and another on consenting processes.

statement: Increase the flexibility around environmental regulations for mining
why: This party says that clear rules are needed for responsible mining, to ensure that resource extraction is done without tax money being used to deal with preventable environmental damage. However, extraction companies should be able to follower fewer regulations if they can demonstrate that there is less risk to the environment.
how: This party would target marine protection at significant ecological features, including important seamounts, habitats and breeding areas. The party says it would give regulators the discretion to allow, in the case of unanticipated effects, the reduction of regulations where evidence demonstrates a lower risk.

statement: Remove the cap on tax deductions for charitable donations
why: This party says that New Zealanders should be encouraged to donate to charity. Charities across New Zealand help people. The $33,333 cap on tax benefits for money spent on charitable donations should be removed so that people donate more money to charity. This would encourage the philanthropic sector to partner with the government to deliver services, such as a proposal to create cancer treatment centres in Auckland and Christchurch.
how: This party would remove the $33,333 cap on tax rebates for money spent on charitable donations.

statement: Keep agriculture as a subject in the Year 11 curriculum
why: This party says that its leader was disappointed that the Minister of Education confirmed that Agricultural and Horticultural Science won't remain as a standalone subject in the Year 11 Science curriculum. It says that 63% of the over 100,000 students who took the subject last year were from urban schools and argues that students should have access to a subject tailored to building knowledge in agriculture, a major export industry.
how: This party would keep Agricultural and Horticultural Science as a standalone subject in Year 11.

statement: Reduce NZ's foreign aid to 2017 levels
why: This party says that NZ is under pressure to tighten its belt and reduce government spending. The party views foreign aid spending as needing to be cut to instead prioritise domestic issues and reducing debt.
how: This party would direct the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade to reduce foreign aid spending back to 2017 levels. The party claims that this would result in annual savings of $283 million. Money being given to Ukraine would be excluded from this reduction.

statement: Reduce new government spending from $2.4 billion to $2 billion
why: This party says that its ambition is to reach a budget surplus earlier without raising taxes, and that savings increase over time. It claims that what starts as saving $400 million will become $1.6 billion annually by 2030/31.
how: This party would reduce new government spending by reducing future operating allowances in government budgets over the next four years.  This party estimates that this policy would save a total $1.6 billion over four years..

statement: Abolish demographic group ministries
why: This party says that issues of duplication arise from ministries tasked with analysing policy impacts on various demographic groups. It says that this analysis is already being done by the ministries and government departments overseeing the delivery of services.
how: This party would abolish all demographic groups ministries. The party is not clear on whether that includes the Ministry for Māori Development's role in helping the government manage the Māori economy, not just the analysis of inquiries between Māori and non-Māori service users. This party estimates that this policy would cost save $187 million annually.

statement: Raise the retirement age to 67 by 2035
why: This party says that increased life expectancy and lowered birthrates mean taxes need to rise to keep up with population ageing. The party wishes to raise the eligibility age of superannuation by three months a year, reaching 67 by 2035.
how: This party would legislate the eligibility age for NZ superannuation be raised 3 months every year until 2035 where the age would reach 67. The party additionally would suspend government payments into the NZ Superannuation Fund. This party estimates that this policy would cost $2.4 billion after four years.

statement: Increase private school subsidies in line with public school operations
why: This party says that independent/private schools provide diversity and choice in NZ’s schooling system. Parents should have greater choice of school options.
how: This party would align/index the independent school subsidy to the increases made to the public school operations grant.  This party estimates that this policy would cost $100 million total over four years.

statement: Give high school students money to teach them how to invest
why: This party says that financial education should be practical and feel relevant to young people. It says that giving a small $500 investment to Year 11 students would give teenagers a reason to engage with saving, risk and business ownership, especially for those who would not encounter investing at home.
how: This party would establish a fund that would provide Year 11 students with a deposit of $500, accompanied by a financial literacy program in school. Students would be allowed to invest the money and would graduate with an understanding. The investment could move from low-risk bank deposits to investing in funds, to higher-risk investments in individual businesses (equities).  This party estimates that this policy would cost $35 million annually.

statement: Establish a Hauraki Gulf marine area
why: This party says that Hauraki Gulf Marine Park needs to have its own catchment area. Instead of the status quo, where rules apply to a much larger area.
how: This party would create a fishery area for the smaller Hauraki Gulf Marine Park where the total allowable catch could be adjusted to sustainable levels. Whatever proportion of the quota present holders have would be maintained if the total allowable catch were to fall. For example, one would retain an entitlement to 5%.

statement: Create daily limits on harvesting from Auckland rock pools
why: This party says that rock pools around Auckland have increasingly faced intensive harvesting of shellfish and other marine life. Patches of rock pools no longer have much life remaining and are being overused. The party says such an issue of overfishing is common across NZ.
how: This party would introduce a nationwide combined recreational daily bag limit of 10 for shellfish and other covered species that do not already have their own individual daily limit. Shellfish with individual catch limits would have those catch limits remain unchanged.

statement: Bad scallop dredging
why: This party says that practice of scallop dredging damages the seabed, so that fisheries can be closed down to recover. Alternative harvesting methods exist, so the particular method of scallop dredging is not needed.
how: This party would permanently ban scallop dredging in scallop fisheries that are currently closed. It would allow selective harvesting technologies as stock numbers recover.

statement: Require Fisheries NZ to write a report that quantifies the economic and environmental cost of fishing methods
why: This party says that existing conservation levies from the fisheries regulator, Fisheries NZ, do not account for the differences in environmental damage that different methods of catching can cause. This issue means taxpayers and other users can be burdened with costs imposed by others. The party is also concerned that present fees are not punitive enough to discourage poor practice.
how: This party would have Fisheries NZ write a report detailing how to quantify environmental harm from different catching methods and then establish a means to adjust conservation levies to match differing environmental impacts and costs. The party would additionally increase fees in a graduated structure to discourage and punish repeat offending.

statement: Seek to progressively increase fish stock levels
why: This party says that current focus from Fisheries NZ on the maximum sustainable catch levels is lacking in ambition. The goal should be, according to the party, to grow fishing as both a hobby and an industry. Over time, it says, Fisheries NZ should look to increase catch levels.
how: This party would look to progressively manage fish stocks at higher levels than the current maximum-sustainable-catch approach.

statement: Increase penalties for illegal rubbish dumping
why: This party says that illegal dumping should be considered another form of vandalism. It says dumping is offensive to those who take pride in their communities.
how: This party would increase the infringement fee for illegal dumping from $400 to $1,000, with repeat offenders facing fines of $2,000. For the most serious offences, courts will have the power to impose higher penalties.

statement: Increase pay for general practice doctors
why: This party says that  average weekly hours for GPs have fallen from 37 to 34 hours a week. That party says that because 35 per cent of GPs intend to retire within five years and 18 per cent are considering moving overseas, NZ needs to make it more attractive for doctors to stay and to recruit from overseas.
how: This party would increase funding for doctors' pay to ensure that doctors are paid more and incentivised to take on more appointments and patients. This party estimates that this policy would cost $400 million over four years.

statement: Introduce a 2.5% annual wealth tax on net wealth over $2 million, with a trust tax
how: A couple would pay nothing on combined net wealth up to $4 million; the party estimates $6.59 billion a year and would resource IRD to enforce it.

statement: Introduce a 33% capital gains tax on realised gains, excluding the family home
how: Covers investment property, shares and business assets, applying only to gains after it starts; revenue estimated to build from $0.54bn to over $2bn a year.

statement: Introduce a 0.1% financial transactions levy on equity and foreign-exchange turnover
how: Estimated at $0.64bn a year; wages, rent and mortgage payments, household bills and KiwiSaver contributions are excluded.

statement: Raise the adult minimum wage immediately to two-thirds of the average wage and index it to inflation
how: Apply the adult rate to workers of all ages and adjust annually for the cost of living.

statement: Provide 52 weeks' paid parental leave for all workers and paid compassionate leave
how: Including part-time, casual and seasonal workers.

statement: Restore national collective bargaining, a broad right to strike and Work Councils in firms with over 50 staff
how: Coordinated wage bargaining, protection for solidarity and some political strikes, worker voice on restructuring and technology, a Minimum Employment Code covering contractors and labour hire, tougher action on wage theft, and a national retraining and redeployment programme.

statement: Replace the Emissions Trading Scheme with a carbon tax
why: The party says a carbon tax sets a transparent price that free allocation and offsets cannot undermine.
how: Revenue directed to renewables, public transport and emissions reduction; mandatory energy-efficiency standards for buildings, appliances, vehicles and industry.

statement: Apply a strict polluter-pays principle and move to a zero-waste, circular economy
how: Polluters pay full repair costs; ban non-recyclable plastic packaging, reusable packaging such as glass bottles, right to repair; keep water in public ownership with stronger pollution controls; a Genuine Progress Index alongside GDP.

statement: Ban mining in national parks, conservation land and the Coromandel, and give the Conservation Minister a veto
how: Restoration bonds for permitted mining, precaution on genetic modification, limits on sales of land and beaches to overseas buyers, and a reaffirmed nuclear-free policy.

statement: Move to affordable and eventually free public transport with restored regional passenger rail
how: Integrated ticketing and timetables, rural services, separated cycleways and transit-oriented planning.

statement: Restore a Universal Child Benefit paid to every child's main carer, plus a Universal Early Years Benefit for under-threes
why: The party says Working for Families and the In-Work Tax Credit leave out some of the families most in need.
how: Non-means-tested, paid directly to the primary carer and indexed to average weekly earnings, as part of a plan to eliminate child poverty.

statement: Pay a universal student income equivalent to the unemployment benefit
how: Independent of parental income, for tertiary and vocational students and trainees.

statement: Guarantee free, accessible abortion and contraception and require gender-impact assessment of government decisions
how: A Gender Audit framework, a Pay Equity Bureau, secure non-contestable funding for women's refuges, affordable high-quality childcare, and support for informed-consent gender-affirming care.

statement: Support small business with a public development bank, maximum payment terms and action against monopolies
how: Legislated maximum payment terms for large firms and agencies, automatic interest on overdue invoices, published payment times, stronger competition law, and support for co-operatives and new enterprises.

statement: Keep NZ Super at 65, raise the married rate to 72.5% of the after-tax average wage, and end means-testing for long-term aged care
how: Also a Ministry for Senior Citizens, independent advocates for older people, subsidised transport and internet, and strengthening KiwiSaver.

statement: Lower the MMP threshold to 3.5% and hold a public review toward a written constitution grounded in Te Tiriti
how: Strengthen the Waitangi Tribunal, consider Matike Mai recommendations, citizens' initiatives, a democratic decision on the monarchy, stronger select committees, OIA reform, conflict-of-interest rules and donation transparency and limits.

statement: Refuse trade deals with investor–state dispute settlement and seek to remove it from existing deals
how: Trade policy that protects jobs, public services and the ability to regulate; retain tariffs as a sparing option; Māori consent on agreements affecting Māori interests; stronger buy-local procurement.

statement: Stop all further privatisation and return ports, water, telecommunications and Air New Zealand to full public ownership
how: Democratic accountability for public enterprises (including extending the OIA to Crown-controlled listed companies), worker board representation, and a Ministry of Development and public development bank.

statement: Make New Zealand non-aligned, restructure defence for peacekeeping and disaster response, and review foreign military and intelligence facilities
how: Withdraw from inconsistent military alliances, remove offensive capabilities, strengthen the nuclear-free Pacific, support Palestinian self-determination and right of return, cancel unsustainable Global South debt, raise aid toward 0.7% of GNI and ease Pacific migration barriers.

statement: Ban the cruellest farming and fishing practices first (intensive winter grazing, fast-growing chicken breeds, live export, mutilations, bottom trawling), with a funded farmer transition
why: The AJP's long-term aim is to end all animal farming; it presents interim reforms to reduce suffering in the meantime.
how: Tighter standards and stronger enforcement of the Animal Welfare Act, and a farmer-led transition scheme with planning, financial help and debt restructuring for moves to plant-based or other land uses.

statement: Recognise animals in law as sentient beings rather than property
why: The AJP says the property classification makes meaningful protection very hard.
how: Write sentience into legislation with enforceable protections and end codes of practice that let industries sidestep the Animal Welfare Act.

statement: Make plant-based meals the default in schools, hospitals and public institutions, and remove GST from fruit, vegetables, legumes and nuts
why: The AJP cites estimates that plant-rich diets could save the health system up to $22 billion.
how: Other options would remain available; clearer food labelling with health and environmental information.

statement: Create an independent Commissioner for Animals with investigative and enforcement powers
why: The AJP says welfare is overseen by MPI, the same ministry that promotes farm exports — a conflict of interest.
how: Modelled on the Children's Commissioner, with funding for welfare research and accountability for enforcement agencies.

statement: Make rehoming the default in council pounds, with euthanasia only as a last resort
why: The AJP says 60% of dogs impounded in Auckland last year were killed rather than rehomed.
how: Public reporting of pound outcomes by every council, fairer reclaim processes and fees, funded foster networks and wide access to desexing.

statement: End lethal and poison-based control of cats; use desexing, Trap-Neuter-Return and habitat restoration
why: The AJP says there is no reliable way to tell a feral cat from a community or companion cat and that habitat loss drives native decline.
how: Also predator-proof fencing and evidence-led conservation.

statement: Remove GST from veterinary services and fund public and mobile vet clinics
why: The AJP says vet bills force impossible choices on families.
how: A national network of publicly funded and mobile clinics plus guaranteed funding for injured wildlife care and desexing.

statement: Get money out of politics: lower donation limits, real-time lobbying disclosure and cooling-off periods
why: The AJP says animal-exploiting industries have outsized access to decision-makers.
how: Also whistleblower protection and support for peaceful protest (manifesto).

statement: Write animal welfare into AI governance and ban AI systems that increase confinement or remove human oversight
why: The AJP says AI already manages hundreds of thousands of farmed animals with no law accounting for it.
how: Independent validation of any AI marketed as improving welfare.

statement: Give up to five days' bereavement leave for the loss of a companion animal and three days when a new one joins the family
how: Emergency leave would also cover urgent animal care.

statement: Abolish all animal farming through a just transition to plant-based and cellular agriculture
why: The AJP's long-term aim is to end all animal farming; it presents interim reforms to reduce suffering in the meantime.

statement: Reform animal breeding and reproduction practices that put production and profit ahead of animal health
why: The AJP's long-term aim is to end all animal farming; it presents interim reforms to reduce suffering in the meantime.

statement: Set legal minimums for farmed animals' shelter, space and environment
why: The AJP's long-term aim is to end all animal farming; it presents interim reforms to reduce suffering in the meantime.
how: Addressing exposure to weather, overcrowding and barren conditions.

statement: Strengthen nutrition and health standards for farmed animals and reduce reliance on pharmaceuticals
why: The AJP's long-term aim is to end all animal farming; it presents interim reforms to reduce suffering in the meantime.

statement: End painful procedures on farmed animals and guarantee prompt veterinary care
why: The AJP's long-term aim is to end all animal farming; it presents interim reforms to reduce suffering in the meantime.
how: Humane handling standards across farming.

statement: Tighten standards for transporting animals
why: The AJP's long-term aim is to end all animal farming; it presents interim reforms to reduce suffering in the meantime.

statement: Extend the live-export ban to animals exported by air
why: The AJP says New Zealand has no control over animals' care once they reach their destination.
how: Exceptions for relocating companion animals and conservation transfers.

statement: Reform slaughter practices to minimise suffering while working toward ending slaughter
why: The AJP rejects the idea that killing animals can be truly humane.

statement: Fund pet-inclusive refuges so domestic-violence victims can escape with their animals
why: The AJP says the safety of companion animals often keeps victims in danger and that New Zealand has only one dedicated pet refuge.

statement: End the private sale and use of fireworks
why: The AJP cites harm to wildlife, marine ecosystems and companion animals.
how: End private sales and use while moving to 'sustainable and animal friendly celebration alternatives'. (The full policy is a Google Drive PDF that was not captured.)

statement: Ban greyhound racing
why: The AJP says over 40% of racing greyhounds suffer injuries and the industry has lost its social licence.
how: Interim: transparency on deaths and injuries, breeding limits, kennel caps and funded transition for workers.

statement: Ban horse racing
how: Covers flat, jumps and harness racing.

statement: Ban rodeo
why: The AJP says rodeos cannot be made safe through regulation.

statement: Ban recreational fishing and fishing competitions
how: An immediate and complete ban.

statement: Replace harmful animal experiments with non-animal research methods
why: The AJP cites MPI figures of over 300,000 animals used in research, testing and teaching in 2021.
how: More funding for alternatives, and consideration of research's environmental impacts.

statement: Move toward a cruelty-free, sustainable fashion industry
why: The AJP says leather, wool, fur, down and exotic skins perpetuate cruel and unsustainable practices.

statement: End 1080, brodifacoum and biological agents such as RHDV for pest control
why: The AJP says these methods cause intense, prolonged suffering.
how: Use humane, non-lethal, species-specific population management instead.

statement: Protect and restore natural habitats and design roads and cities to protect wildlife
how: Wildlife impact assessments in urban planning and road design; help wild animals facing natural threats where appropriate.

statement: Cut emissions rapidly by shrinking animal agriculture
why: The AJP says animal agriculture produces around half of New Zealand's emissions.

statement: Shift to an economy of 'sufficiency within planetary boundaries' with circular and sharing economy policies
how: Include environmental externalities in economic measures.

statement: Cut personal and company tax, align the company rate with the top personal rate, and lower GST to 12.5%
why: The party says lower taxes improve compliance and investment and that New Zealand's rates should be no higher than Australia's.
how: Also tackle public debt; a 2025 release calls for a 'flat tax rate' for individuals and companies.

statement: Stop taxing NZ Super (including for over-65s still working) and boarders' income in private homes
how: Remove NZ Super from taxable income, and exempt genuine home-sharing/boarder income with safeguards against commercial use.

statement: Let mayors become full-time council CEOs and give ministers power to appoint and sack senior public servants
why: The party says unelected bureaucrats and advisers usurp the mandate of elected representatives.
how: Elected representatives at local and national level would get wide powers to dismiss obstructive or incompetent staff; legislate to curtail 'unconstitutional bureaucratic power'.

statement: Make cutting hospital waiting times the top health priority, funded from bureaucracy, procurement and productivity savings
why: The party says the key issue is whether patients are treated in time, not how much is spent.
how: Measure waits for elective surgery, specialists, diagnostics, cancer and ED; buy private capacity where it is quicker and competitive; grow the domestic workforce; link any extra funding to measurable results.

statement: Tighten immigration toward skilled migrants and cap other net migration by the supply of housing, doctors and school places
why: The party says population growing faster than 'social goods' makes everyone poorer.
how: A stable points system; end 'golden' investor visas; NZ licence tests for foreign truck drivers; tougher document checks and audits; report GDP per capita.

statement: Hold a Royal Commission of Inquiry into police under-performance and corruption
why: The party cites fabricated drink-drive tests and lost public trust.
how: Also: refer prima facie criminal allegations against police and all deaths caused by police action to the courts; protect identities of police witnesses in international drug cases; review drone laws.

statement: Strengthen the IPCA: double its staff, quadruple its budget, and let it prosecute and name officers
how: As set out in its 'Sharpening the Teeth of the IPCA' statement.

statement: Improve access to justice for self-represented litigants
how: Procedural changes, support services, legal aid reform, tax deductions and cost awards for pro bono work, and wider Family Dispute Resolution.

statement: Leave the Paris Agreement, scrap the ETS and repeal all 'climate'-based taxes, laws and agencies
why: The party says there is no climate emergency and that climate policies raise food and energy costs and hurt the poor most.
how: Remove fossil-fuel taxes and restrictions, abolish climate units in government, end energy subsidies of any kind, and stop public funding of methane research such as AgriZero.

statement: Oppose converting farmland to carbon forestry and oppose the Gene Technology Bill
how: No incentives for permanent carbon forestry on productive land; keep restrictions on GMO field trials and release; revisit the Planning and Natural Environment Bills to make them workable and protect property rights.

statement: Encourage oil and gas exploration with a Norway-style resource joint venture and sovereign investment fund
why: The party says New Zealand has failed to secure a fair share of its resources.
how: Public-private resource partnerships, royalties shared with local communities, environmental bonds, returns held in a New Zealand Investment Fund.

statement: Buy a fleet of oil tankers and build new oil refineries for fuel security
how: Tankers would guarantee supply and floating storage until refineries able to process local and Pacific crude are built; also bring back manufacturing.

statement: Ensure 'cheap, reliable and abundant' energy without relying solely on solar and wind
how: Renewables have a role but cannot be relied on alone because of variability.

statement: Create a Kermadec Ocean Sanctuary and overhaul fisheries management with cameras on all commercial vessels
why: The party says the sustainable fisheries regime is widely abused.
how: Promote the Kermadec Ocean Sanctuary Bill and reinstall surveillance cameras on commercial vessels.

statement: Increase penalties for child sexual offending and online exploitation
how: Longer sentences for serious and repeat offenders, review of sentence reductions, better monitoring after release, more online-exploitation investigation resources and victim support.

statement: Restrict irreversible gender-related medical procedures for minors and require parental involvement
how: Independent assessment before significant intervention, evidence-based practice, parental involvement subject to safeguards, and independent review mechanisms.

statement: Recognise an unborn child as a legal person from the third trimester
why: The party says every human life has inherent dignity.
how: An Unborn Child (Legal Personhood and Rights) Act with a protected right to life, without criminalising pregnant women, plus a Pregnancy and Family Support Programme (support payment, housing security, support services, adoption options).

statement: Review all trade agreements and pursue a neutral foreign policy with a support- and reconstruction-focused military
how: Seek a balance between free trade and protectionism ('Trade before War'); avoid being drawn into conflicts that do not threaten NZ territory.

statement: Employment and services based on merit, 'one law for all', and 'a man is a man, and a woman is a woman'
why: The party opposes policies that divide people by race, ancestry, sex or identity.
how: Listed among its 'policies that work' alongside limiting unskilled immigration and defending free speech and Judeo-Christian traditions.

statement: Support the right of return of Palestinian refugees and the dismantling of Israel's current state structure, rejecting a two-state solution
why: The party says a just peace depends on refugees' return and that further partition would bring more injustice.
how: Founding principle 1 (website) / constitution clause 2.

statement: Establish a single secular, democratic, bi-national state in all of historic Palestine with equal citizenship
how: Founding principle 4: one state with full and equal citizenship and ethnic and religious rights protected in a democratic constitution.

statement: Press the New Zealand government to uphold international law and UN resolutions on Palestine and support war-crimes and genocide prosecutions
why: The party says its aim is to change public opinion and put sustained parliamentary pressure on the government.
how: Accept the primacy of international law and UN resolutions; call Israel to account under the Universal Declaration of Human Rights; have New Zealand support prosecutions and use its independent voice internationally.

statement: Give 'unconditional and complete solidarity' to Palestinian resistance 'in all forms accordant with International Humanitarian Law'
how: Founding principle 5 (the press release lists 'unconditional support for all forms of Palestine resistance' without the IHL qualifier).

statement: Adopt an independent foreign policy and withdraw from formal military and security alliances with the United States
how: Founding principle 6: leave any formal US security alliances and distance foreign policy from 'Anglo-U.S. economic hegemony and military interventionism'.

statement: Build a mass democratic movement and global solidarity links for Palestinian liberation
how: The party's stated objectives: a broad party uniting Palestine supporters from all traditions, and links with others resisting inequality and injustice; it also seeks to persuade other parties to adopt stronger pro-Palestine policies.
