statement: Return the tax rate to 33 percent for New Zealand's biggest corporations
why: This party says that multi-national businesses send profits offshore and don't pay the same taxes as local businesses. This increases prices and decreases wages. Lower corporate taxes have not led to improvements for working New Zealanders. The corporate tax rate increase would only be on the 0.7 percent biggest businesses in NZ, including banks, supermarkets and energy companies. This would level the playing field for small and medium businesses.
how: This party would increase the tax rate to 33% for large corporations while keeping it at 33% for small and medium businesses. A bank levy of 0.06 percent would be added to the liabilities of the four big banks (ANZ, BNZ, Westpac and ASB).

statement: Enforce the 5 percent withholding tax on major international tech and finance companies
why: This party says that big corporations like Google, Meta, Microsoft, Visa, Uber and Mastercard use loopholes to avoid taxes in NZ. Withholding tax requirements must be enforced so that these companies contribute their fair share.
how: This party would enforce a 5 percent withholding tax on the services and licences of big tech and finance companies.

statement: Create a 2.5 percent tax on assets worth over $10m
why: This party says that the richest 311 households in NZ pay an effective tax rate of 9 percent, half that of most working people. This is because much of this wealth sits in asset portfolios, rather than being taxed as income. The wealthy need to contribute to solving shared problems with the rest of New Zealand. With the 150 richest people in NZ holding as much as 917,000 households, it is important to ensure the wealthy contribute through taxes.
how: This party would implement a 2.5 percent annual tax on the net assets of people holding over $10m in wealth. This would affect 0.3 percent of New Zealanders.

statement: Keep and expand the free school lunches programme
why: This party says that children learn best when they are not hungry. Every child deserves healthy and nutritious food that helps them succeed at school.
how: This party would keep and expand the Ka Ora, Ka Ako programme in schools. It would extend the programme to approximately 400 more schools and fund the programme permanently so schools and families have long-term certainty.

statement: Implement a tax on wealth received over $1m
why: This party says that more than $1.6 trillion in wealth is passed on intergenerationally. The party believes that being rich shouldn't be determined by who your parents are.
how: This party would introduce a Capital Acquisitions Tax on assets and gifts received worth more than $1m. Family farms and family homes would be exempt.

statement: Increase the corporate tax rate to 33 percent for big corporations only
why: This party says that large corporations in NZ are profiting from the public without contributing back towards society. It says that cuts to the corporate tax rate have not increased wellbeing, growth or investment for most New Zealanders; rather, corporations see more profits.
how: This party would return the corporate tax rate to 33 percent for the 0.7 percent biggest corporations, such as the supermarket duopoly, energy companies, and banks. It would keep the corporate tax rate at  28 percent for small and medium enterprises. It would also introduce a Bank Levy of 0.06 percent on the liabilities of the four main banks. It would also enforce the 5 percent tax rate on service and license fees for large tech companies.

statement: Reverse interest deductibility for residential property investment
why: This party says that says that a landlords' tax cut means housing speculators and landlords can spend more on house-buying than first home buyers. This makes it harder for New Zealanders to get onto the property ladder.
how: This party would  remove interest deductibility for residential property investment and restore the bright-line test period to 10 years. The bright-line test will require income tax to be paid on gains from selling residential investment property if sold within 10 years of being purchased. The profit from the sale is applied to the seller’s annual personal income and taxed at the marginal income tax rate.  The family home would be exempt.

statement: Make the first $10,000 that people earn tax-free
why: This party says that people working for a salary or wage pay double the effective tax rate of the very richest people in NZ. It believes this tax cut will help support New Zealanders and ease the high cost of living. This party says 96 percent of New Zealanders would get a tax cut with this policy.
how: This party would create a new tax-free threshold of $10,000.

statement: Create a new tax bracket for income earned over $160,000
why: This party says that says that NZ has low income taxes for people who earn high salaries compared to most other countries. It believes the tax system should be updated so that those who earn the most should contribute more and those who earn less should contribute less.
how: This party would reset NZ's income tax settings, including a 45 percent threshold for income above $160,000. Everyone earning under $160,000 per year will receive a tax cut, with those earning the least benefiting most. It would reduce taxes for lower and middle-income earners by implemening progressive tax brackets between $10,000 and $160,000. For example, people would pay just 10 percent of the income they earn between $10,000 and $19,999, and so on.

statement: Set science-based national standards for freshwater
why: This party says that it supports taking a precautionary approach to protect people's health. It says there is emerging evidence of a link between nitrate contamination in drinking water and bowel cancer and preterm births. The Danish government has committed to lowering nitrate levels in drinking water by almost 90%.
how: This party would lower the nitrate limit in drinking water based on scientific evidence. It would also create a drinking water regulator to monitor, report on and enforce protections for drinking water sources.

statement: Strengthen rules for wastewater discharges
why: This party says that NZ's favourite swimming spots are often too polluted to safely swim in due to weak rules for discharging wastewater into our rivers and coastlines.
how: This party would strengthen rules for wastewater discharges to ensure rivers, lakes and seas are swimmable.

statement: Phase out synthetic nitrogen fertiliser
why: This party says that synthetic nitrogen fertiliser is harming our environment by polluting our rivers, lakes and groundwater. Between 1991 and 2019, the use of synthetic nitrogen increased by more than 600%. At the same time, more than a third of monitored groundwater sources saw an increase in nitrate levels. It says that contamination of community water supplies poses a risk to human health.
how: This party would lower the current cap on synthetic nitrogen fertiliser for the dairy industry. This is because the dairy industry uses more than 60% of synthetic nitrogen. It would work with farmers across other sectors to cut fertiliser. There is no timeframe set for the phase-out. It would work alongside the Ministry for Primary Industries to develop a clear implementation plan with milestones and would support regenerative farming initiatives such as the Sustainable Food and Fibre Futures fund.

statement: Protect at least 30% of  New Zealand’s oceans and seas
why: This party says that current rules allow overfishing and enable the pollution of NZ's oceans. It believes marine ecosystems should be protected and restored so New Zealanders can enjoy health oceans to swim in and abundant fish stock to feed their families with.
how: This party would reform marine-protected area legislation to make it fit-for-purpose, consistent with the Tiriti o Waitangi, and guided by tikanga values. This would include supporting kaitiakitanga Māori in marine management and iwi- and hapū-led conservation and restoration initiatives.

statement: Phase out certain fishing practices
why: This party says that bottom trawling, set netting, dredging and seamounts are destructive fishing practices, destroying native ecosystems and catching endangered species such as the Māui and Hector's dolphins. Banning these fishing practices would protect NZ's ocean ecosystems for generations to come.
how: This party would phase out bottom trawling, set netting and dredging, starting with an immediate ban on seamounts. The focus on banning these fishing practices would begin in ecologically sensitive areas such as Tīkapa Moana/Hauraki Gulf and the habitats of Māui and Hector's dolphins.

statement: Review the quota system for fisheries
why: This party says that the current fisheries rules allow for overfishing, depleting NZ's oceans. It wants to replenish our fish stocks with an improved management system which is founded on ecosystem protection.
how: This party would review the Quota Management System and move towards ecosystem-based fisheries management that prioritises abundance and long-term sustainability.

statement: Establish a government backed clean energy loan scheme
why: This party says that this policy would help make household power bills more affordable so people would not have to choose between heating or eating. This party says that since 2021, 100,000 more households cannot afford to heat their home and 76,000 could not pay their bills on time. The easiest way to lower household power is to help people generate and store solar power but most people are barred from this due to the expensive upfront cost of equipment purchase.
how: This party would establish a government-backed loan scheme to enable zero-interest clean energy loans for up to 90% of homeowners. Homeowners can use these loans for rooftop solar, batteries and making energy efficiency upgrades. Some borrowers will have the option to defer repayments until property sale, while loans will be paid off over time via a separate levy. Central government would be a 20 percent shareholder, with participating councils and the Local Government Funding Agency (LGFA) splitting the remaining 80 percent. The Energy Efficiency and Conservation Authority (EECA) would implem

statement: Legalise plug-in solar and establish a renters’ right to solar
why: This party says that says that a warm, dry home should be possible for everyone. This policy would help lower power bills for renters by improving access to affordable, renewable solar power. Plug-in solar systems can save up to $350 a year on people's power bills. It is also smaller and cheaper to install than rooftop solar.
how: This party would urgently progress regulation to legalise plug-in solar and establish a renters' right to solar in law. It would amend tenancy and body corporate law to allow this to happen.

statement: Reform pricing so people are paid fairly for excess solar power exported to the grid
why: This party says that households and businesses with rooftop solar should receive a fair price for the electricity they export back to the grid.
how: This party would regulate energy pricing to ensure that households and businesses with rooftop solar receive a fair price for the electricity they export back to the grid.

statement: Invest $200m in community energy projects across the country
why: This party says that restoring public ownership of energy projects would make power more affordable and grow community resilience. It would ensure clean-energy benefits go back into the community rather than to shareholders. Building renewable energy close to where the demand is can cut costs.
how: This party would fund this policy by reallocating subsidies for fossil fuel companies to community energy projects. Locally-led projects such as schools, marae, libraries, recreation centres, community energy groups, iwi/Māori, local government and other locally governed organisations would be eligible for funding. Small-scale wind, solar and geothermal projects that deliver benefits to the community would be included.  This party estimates that this policy would cost $200m over 4 years.

statement: Mandate the installation of solar on new or renovated public homes, where appropriate
why: This party says that installing solar panels on public housing would reduce the power bills of those dwelling there.
how: This party would install rooftop solar panels on more than half of all public homes within four years. It would also mandate the installation of solar on new or renovated public homes, alongside energy  efficient appliances that cut bills.  This party estimates that this policy would cost $460 million over four years..

statement: Invest $80 million into renewable energy for Māori housing
why: This party says that Māori are two to three times more likely to experience energy hardship compared to the general population. This policy would ensure Māori can access clean energy, resulting in cheaper power bills that also uphold kaitiakitanga, rangatiratanga and tikanga.
how: This party would invest in projects ranging from solar on kaumātua homes and papakāinga (communal housing built by families on ancestral Māori land) to geothermal energy to local distribution solutions that help manage energy on Māori land. This party estimates that this policy would cost $80 million over four years.

statement: Create a self-governance trust to restore and sustain marae
why: This party says that marae are a key part of New Zealand's national identity for Māori and non-Māori. They are a central hub during states of emergency, serving and connecting communities. Despite this significance, marae across NZ are ageing with failing infrastructure and need long-term financial support to be sustained.
how: This party would create Te Rangatiratanga Trust, which provides immediate support and long-term funding certainty for marae, owned and operated by hapū and iwi. The Crown would provide $2.44bn to establish the trust and two funds: Te Rākau Whakarauora Restoration Fund, which would provide $400m over four years for urgent needs, and Te Tōtara Haemata Intergenerational Fund, to protect and grow capital for future generations. The latter would be funded by returns from a $2bn diversified portfolio. Trust funding decisions would be made independently of ministers and successive governments.

statement: Advocate for universal membership to international agreements that support biodiversity
why: This party says that there is a global biodiversity crisis, and the rates of species extinction have increased due to pressures from human activity. As this is a global problem, it requires a global commitment to respect biodiversity.
how: This party would ensure NZ becomes party to and advocates for universal membership of international agreements that support biodiversity, such as the Convention on Biological Diversity.

statement: Minimise climate change's impact on biodiversity
why: This party says that human activities have resulted in a warming climate. This climate change is harming the Earth's biodiversity, with species unable to quickly adapt to their changing habitats.
how: This party would consider climate change impacts and adaptation strategies when designing conservation programmes.

statement: Strengthen New Zealanders' relationship with nature and conservation efforts
why: This party says that NZ's priorities need to urgently change to prevent rapid biodiversity loss and the increased rates of species extinction. Biodiversity is declining at such a rate it is threatening ecosystems and the human systems that rely on them.
how: This party would explore redirecting DOC's purpose to focus solely on conservation. It would enable this to happen by reallocating its tourism, recreation and heritage priorities to other agencies. It would also support practices that recognise the rights and wellbeing of the natural world.

statement: Support criminalisation of "ecocide"
why: This party says that human activities such as resource extraction are leading to pollution, habitat loss and an increasing rate of biodiversity loss. Criminalising ecocide would disincentivise environmentally destructive activities.
how: This party would explore and support criminalising "ecocide" in domestic and international law. This would incorporate a Te Tiriti o Waitangi perspective.

statement: Create a job guarantee programme for jobs focused on ecosystem regeneration
why: This party says that the NZ economy currently incentivises the exploitation of the environment for short-term gain. This has resulted in ecosystem loss and degradation. This policy would incentivise environmental protection by providing jobs that focus on that goal.
how: This party would establish a job guarantee programme focused on understanding, protecting, and regenerating ecosystems.  It would expand funding for Jobs for Nature – Mahi mō te Taiao.

statement: Create a fund to resource ecosystem protection projects
why: This party says that loss and degradation of ecosystems are occurring due to human activity encouraged by an economy focused on short-term gain. This would provide reliable funding that instead encourages environmentally protective activities.
how: This party would fund Action for Nature, implement the biodiversity strategy, and also national guidance to protect indigenous biodiversity, including the protection of taonga species.

statement: Encourage landowners to regenerate and maintain native biodiversity
why: This party says that prioritising the health of indigenous species and ecosystems will allow NZ's environment to thrive.
how: This party would introduce a biodiversity credits system that incentivises private and Māori landowners to establish areas of indigenous biodiversity and regenerate indigenous ecosystems. A strong emphasis would be placed on protecting areas such as wetlands, as they are particularly affected by biodiversity loss. Resource management legislation and plans would take an ecosystem-based approach, encouraging this indigenous regeneration. It would also require new developments to undergo in-depth analysis of environmental impacts.

statement: Ensure New Zealand's activity in Antarctica protects its biodiversity
why: This party says that says humans are interdependent with other species and environments. Our survival requires a functional biosphere, including protecting Antarctica's biodiversity and environment.
how: This party would develop and fund an environmental regeneration plan for the Ross Dependency and establish an environmental impact assessment system for human activities in Antarctica, such as research and tourism. It would also collaborate with other Antarctic Treaty signatories to uphold responsible management of the region.

statement: Minimise light pollution
why: This party says that this would help protect ecosystems that rely on natural dark and light cycles. Aoraki Mackenzie is the largest Dark Sky Reserve in the Southern Hemisphere. Protecting more areas from light pollution protects both natural and cultural heritage, with te ao Māori seeing the night sky as an important connection to ancestral knowledge and navigation.
how: This party would support research and development on efficient light technologies that minimise light pollution. It would also increase the number of protected dark sky reserves.

statement: Restore native species populations so they do not become extinct
why: This party says that New Zealand is known as a hotspot for its native biodiversity that has evolved with unique characteristics due to the island environment. For example, there are many native birds that can't fly, as they evolved in a land without predators. In the last 150 years, any native species have been placed at risk of extinction due to habitat loss, predators and pollution.
how: This party would broaden and update recovery plans to cover more threatened species. It would broaden legal protections and conservation strategies to cover indigenous fish, plants, invertebrates, and fungi to recognise the importance of diversity. It would also investigate appropriate regulation that limits or suspends the harvesting of vulnerable aquatic species, such as whitebait, to allow populations to regenerate.

statement: Exterminate, manage and monitor invasive species
why: This party says that many of New Zealand's unique flora and fauna are at risk of extinction due to invasive species. There are many efforts in place to control and eliminate these invasive species and they need continued support.
how: This party would expand the "mainland islands" where intensive invasive species management occurs, as well as significantly increasing funding for organisations that eradicate and control invasive species and prioritising the elimination of high-risk species. It would also strengthen regulation and enforcement around introducing, releasing, and commercial use of invasive species and develop human and effective chemical, biological and physical invasive species control options, while still using effective options currently available like 1080, cyanide and trapping.

statement: Ensure that diseases that negatively affect indigenous species are controlled
why: This party says that New Zealand's unique biodiversity is particularly vulnerable to the negative impact of invasive species, pollution and disease such as Kauri dieback and myrtle rust.
how: This party would fund research to understand diseases that affect indigenous species and establish strategies to combat the spread of these diseases.

statement: Ensure genetic diversity and variation of indigenous species are protected
why: This party says that New Zealand's biodiversity has evolved uniquely, which means our indigenous species are particularly vulnerable to extinction and human pressures, including genetic bottlenecks.
how: This party would research and monitor genetic bottlenecks and inbreeding depression in indigenous species. It would fund genetic rescue programmes to increase genetic variation, establish genome and seed banks for indigenous species and explore ways to use eco-sourcing in nurseries and re-wilding programmes.

statement: Tighten biosecurity measures to prevent the introduction of new species
why: This party says that the introduction of new species and biological hazards threatens New Zealand's unique biodiversity and agricultural sector.
how: This party would ensure biosecurity measures that prevent the introduction of new species and biological hazards are vigorous, well-resourced, and effective.

statement: Regenerate indigenous forests in New Zealand
why: This party says that indigenous forests provide a home and habitat to many of New Zealand's native fauna. Protecting these forests will ensure the whole ecosystem can thrive.
how: This party would strengthen the existing restrictions and penalties on the harvesting and export of indigenous logs and chips, including swamp kauri. It would ensure that any removal of windthrown trees on public conservation land is ecologically and culturally sound. It would also prioritise the control of introduced pests that contribute to forest collapse (i.e. possums, pigs, and deer) over recreational hunting.

statement: Take a collaborative, Te Tiriti o Waitangi and te ao Māori approach to conservation
why: This party says conservation has become disconnected from, and is failing to uphold, Te Tiriti o Waitangi. This is further distancing Māori from their ancestral lands and undermining their kaitiaki guardian role of looking after the environment. Te ao Māori principles can help all New Zealanders better care for their environment.
how: This party would ensure all environmental protection and resource management legislation reflects Te Tiriti o Waitangi and Māori cultural values, and upholds the tino rangatiratanga of iwi and hapū to protect their environment. In cooperation with local government, this policy would also ensure conservation efforts uphold kaitiaki through enabling customary use of indigenous resources and implementing the recommendations of the Ko Aotearoa Tēnei Waitangi Tribunal (WAI262) report. It would recognise native species as tāonga, Māori treasures, and increase public awareness of the colonial history

statement: Ensure conservation projects are provided with sufficient funding and resources to achieve their goals
why: This party says that despite decades of conservation efforts across New Zealand, biodiversity is continuing to decline.
how: This party would expand DOC's core capacity to work on conservation efforts by increasing resource funding and employing more field and research personnel. It would also enable the purchase, protection and regeneration of special places that are threatened in the public conservation estate and strengthen the role of conservation boards as individual advocates representing the community. Community efforts to regenerate urban biodiversity would also be supported, with funding increased for evidence-based landscape-scale conservation projects.

statement: Support Māori autonomy in their responses to climate change
why: This party says that climate change is damaging Māori customary practices, cultural identity, well-being and connection to the land. Historical and current injustices have also weakened the resources of Māori communities and businesses to mitigate and adapt to climate change.
how:
This party would ensure Māori communities and leadership networks are resourced to research, monitor and provide advice on climate change on policies and legislation that might negatively affect them. It would also fund Māori-led initiatives for transitioning away from fossil fuel and agribusiness ventures into sustainable industries. 
This policy would ensure overarching support for the autonomy and self-determination of hapū, iwi and Māori businesses in leading their own climate change responses, with funding provided to redress inequities.

statement: Ensure all sectors are covered by an effective emissions pricing system
why: This party says that all sectors need to be incentivised to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions, in order to prioritise the health of the environment and humanity over profit.
how: This party would phase out the free allocation of NZUs to emission-Intensive and trade-exposed industries, and implement a framework for pricing agricultural greenhouse gas emissions. It would also include emissions from international aviation in pricing schemes. Marine-based 'blue carbon' - carbon dioxide captured and stored by the world's ocean and coastal ecosystems - would be included in the ETS. Alternative emissions pricing mechanisms would be implemented when the ETS is not doing its job in reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Lastly, existing foresters would received equitable treatment

statement: Advocate internationally for strong climate action from other countries and partners
why: This party says that that New Zealand has a legal and moral responsibility, supported by the Te Tiriti o Waitangi, to lead climate action on a global scale. New Zealand is relatively wealthy but currently ranks poorly against other countries for its climate change policies. This party says we need to do better to help our vulnerable neighbours, like Pacific Island nations.
how: This party would advocate internationally for the strengthening of international climate agreements and encourage all countries to increase their Nationally Determined Contributions so that global emissions halve by 2030 and reach net carbon-negative by 2050 to limit global average temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius. The party would also advocate for urgent climate action to be embedded in all international agreements and institutions, with a legally binding mechanism created to ensure international compliance with climate commitments and ramped-up funding made available to finance climat

statement: Support Pacific nation's leadership on global climate change action
why: This party says that as a relatively wealthy nation, New Zealand has a duty to support our Pacific Island neighbours who are on the frontline of climate change.
how: This party would actively support Pacific states' leadership on climate change issues of concern, including security and sovereignty related to the future survival of island nations. It would advocate for legal protection for people displaced by climate change and systems for loss and damage compensation from climate damage. Even in the case of climate-caused migration, it would advocate for sovereign cultural and political identities to be maintained.

statement: Ensure all environmental protection and resource management legislation is in line with climate change policies
why: This party says that climate-exacerbated pressures are threatening ecosystems and biodiversity. If ecosystems fail, the ability to hold greenhouse gases and adapt to climate change will also fail.
how: This party would ensure that all environmental protection and resource management legislation integrates climate change goals. The legislation must also work to protect and restore the resilience of biodiversity and ecosystems and their ability to adapt to climate change.

statement: Ensure marginalised groups are proactively protected from climate change
why: This party says that both climate change and the necessary actions needed to mitigate and adapt to its negative consequences will worsen socioeconomic inequalities. Initiatives need to be put in place to protect already marginalised groups.
how: This party would proactively identify those disproportionately impacted by climate change, such as people living in remote communities or people living with a disability, and support them to develop and implement inclusive plans to avoid harm. It would also strengthen human and labour rights to reduce inequitable vulnerabilities to the impacts of climate change and provide resources to grassroots climate change organisations focusing on community empowerment.

statement: Support people whose work has been impacted by climate change responses
why: This party says that both climate change and the necessary actions needed to mitigate and adapt to its negative consequences threaten to worsen socioeconomic inequalities. In moving towards a carbon-negative economy, people who work in high-emission industries may lose their jobs.
how: This party would fund free vocational training and redeployment opportunities for those in high-emission industries to transition to climate-safe work. It would also provide access to redundancy compensation for people working in sectors that are adversely affected by climate change mitigation and adaptation actions.

statement: Support effective climate adaption decision making and action
why: This party says that climate change adaptation measures must be adopted by all of New Zealand, meaning everyone needs to work together from the government down to the individual.
how: This party would increase resourcing and accountability for climate adaptation within local government, including providing additional resources to those lease resourced to take climate action. It would also prioritise long-term, nature-based solutions aligned with tikanga Māori and culturally appropriate values and ensure every student knows how to respond and stay hopeful in the face of climate change. This party would also expand the role of the Natural Hazards Commission to include cover for climate-related weather events and ensure it plays a key role in managing community-led adaptation

statement: Establish a fund for implementing climate adaptation and resilience measures
why: This party says that as the impacts of climate change are felt more widely with more intense and frequent storms, community groups are often on the front lines of the emergency and clean-up response. Central and local governments must provide support for their communities to proactively plan and adapt.
how: This party would establish a dedicated fund for central and local government to implement climate adaptation and resilience measures, including funding for partnerships with tangata whenua and community organisations.  It would also develop and implement strategies to support the wellbeing of people displaced by climate change, including supporting Māori communities to deal with detachment and loss of identity from places of historical and customary significance.

statement: Increase the reporting and transparency aspects of the Zero Carbon Act
why: This party says that by urgently phasing out fossil fuels, NZ can ease the cost of living pressures and reduce our country's vulnerability to global price shocks. To do this, NZ needs to be led by strong domestic targets that stop emissions at the source and make polluting corporations pay.
how: This party would require the government Budget process to be consistent with limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees, gross emissions-reduction targets, and international commitments.  It would also improve public transparency on the costs of inaction by including the fiscal impact of the Nationally Determined Contribution obligation in the financial statements.

statement: Implement Waitangi Tribunal recommendations to ensure governance of the agricultural sector upholds Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
why: This party says that governance of the agricultural sector should recognise the expertise and rights of Māori and have self-governance over mahinga kai (food production). The agriculture sector and regional councils should work in partnership with Māori, in line with Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
how: This party would implement the recommendations of the Waitangi Tribunal to ensure that governance of the agricultural sector upholds Te Tiriti o Waitangi.

statement: Support Māori to address barriers to traditional food production
why: This party says governance of the agricultural sector should recognise the expertise and rights of Māori and have self-governance over mahinga kai (traditional food gathering practices). The agriculture sector and regional councils should work in partnership with Māori, in line with Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
how: This party would support Māori to address barriers found in banking, tax, company and co-operative laws that prevent te ao Māori principles from being applied to the production of food and fibre and/or Māori land use and development.

statement: Establish an Agricultural Standards Framework
why: This party says that New Zealand needs strong agricultural standards to ensure it remains known for its premium-quality and environmentally sustainable products.
how: This party would establish an Agricultural Standards Framework that includes requirements to measure all agricultural inputs and outputs, and robust and consistent measures of environmental impacts caused by agriculture. The framework would also include sustainability standards for all food and fibre sectors and incentives and other support to farmers to continuously improve ecosystems on productive land.

statement: Prohibit palm kernel expeller (PKE) imports
why: This party says that New Zealand needs strong agricultural standards to ensure it remains known for its environmentally sustainable products. NZ should not import products known for their link to tropical deforestation and habitat loss.
how: This party would prohibit palm kernel expeller (PKE) imports. This is a solid by-product left over from extracting oil from the seeds of oil palm fruit.

statement: Impose nitrogen caps on all agricultural practices
why: This party says that New Zealanders should be able to swim in unpolluted rivers and lakes. However, nitrogen fertilisers used on farms are polluting our freshwater. Fossil fuels are used in the production of nitrogen fertiliser, contributing to the climate emergency.
how: This party would impose nitrogen caps on all agricultural practices, and it would also prohibit the production of nitrogenous fertilisers from fossil fuels.

statement: Phase out most grazing concessions on public conservation land
why: This party says that that New Zealand should be working to look after its environment so that its communities and biodiversity are sustained. Allowing animals to graze on conservation land is prioritising economic opportunities over the core purpose of conservation land: preserving and protecting our native ecosystems.
how: This party would phase out most grazing concessions on public conservation land and require sustainable farm plans for active concessions.

statement: Support farmers in sensitive ecosystems to work collaboratively to protect indigenous biodiversity
why: This party says that NZ should be working to look after its environment so that its communities and indigenous biodiversity are sustained.
how: This party would support farmers in sensitive ecosystems to work collaboratively to protect indigenous biodiversity.

statement: Reduce agricultural emissions in New Zealand
why: This party says that the agriculture industry in New Zealand should be working to positively contribute to clean air and a safe climate. To do this, all agricultural businesses must work together to achieve a significant cut in gross emissions.
how: This party would adjust stocking rates according to the holding capacity of the land, protect existing wetlands and encourage wetland restoration, phase out the use of fossil fuels for agricultural processes, and phase out synthetic nitrogen fertilisers. It would also require the agriculture sector to provide data that enables greenhouse gas emissions to be measured and incentivise low greenhouse gas agricultural initiatives.

statement: Create a resilient agricultural sector
why: This party says that to protect New Zealand's food and agricultural products for generations to come, the agricultural sector needs to become resilient, diversified and agile. It will continue to face changing weather patterns, markets, and consumer demands.
how: This party would require imported foods to meet our own national growing and production requirements and support a transition to agroecological practices (such as regenerative and organic approaches). It would also encourage preserving and growing heritage seeds for personal use and commercial production and strengthen the collective resilience of grassroots community collaborations like local catchment groups.

statement: Provide resources and funding for innovative agricultural projects
why: This party says that communities benefit from local and seasonal produce that is nutritious, safe, fresh, and affordable. We should be supporting innovative agricultural practices and systems that encourage a thriving sector.
how: This party would provide startup funding for innovative systems and/or new food and fibre trials, and fund ongoing research to explore sustainable agricultural livelihoods that require less energy, time and costs. It would also provide resources for projects addressing the food and fibre needs of local communities.

statement: Honour traditional Māori agricultural practices
why: This party says that in meeting New Zealand's commitment to Te Tiriti o Waitangi, mātauranga Māori must be recognised, and Māori communities should be supported to grow, forage and hunt for food on their land.
how: This party would prioritise iwi-based initiatives in the management and restoration of retired and/or degraded agricultural land. It would fund research and development that supports hapū and iwi, Māori agribusiness and resources. A Māori-led authority would be set up to oversee the distribution of start-up funding for locally-led and sustainable Māori agricultural initiatives.

statement: Ensure the agricultural industry uses an ethical and human approach to animal management
why: This party says that animals in New Zealand's agricultural industry should enjoy the highest animal welfare standards. Welfare standards need to be properly enforced so that any animal death is managed as humanely as possible.
how: This party would ban the importation of animals and animal products when living conditions in their country of origin have not met Aotearoa New Zealand’s animal welfare standards and would empower resource animal welfare inspectors and prosecutors to fully uphold the Animal Welfare Act. It would also address the requirements of the Global Animal Protection Index to improve animal welfare in New Zealand, and prohibit new, and phase out existing factory farming of animals, including highly intensive outdoor facilities like feedlots. Transport standards that are fit-for-purpose and animal-focused

statement: Create national standards for the registered breeding of companion animals
why: This party says that humans have a duty of care towards animals they interact with. They should not be violated or exploited, and their distress and pain should be minimised.
how: This party would create national standards for the registered breeding of companion animals and limit the number of litters an individual animal can have over a lifetime. People who breed companion animals for sale and rescue centres must register and hold a current licence. It would also review the appropriateness of breed-specific legislation, and ban breeding of lineages with high susceptibility to genetic welfare issues.

statement: Implement improved welfare regulations for companion animals
why: This party says that people have a duty of respect for animals' rights. They should not be violated or exploited, and their distress and pain should be minimised.
how: This party would limit the number of companion animals an individual can have at once, with pathways for exemptions, such as for owners who can demonstrate being able to uphold welfare. It would implement codes of welfare for highly social animals, such as guinea pigs, rabbits, birds, rats, goats, horses and pigs, that require them to always be kept with others of their species. The party would also ban prolonged close confinement of animals and amend the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 to ensure that renters are able to own a registered companion or support animal when the animal meets local b

statement: Ensure animal welfare regulations upholds Te Tiriti o Waitangi and incorporates Māori cultural values
why: This party says humans have an ethical obligation to make informed decisions on behalf of animals, drawing on the best available knowledge of their needs and behaviours. This includes tikanga and mātauranga Māori.
how: This party would reform animal welfare legislation to recognise Māori concepts and values, in partnership with tāngata whenua, and ensure Māori representation on decision-making bodies for animal welfare. It would establish a Department of Animal Welfare, led by a Minister for Animal Welfare.

statement: Reform animal welfare legislation so that it protects indigenous biodiversity
why: This party says that we need to carefully balance the needs of indigenous species and introduced animals. Indigenous species and ecosystems are essential for maintaining ecological balance, so their interests should be prioritised over invasive species.
how: This party would develop local regulations around pet ownership to cater for the indigenous species residing in that locale, such as requiring catios to keep cats safe and protect local biodiversity. This includes funding free spaying and neutering for pets, introducing national standards for desexing dogs and registering, desexing and microchipping cats, and regulating recreational activities like hunting and fishing when they negatively affect indigenous species.

statement: Uphold the leadership of Māori during emergency management
why: This party says that the government has a responsibility to protect Māori interests, work in partnership with Māori, and respect Māori autonomy in disasters.  Decisions made during emergencies should also respect local knowledge.
how: This party would guarantee Māori representation at all levels of emergency management planning. It would formalise the role of iwi and hapū Māori in risk reduction, adaptation and recovery. It would also invest in the capacity and capability of iwi and hapū to respond in emergencies, and resource rural marae that want to be autonomous hubs for emergency preparedness and response.

statement: Make nature-based solutions the primary mechanism for hazard mitigation
why: This party says that New Zealand faces certain and increasing threats of many kinds, both natural and man-made.  Looking after the natural world is critical for minimising the risks and impacts of emergencies.
how: This party would set nature-based hazard mitigation as the default approach to hazard mitigation, but only if that approach does not negatively impact people and communities. The emergency response approach should be flexible and outcome- and needs-oriented, preserving local ecosystems, tikanga, and communities. To ensure this, the party would standardise Fire and Emergency NZ's chemical, biological, radioactive and nuclear response procedures and prepare a rapid, coordinated response plan covering marine emergencies and the impacts of land-based emergencies on the marine environment.

statement: Adequately resource national, regional and local emergency systems so communities are prepared for future emergencies.
why: This party says that New Zealand faces certain and increasing threats of many kinds, both natural and man-made. The government should provide the financial, material and training resources that agencies and community organisations require to effectively plan for and respond to emergencies of all kinds.
how: This party would fund critical roles and equipment for all emergency response services, including energy and communications providers, so they can prepare to maintain service resilience in emergencies. Stockpiles and systems providing lifesaving supplies would be organised in local and regional hubs, with regional preparedness plans created. Community organisations would receive training in emergency response, with multilingual, community-led education about emergency preparation and response for the public. It would also fund scientific research on resilience, risk mitigation, and adaptation

statement: Take a preventative approach regarding emergency management responses
why: This party says that that all people should be empowered to pre-emptively shape the emergency management systems that affect them through community engagement enabled by good evidence, co-design, and adequate resourcing.
how: This party would prioritise collaborative plans and strategies for targeted support towards communities at risk, including isolated people or communities, people at risk, and marginalised groups. It would ensure these communities were supported through developing and resourcing individualised preparedness plans. This would include providing tailored emergency preparedness and response information in various formats and languages to communities and households.

statement: Prioritise making critical utilities resilient in preparation for future emergencies
why: This party says that emergency management should prioritise basic needs and restoring essential services. Emergency financial support systems should maintain basic living standards and avoid exacerbating existing inequities.
how: This party would set minimum standards for regional resilience in critical utilities, including the electrical grid and satellite communications and provide resources to remote communities so they can establish local alternatives to these centralised critical systems. It would also provide easily accessible basic resources as needed, including food, shelter, repairs, and clothing,  regardless of people’s immediate ability to pay.

statement: Support Māori led education for growing and preparing food
why: This party says that food is deeply connected to wellbeing, culture, identity, and the health of the planet. By restoring Māori-led kaitiakitanga of mahinga kai and prioritising nutritious, sustainable food systems, we can strengthen relationships with the environment and support healthier communities.
how: This party would support learning opportunities for children and communities to grow, harvest, prepare, and share nutritious wholefoods through school gardens and food education programmes. It would strengthen Māori-led approaches to caring for mahinga kai and ensure traditional knowledge and practices are valued and supported. A national whole food system strategy will guide decision-making by honouring Te Tiriti o Waitangi and prioritising the health of people and the planet alongside sustainable practices.

statement: Support access to food security and traditional food practices
why: This party says food security and sovereignty are essential for the health, wellbeing, and resilience of communities. It believes all consumers should have agency over their food and be able to make informed choices. There should also be a wide range of options close to where people live so they can choose nourishing food that meets their cultural needs.
how: This party would support tangata whenua-led food production, distribution, and decision-making processes It would protect and promote foods and practices that reflect mana whenua (the people of the land). This party would work to ensure consumers have access to clear, accurate information about the nutritional, environmental, and ethical impacts of food choices. It would revise relevant legislation to protect the human right to be free from hunger and malnutrition.

statement: Ensure everyone has reliable access to affordable, fresh, and nutritious food
why: This party says that access to nourishing food is essential for people’s health, well-being, and ability to participate fully in society. A food system therefore should support communities by reducing food insecurity, strengthenen local connections, and ensuring that healthy choices are available to everyone.
how: This party would support community food hubs, distribution programmes, and local food initiatives that improve access to fresh and nutritious foods. It would address unfair practices within the grocery sector through stronger legislation that promotes competition and fairness. Actions would also focus on making nourishing foods and drinks more affordable and accessible.

statement: Make a child's voice central in all decisions that matter to them
why: This party says that our children and young people deserve to be loved, nurtured and safe. We have a shared responsibility to make sure tamariki's voices are heard, centred and reflected in all decisions that impact them.
how: This party would create and amend legislation so that the child’s voice is central in all decisions that matter to them. It would do this by using the Child Impact Assessment Tool consistently in all government policy and planning, and fully incorporating the Rights of the Child into legislation.

statement: Make the Best Start payment for children universal
why: This party says that our children and young people deserve to be loved, nurtured and safe. We have a shared responsibility to make sure children are free from poverty as soon as they are born.
how: This party would increase the Best Start payment and extend it to every child under three as a universal child benefit for the early years.

statement: Improve workforce safety in the child protection system
why: This party says that children and young people deserve a skilled, well-supported workforce that is trauma-informed, culturally responsive and properly trained when dealing with their safety, health and education.
how: This party would would fund training and create a workforce development strategy. This would prioritise Māori, Pacific, rainbow, disabled and community provider pathways.

statement: Improve access for diagnosis services for children with disabilities or learning support needs
why: This party says that children deserve to be supported in each of their unique journeys through life. A functioning society should ensure children with disabilities or learning support needs get the help they need to have a great quality of life.
how: This party would improve access to both diagnosis and support services for children with disabilities or learning support needs.

statement: Amend the Oranga Tamariki Act to explicitly protect Māori children
why: This party says that young Māori children are disproportionately impacted by New Zealand's current child protection system. This is because it excludes meaningful partnership and underinvests in culturally grounded, whānau-led solutions. The party says that to uphold our commitment to Te Tiriti o Waitangi, we need to address the inequities tamariki Māori face in everyday life and in the state care system.
how: This party would amend the Oranga Tamariki Act to protect tamariki Māori and explicitly embed whānau participation in decision-making to exercise iwi or hapū authority. It would implement the Waitangi Tribunal recommendations regarding Oranga Tamariki.

statement: Increase overall public conservation funding
why: This party says that New Zealand's flora and fauna are central to our national identity and way of life. Yet they are often threatened by economic goals, as well as introduced predators. This party says that conservation decisions should be made for the public good, not in the interests of private profiteers.
how: This party would increase overall public conservation funding, including increasing funding and support for the Predator Free 2050 goal.

statement: Require all publicly funded projects to pay at least the living wage to artists
why: This party says that artists and creatives deserve to be valued, respected and recognised for their work. Yet currently, too many are without the certainty of a stable income, and many lack access to the training and education needed to foster their skills and talents. Creatives should be supported in their work.
how: This party would require that all publicly funded projects pay at least the living wage to artists and expand paid artist residencies so creatives can upskill and grow their practice while building a meaningful livelihood.

statement: Provide stable funding for creative organisations and events
why: This party says that artists and creatives deserve to be valued, respected and recognised for their work. Yet currently, too many are without the certainty of a stable income. Creatives should be supported in their practice and provided opportunities to participate in events where they can grow and showcase their work.
how: This party would provide stable funding for creative organisations and events such as Te Urungi, including long-term funding for significant creative initiatives such as Te Matatini and Polyfest.

statement: Provide long-term arts funding for creatives
why: This party says that artists and creatives deserve to be valued, respected and recognised for their work. Yet currently, too many are without the certainty of a stable income. Creatives should be supported in their practice and provided opportunities to participate in events where they can grow and showcase their work.
how: This party would provide sustainable long-term arts funding that is not reliant on gambling revenue, alongside alcohol-free venues for performers.

statement: Support the repatriation of taonga overseas back to the Māori community
why: This party says that repatriation of items of cultural significance is an act of reconciliation, restoring dignity to ancestors taken illegally from iwi and hapū during the colonial era. These taonga are part of New Zealand's cultural identity and should live within its shores.
how: This party would invest in repatriating taonga currently overseas back to iwi, hapū and whānau Māori, as well as keeping taonga in NZ.

statement: Establish infrastructure across ministries to strengthen our creative and cultural economy
why: This party says that arts, culture and creativity are vital for creating vibrant cities and communities. Like other community infrastructure, the arts, culture and creative sectors need proper support.
how: This party would establish infrastructure across ministries to strengthen our creative and cultural economy and maximise opportunities for local artists.

statement: Increase funding for non-commercial public media
why: This party says that non-commercial public media can nurture and promote our talent and creativity as a nation, providing original opportunities without the need to prioritise profit.
how: This party would increase funding for quality, non-commercial public media, including sustainable funding for Radio New Zealand and Whakaata Māori.

statement: Increase funding for community media
why: This party says that young people and local communities deserve opportunities to foster their skills and talents in media and radio. This promotes culture and creativity that is vital for creating vibrant cities and communities, alongside encouraging young New Zealanders to grow their careers in the country.
how: This party would fund and resource student, community, regional, Māori and Pacific media and radio.

statement: Provide $200m towards te reo Māori initiatives
why: This party says that te reo Māori is a national treasure and initiatives that help it thrive should be supported so future generations can learn and enjoy the language. Supporting te reo Māori also supports whānau, hapū and iwi to be connected to their culture.
how: This party would fund an additional $50m towards te reo Māori initiatives each year. This would be made up of: $30m a year to programmes that provide continuous education and professional development for teachers in te reo Māori, and $20m a year towards increased funding for Te Taura Whiri and Te Mātāwai.

statement: Resource a national conversation for constitutional change
why: This party says that that democracy in New Zealand should uphold Te Tiriti o Waitangi and the vision of Matike Mai Aotearoa, creating a decision-making process that reflects genuine partnership.
how: This party would resource a national conversation for constitutional change that upholds He Whakaputanga (the Declaration of Independence of the United Tribes of New Zealand) and Te Tiriti o Waitangi as our founding constitutional documents, utilising Matike Mai Aotearoa to facilitate community discussions.

statement: Expand voting rights in New Zealand
why: This party says that expanding voting rights creates a more representative democracy where everyone's voices are respected and heard.
how: This party would uphold the right to vote by extending the voting age to 16, extending the right to vote to all people in custody and restoring enrolment up to election day.

statement: Entrench the Māori electoral seats
why: This party says that that democracy in New Zealand needs to represent our entire population. It should appreciate Te Tiriti o Waitangi as a decision-making process that reflects a genuine partnership.
how: This party would entrench the Māori electoral seats to guarantee Māori representation in Parliament and extend the time in which Māori can switch rolls.

statement: Reform electoral funding policies
why: This party says that democracy should work for everyone, not just those who are wealthy. The richest few can currently spend millions of dollars backing different political parties and ministers.
how: This party would limit donations to registered voters, increase public financing of campaigns and cap a donor’s donations at a level that does not risk donor influence over policy.

statement: Strengthen political lobbying rules
why: This party says that the wealthiest few in New Zealand have the resources to influence government policies and decisions through political lobbying. Yet this excludes the rest of the country from advocating for the issues that matter most to them.
how: This party would strengthen the rules and transparency over political lobbying, through creating a lobbyist register and a code of conduct.

statement: Regulate social media platforms to address harmful content
why: This party says that digital environments need to support our wellbeing, especially for young social media users who are often more vulnerable in the digital space.
how: This party would introduce a Digital Duty of Care to address harmful content and behaviour on social media platforms. This would require algorithmic transparency and accessible and responsive complaints systems, as well as strengthening enforcement with an independent national regulator.

statement: Regulate artificial intelligence to limit the harm from scams and deepfakes
why: This party says that digitial platforms should be held accountable for protecting the public and its information. This party believes a harm-reduction approach should be taken to digital technology.
how: This party would regulate artificial intelligence to ensure its use is safe, transparent and accurate. It would also create stricter rules around "deepfakes" and scam material.

statement: Crack down on tax avoidance by offshore corporations
why: This party says that multinational tech giants are part of New Zealand's digital infrastructure. However, they are not adequately regulated, meaning profits are going overseas rather than back into the New Zealand economy.
how: This party would crack down on tax avoidance and the offshoring of profits by multinational tech giants such as Meta, Amazon and Microsoft.

statement: Protect Māori data sovereignty
why: This party says that without the regulation of AI models, Māori culture is being exploited and stolen by overseas platforms.
how: This party would adopt and implement the Māori Data Governance Model and Māori AI Governance Framework from Te Kāhui Raraunga across the public sector to protect Māori data sovereignty.

statement: Strengthen obligations for data-holders to protect user data
why: This party says that that the companies that are holding public data, including health biometrics and personal information, cannot always be trusted to protect it.
how: This party would strengthen obligations on data-holders to protect user and biometric data by increasing penalties for privacy breaches, and strengthen the Privacy Commissioner's enforcement powers to protect personal information better.

statement: Expand media and digital literacy education
why: This party says that digital environments should support our wellbeing, yet many young people have been exposed to harmful and toxic content. We should equip our young people with adequate tools so they can use digital technologies without compromising their privacy and online safety and keep up with the rapid development of technology.
how: This party would expand media and digital literacy education to equip New Zealanders to navigate AI-generated media and other emerging digital technologies.

statement: Reduce barriers to digital inclusion
why: This party says that in NZ, there is a great digital divide, which only increases inequalities. Every person should be able to access the digital infrastructure necessary to actively participate and thrive in society.
how: This party would reduce barriers to digital inclusion by ensuring all communities have access to the internet, have suitable devices and have offline alternatives for essential services.

statement: Create a disability rights law based on Te Tiriti o Waitangi
why: This party says that disabled people are often denied the same rights as others. They can also be excluded from places and activities that non-disabled people take for granted. These barriers are often worse for tāngata whaikaha Māori.
how: This party would introduce a disability rights law based on Te Tiriti with enforceable accessibility standards. Policy-makers would need to collaboratively design laws, policies, and systems in ways that work for disabled people.

statement: Provide accessible and timely income support for disabled people
why: This party says that in New Zealand, disabled people are often denied the same rights as others. They can also be excluded from places and activities that non-disabled people take for granted. All disabled people deserve enough support so that they can participate equally in life and in their communities.
how: This party would provide easily accessible and timely income support to meet all disability-related living and medical costs. This income support would be regardless of relationship status and cause of disability.

statement: Ensure all disabled people can access and live in safe housing
why: This party says that our current laws, policies and social norms mean disabled people are often denied the same rights as others. They are often excluded from places and activities non-disabled people take for granted, such as the basic human right to shelter.
how: This party would address homelessness and work towards ensuring all disabled people can live in safe, accessible, affordable housing in the community of their choice, including by setting robust universal design standards for public and private housing. Institutional group home settings would be phased out.

statement: Make travel accessible for disabled people
why: This party says that our current laws, policies and social norms mean disabled people are often denied the same rights as others. They are often excluded from places and activities non-disabled people take for granted, such as accessing public transport and travelling around their communities.
how: This party would make getting around accessible through continuing to fund the 75% subsidy for the Total Mobility taxi scheme, making it easier to use and increasing the number of mobility vehicles to meet demand.

statement: Remove barriers to accessing essential services for disabled people
why: This party says that our current laws, policies and social norms mean disabled people are often denied the same rights as others. They are often excluded from places and activities non-disabled people take for granted, such as accessing public transport, basic health care and inclusive education. Interactions with public services should effectively support disabled people's wellbeing.
how: This party would remove barriers to accessing the essentials like health care, transport, inclusive education and disability support for all who need it. The party would do this by drawing on the Enabling Good Lives approach as a guide to how government agencies work with disabled people. It would provide public service staff with resourcing and training to meet access needs and counter ableism and operate using a high-trust model that recognises disabled people as experts in their own lives, while making support and services available when needed.

statement: Ensure national and local emergency response plans address the needs of disabled people
why: This party says that disabled people are often more vulnerable than non-disabled people during emergencies. It does not want disabled people to be left behind in times of emergency. Their needs must be considered and supported.
how: This party would resource a coordinated approach to disability in emergency management, including a national disability emergency management strategy. It would prioritise disabled input and leadership locally and nationally within emergency response planning and communication.

statement: Uphold legal capacity for everyone in New Zealand
why: This party says that everyone, with the support of people of their own choosing when appropriate, should have autonomy and equal recognition before the law. Disabled people, like others should be in charge of decisions about our own lives.
how: This party would uphold legal capacity for everyone, moving from legal capacity assessments to rights-based systems of supported decision-making. This includes disabled people and their families being able to rely on accessible, timely, and affordable healthcare, mental health support and palliative care, without fear of judgement.

statement: Repeal and replace the Misuse of Drugs Act
why: This party says that drugs exist and people use them. This party wants to reduce harm that can arise from drug use by taking a health-based approach rather than a punitive approach to drug use. Drug criminalisation leads to unsafe drug use, fosters organised crime, and traps those convicted in a cycle of poverty that, in turn, contributes to harmful drug use.
how: This party would repeal and replace the Misuse of Drugs Act with an evidence-based approach that reduces harm, treats drug use as a health issue and provides for regulated access to cannabis for personal use. As a short-term measure, it would implement the recommendations of the Law Commission’s 2011 review of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975. The new Act would be co-designed with Māori under a Te Tiriti o Waitangi framework and would promote the rights and interests of whānau, hapū, and iwi.

statement: Increase resourcing for rainbow community organisations
why: This party says that all New Zealanders need to live with dignity and safety. Rainbow New Zealanders, in particular, need access to public services and healthcare that meet their needs.
how: This party would work with rainbow communities and organisations to develop strategies for wellbeing, especially for access to health care. Māori and Pasifika services specifically would also be included. Rainbow community organisations would receive dedicated resources for their work and be involved in developing and delivering services.

statement: Ensure rainbow communities can access gender-affirming healthcare
why: This party says that all New Zealanders need to be able to live with dignity and safety. Rainbow New Zealanders in particular need access to public services and healthcare that serve their needs. This includes healthcare that supports their gender identity and removing barriers, such as surgery for intersex people and the ban on puberty blockers.
how: This party would provide timely, non-discriminatory access to gender-affirming healthcare, such as hormones and surgery. These treatments would be given more resources in the health system, and the focus would be on informed consent and self-determination. The ban on puberty blockers would be revoked.

statement: Promote the human rights of takatāpui, intersex and rainbow people against discrimination
why: This party says that all New Zealanders need to be able to live with dignity and safety. Rainbow New Zealanders in particular need their identities to be recognised and protected, as recommended by the Law Commission’s Ia Tangata report. Protecting human rights means being protected from non-consensual surgeries, and that rainbow migrants have their identities recognised and protected.
how: This party would amend the Human Rights Act to clarify that all forms of sexual orientation, gender identity and variations in sex characteristics, are prohibited grounds of discrimination and adopt the recommendations of the Ia Tangata report. Non-consensual and medically unnecessary surgeries for intersex people would be prohibited. Migrants, asylum seekers and refugees with rainbow identities would be able to access legal services, have their gender and partners legally recognised, and reunite with their families.

statement: Form a strategy for a zero-waste economy
why: This party says that all our activities should aim to eliminate waste, circulate resources and regenerate nature. It believes in transitioning to a zero-waste economy, where single-use plastics are largely eliminated and a circular product stewardship system, from design to disposal, is in place across the economy.
how: This party would work towards phasing out landfills and resource zero-waste strategies and legislation. It would develop and resource a national resource recovery network. It would promote moderate consumption and ban most single-use plastics. It would lead international efforts to clean up waste from the Pacific Ocean.

statement: Ban single-use plastics and require plastics or rare earth materials to be recycled
why: This party says that NZ needs to transition to a zero-waste economy, where single use plastics are largely eliminated, wasteful consumption is ended, and a circular product stewardship is in place across the economy.
how: This party would require all products using plastics and rare earth metals to be readily recycled. Most single-use plastic products and non-recyclable and non-home-compostable packaging would be banned, with necessary exceptions.

statement: Support better working conditions including pay equity rules
why: This party says that everyone is entitled to secure and meaningful work in innovative, environmentally sustainable, and socially responsible workplaces. That includes fair pay, freedom from discrimination and an equitable relationship between employers, union and workers.
how: This party would ensure pay equity, such as requiring pay transparency and pay-parity management, and ensure everyone including marginalised groups get the training and information they need to have equitable employment opportunities. It would support people whose work has been affected by climate change, and progress towards a shorter standard working week It would ensure time in lieu or overtime is provided for work out of contracted hours.

statement: Support default union membership for new workers
why: This party says that everyone is entitled to secure and meaningful work in innovative, environmentally sustainable, and socially responsible workplaces. That includes fair pay, freedom from discrimination and an equitable relationship between employers, unions, and workers.
how: This party would make union membership an opt-out option when people start a new job. Newly hired employees would be default, be members unless they wish not to be.

statement: Improve training in te reo Māori and Te Tiriti o Waitangi for all public servants
why: This party says that public services are investments in our shared future. Capable public servants need a strong grasp of Māori language, culture, and Te Tiriti o Waitangi as NZ's founding document in order to deliver services effectively.
how: This party would improve training in Te Tiriti and te reo Māori for all public servants, so that results across agencies are more consistent.

statement: Restore the monitoring role of the Children's Commissioner
why: This party says that that independent commissions with expertise, like the Climate Change Commission, Human Rights Commission and Children's Commission play an important role. Public services ensure that all New Zealanders can thrive, and these commissions are part of how issues are monitored.
how: This party would restore the "monitoring" function of the Children's Commissioner, in addition to the advocacy function. It would also support the importance of independent commissions in the government more broadly.

statement: Support measures to reduce violence
why: This party says that everyone must be able to live free from violence and abuse. Aotearoa has among the highest rates of intimate partner violence, sexual violence and child abuse, and this is disproportionately harmful to people in vulnerable professions and families.
how: This party would invest in services to help victims and increase awareness of the drivers of violence and of restorative practices. It would fund a national strategy to eliminate family and sexual violence (Te Aorerekura) and amend the Crimes Act to criminalise coercive control. It would also amend the definition of consent. and restore relationship and sexuality teaching guidelines in all schools. Funding would be lifted for mental health support for victims and others in the justice system.

statement: Fund community organisations and marae to fulfil the needs of their communities and regions
why: This party says that NZ has enough to invest in services for everyone, and community organisations, marae, iwi and hapū fulfil important roles in responding to the needs of their communities. These organisations should receive more money to meet the needs of their communities.
how: This party would fund Māori organisations, marae, iwi and hapū for community and environmental work. It would also provide secure and flexible funding arrangements to the community sector to recognise the importance of its work and ensuring community work and remain independent.

statement: Standardise pay and other support across the public sector
why: This party says that underinvestment has hurt public services and damaged their ability to fulfil their responsibilities to the public, leaving services stretched. Staff members in any part of the public sector should have access to the same pay and career progression to make things equal, improve retention and develop capacity and skills. The public service should also lead the way in providing flexible employment options for disabled people.
how: This party would ensure all public servants can access career progression, pay, community secondment opportunities and training in all sectors. It would provide resources and training to meet disabled employees access needs and counter ableism.

statement: Allow people with Māori whakapapa to become New Zealand citizens no matter where they are born
why: This party says that increasing numbers of New Zealanders are moving or living overseas, and the government represents these people too. New Zealanders living overseas deserve to connect to Aotearoa, and tangata whenua should always be able to return to their turangawaewae by being New Zealand citizens, regardless of where they were born.
how: This party would allow all people with Māori whakapapa to become New Zealand citizens, even if they have been born in another country.

statement: Extend the time New Zealanders can live overseas and retain voting eligibility
why: This party says that increasing numbers of New Zealanders are moving or living overseas, and the government represents these people too. New Zealanders overseas are still invested in the future of the country and should be able to vote. If they return to New Zealand and contribute here again, they should be able to receive superannuation.
how: This party would extend the time New Zealanders can live overseas and retain voting eligibility. Currently, overseas-based New Zealanders must have lived in NZ continuously for 12 months at some point in their life and been in NZ at some point in the last three years.

statement: Return to a 10-year period based in New Zealand for superannuation eligibility
why: This party says that overseas New Zealanders deserve to remain connected to NZ, and have a interest in the future of the country. Nearly 15 percent of New Zealanders live in other countries. The government should take a compassionate approach to New Zealanders who have lived or are living overseas.
how: This party would restore the 10-year period of being based in NZ for superannuation eligibility.

statement: Make it easier for people based in other countries to repay student loans
why: This party says that overseas New Zealanders deserve to remain connected to NZ, and have an interest in the future of the country. Nearly 15% of New Zealanders live in other countries and many have moved overseas recently. The government should take a compassionate approach to New Zealanders who have lived or are living overseas. People with student loans should not face harsh consequences or border arrests.
