how: This party would reduce student loan interest rates for New Zealanders in other countries. It would cease the practice or arresting people at the NZ border for not repaying their student loans and extend the repayment holiday for people living overseas.

statement: Pursue reciprocal healthcare, welfare and visa-waiver arrangements with other countries
why: This party says that overseas New Zealanders deserve to remain connected to NZ, and have a interest in the future of the country. Nearly 15% of New Zealanders live in other countries. The government should take a compassionate approach to New Zealanders who have lived or are living overseas. These people, and visitors from other countries to New Zealand, should be able to access public services like healthcare wherever they are.
how: This party would seek further reciprocal arrangements with other countries where New Zealanders might live. These would include access to public healthcare, welfare support or benefits and visa waivers. In return, the citizens of those countries would be offered the same services in New Zealand. Existing arrangements, as already exist in some form with the UK and Australia, could be widened to include temporary visitors as well as people working.

statement: Introduce free public transport fares for young people, the disabled and CSC card holders
why: This party says our rail system has fallen into disarray, and our spread-out communities are poorly served by bus networks. Young people, non-car owners, families and minority groups all benefit from better transport options, as does the environment.
how: This party would extend the Community Connect programme to provide free fares for young people, disabled and community service card holders. It would also work towards more bike lanes, and e-bike sharing.

statement: Build mass rapid transit in three major cities and invest in better rail and bus links
why: This party says that our rail system has fallen into disarray, and our communities are poorly served by our bus networks, particularly on the outskirts of towns. Young people, non-car owners, families and minority groups all benefit from better transport options, as does the environment.
how: This party would build mass rapid transit in Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch and invest in a national passenger and freight rapid rail system to connect major cities and regions better. It would also fund affordable inter-regional and rural bus services and beef up bus lanes in cities.

statement: Phase out fossil-fuel vehicle imports and incentivise electric vehicles
why: This party says that NZ's public transport system has left many people with no option but to rely on cars to get around, adding to congestion and making people vulnerable to oil price shocks. Young people, non-car owners, families and minority groups particularly benefit from better transport options, as does the environment.
how: This party would phase out the importation of fossil-fuel vehicles, and build more electric vehicle charging stations, promote EV charging stations, car-sharing and introduce incentives for EV uptake.

statement: Introduce fees-free tertiary education, universal student allowances and paid placements
why: This party says that our education system should be lifelong and accessible to everyone. But currently students struggle to pay for and stay in tertiary education - including vocational and community adult education - and providers are struggling to provide courses and attract and retain talent..
how: This party would provide fees-free tertiary education, reduce student loan repayments, and work towards a write-off of student loan debt. It would also introduce a universal student allowance for tertiary students to cover their needs, and training allowances for those doing compulsory work placements.

statement: Increase visa-free travel and work visa set-ups for Pasifika visitors and workers in NZ
why: This party says that Pacific peoples are an important part of building NZ's sustainable and flourishing future. Pacific communities are some of the youngest and fastest-growing in NZ. However, it can be hard for their family from Pacific Island countries to visit NZ, and workers under the RSE (Recognised Seasonal Employer) scheme can be mistreated.
how: This party would extend visa-free travel to NZ for citizens of Pacific countries. It would also replace the current RSE scheme with an alternative that guarantees housing and fair wages, and create an open work system where it is easier for these workers to change employers if they are not being treated well. Workers under the new scheme would have a clearer path to NZ residency.

statement: Ensure proper resourcing for tertiary education providers
why: This party says that education should be lifelong and accessible to all. In reality, tertiary education is cost-prohibitive to many, and the institutions themselves struggle with funding to keep courses open and attract and retain good teachers and researchers. Polytechnics are underfunded and don't always meet community needs and  more apprenticeship programmes are needed.
how:
This party would ensure polytechnics have adequate funding and strong local control to meet workforce and community needs, and protect staff and courses. 
Tertiary organisations would receive a funding formula that prioritises teaching, pastoral care, and research, with a focus on collaboration rather than competition between providers. 
Apprenticeship programmes would be expanded and all tertiary education would be fees-free.

statement: Uphold te Tiriti in the Treaty of Waitangi Act and across government decision-making
why: This party says that te Tiriti must be upheld as the fundamental document that the Treaty of Waitangi Act is based on. In its view, successive governments have consistently breached Te Tiriti, eroding the true partnership that was intended. Te Tiriti o Waitangi references have recently been weakened or stripped out of 19 acts of Parliament. And in government decision-making, iwi and hapū are often treated as advisors, rather than the partners which they are meant to be.
how:
This party would amend the Treaty of Waitangi Act so Te Tiriti is the authoritative text. It would implement genuine Te Tiriti decision-making models across government, and ensure iwi and hapu are resourced to participate as partners.
It would increase resourcing for the Waitangi Tribunal and give it the power to make binding recommendations for the return of Crown and private land. 
It would facilitate the return of whenua outside of Treaty Settlements that was wrongfully alienated from tangata whenua, including a possible right-of-first-refusal process at point of sale. It would also reform

statement: Support NZ made products, small business and sustainable industries
why: This party says that small businesses are facing an economy that is stacked against them. Liquidations are the highest in almost 15 years and a lack of supermarket competition is squeezing shoppers and local suppliers. International corporates are flourishing while factories close and local businesses struggle. This party will work for an even playing field for local businesses and support sustainable low-carbon industries.
how: This party would encourage consumer to support local by revitalising ‘Buy Kiwi Made’ and expanding country of origin labelling; commit government departments to buying more NZ goods and services; reform competition laws to create a fairer playing field for small businesses and consumers. It would foster sustainable, low carbon jobs in the ICT sector, particularly smaller firms. And it would invest in community-led regional development with a focus on sustainable building, regenerative agriculture, low-carbon infrastructure and iwi/hapū led economic activity.

statement: Better resource the agencies fighting anti-competitive practices
why: This party says that small businesses are faced with a challenging landscape including a 15-year high in liquidations and a lack of supermarket competition which is squeezing local suppliers. Small businesses need an even playing field against international corporates where the profits go offshore.
how: This party would reform competition laws to create a fairer playing field for small businesses and consumers. It would also increase the resources and powers of regulatory agencies investigating anti-competitive behaviour.

statement: Create a state-owned retirement village system and more support for seniors
why: This party says that seniors have cared for us and many continue to do so during retirement. They should feel valued, connected and able to live with dignity. Seniors should have warm, accessible homes, and the community spaces and marae-based centres that support them should they need assistance. The says that, additionally, there should also be more support for the conditions and pay of aged care workers.
how: This party would launch a long‑term seniors strategy that addresses kaumātua wellbeing, elder abuse, equitable incomes, and the creation of a state‑owned, not‑for‑profit retirement village system. It would boost funding for senior community spaces and activities, expand housing options such as papakāinga and address social housing waitlists for kaumātua. It would support warm, accessible, smaller home designs and back fair pay and conditions for aged care workers.

statement: Transfer responsibility for local elections to the Electoral Commission
why: This party says that democratic engagement in local government is low, especially at turnout for local elections. Local government should have a mandate from communities and local elections should be consistent across the country, rather than being run by different private companies.
how: This party would transfer responsibility of local elections to the Electoral Commission. Sixteen year olds would be allowed to vote in local elections and all councils would use a Single Transferable Vote (STV) system. To enhance democracy and community input, councils could use tools like citizens assemblies to make decisions, especially regarding reorganisation of council bodies.

statement: Ensure that fulfilling Te Tiriti and wellbeing goals is a core responsibility of local government
why: This party says that tino rangatiratanga is often sidelined in council decision making. Local government shapes a lot of people's everyday life, and community wellbeing should be a priority.
how: This party would reinforce the role of local government to give effect to Te Tiriti o Waitangi, and formally establish local councils as Te Tiriti partners. Councils would be allowed to reinstate Māori wards. Councils should also consider multiple sphere through the "four wellbeings" (social, economic, environmental and cultural) and take responsibility for more areas from central government, with appropriate resourcing.

statement: Reject the proposed rates cap and allow councils to use more funding tools
why: This party says that councils have been loaded with new responsibilities like emergency management and tourist influxes, but not given enough money to carry out these responsibilities. To carry out their role in communities, councils should not have limits on rates set by central government. Instead they need appropriate resourcing from a range of tools.
how: This party would reject the proposed rates cap where councils could only increase rates between 2 and 4 percent annually. Councils could set rates as they chose. Councils would also be allowed to use bed levies, congestion charging and charge GST on rates and other growth.

statement: Connect primary and secondary mental health care with clear referral pathways
why: This party says that everyone deserves to access quality mental health care in the community where they live. Services should be culturally relevant and focused on the area of greatest need. With demand high and mental health workers burned out, making referral to secondary services clear, fast and consistent will lead to good outcomes.
how: This party would link primary health and secondary mental health services with clear referral pathways in every health region. The focus would be on areas that have disproportionate need.

statement: Create an independently enforced Rental Warrant of Fitness
why: This party says that a warm safe home should be a basic right, but much of NZ's housing is a source of misery and expense, while people who can afford to own their homes get richer. Housing should be affordable and healthy.
how: This party would increase the stringency of the current Healthy Homes Standards for rental housing. It would also introduce a "Rental Warrant of Fitness" to certify that a house was appropriate to rent out, which would be independently certified.

statement: Increase public housing supply and housing support
why: This party says that housing should be a basic right, not a "get rich quick" scheme only for those who can afford it. Building affordable, sustainable homes in the places where people want to live will focus on housing for homes, rather than housing as an investment.
how: This party would increase public housing stock by building tens of thousands of new homes. It would fund papakāinga to be built on Māori land. People in need of emergency housing would be guaranteed "same-day" placement, and concepts like "housing first" and supported housing would be used for those in most need to support them to build a life in a stable home.

statement: Limit annual rent increases to 2 percent
why: This party says that housing should be a basic right, not an investment that a lucky few can get rich from. Renting should be fixed so that healthy homes in places where people want to live are affordable.
how: This party would limit annual rent increases to no more than 2 percent per year. The amount charged in rent for a new tenancy would be linked to what previous tenancies paid, so that there is not a jump in price between tenants.

statement: Implement a one-year pause on AI data centers
why: This party says that AI data centres can currently be consented by councils with no community input. Overseas, data centres have had adverse effects on local water supplies and are high energy users, driving up power prices. The Datagrid data centre in Southland is expected to use 6 per cent of the country's electricity supply. This party says there needs to be more transparency and a chance for regulation to be developed.
how: This party would call for a one-year moratorium on new AI data centres while proper rules are put in place to ensure there are benefits and don't unduly strain our resources. Solutions could include forcing centres to build their own energy or use closed loop water cooling systems, but currently there are no requirements for these under NZ rules.

statement: Encourage mixed-use areas and walkability in new housing developments
why: This party says that a home is a place to build a life with loved ones. Building houses in existing urban areas will prevent cities from encroaching into rural areas, and mean homes are more sustainable for the next generation.
how: This party would require councils to collaborate with communities, including mana whenua on decisions about new housing. Housing should be in mixed-use areas with shops and housing, within existing urban areas, and prioritise being able to walk around easily.

statement: Increase funding for food grants, food banks and other food security programmes
why: This party says that NZ produces enough food to feed 40 million people, but somehow food prices are too high for many. Dismantling the supermarket duopoly alone is not enough to deliver food security, and demand for community solutions like food banks is immense. This party would offer more support to those building alternative models for food security, processing and distribution.
how: This party would double the cap on food grants at the cost of $94-$100m annually. It would lift funding for regional food distribution hubs and community food providers from up to $8m to $25m a year and set up a $150m a year Fair Food Fund for community-led food security, such as food rescue programmes, marae and social supermarkets.

statement: Make early childhood education free
why: This party says that that early childhood education costs are a stress and barrier for many families, and that education should be a public good. This party says the competitive market in education has reduced trust, creativity and maintained exclusion.
how: This party would first cap charges at $10 per day per child, on top of the 20 hour per week entitlement that is currently funded. This party would raise the funded entitlement to 35 hours a week by 2029.

statement: Expand the school lunch program
why: This party says that children learn better when they are well-fed and every child deserves healthy, delicious and locally prepared food.
how: This party would restore Ka Ora, Ka Ako, the healthy school lunch programme, so lunches are provided by schools and local providers. Expand the school lunch programme to 400 more schools, providing lunches to 150,000 more schoolchildren. It would permanently fund the school lunch programme.

statement: Restore the Ministry for the Environment
why: This party says that that restoration and protection of the environment is important for the future and that a strong ministry is important for this.
how: This party would restore the Ministry for the Environment, and increase resources for the Environmental Protection Authority to identify risks to the environment and to support compliance, monitoring and enforcement. It would also re-establish resources for the Community Environment Fund.

statement: Develop a long-term plan to support the teaching workforce
why: This party says that education is vital for social cohesion and democracy and should be planned and funded to deliver this.
how: This party would support the workforce to get fair wages and reach staffing levels that support quality teaching, and co-develop a long-term workforce plan with the sector.

statement: Regulate lobbying and party donations
why: This party says that democracy should work for everyone, not just the wealthy. Capping donations and increasing the transparency around lobbying mean big money and professional lobbying can have less influence over politics.
how: This party would bring in a package of reforms, including a public register for lobbying so meetings with politicians are on the record. Former ministers would have to wait two years before they can be employed by a lobbying group. A new bill would cap party donations at $30,000 per individuals, and companies will not be able to donate. Donors above $1000 would have to be named.

statement: Expand access to learning support
why: This party says that people with disabilities and diverse learners should be fully supported to learn, belong and thrive.
how: This party would expand the criteria for access to learning support and establish a single agency for specialist supports for learners with health and disability needs. It would implement all actions in the Ministry for Educations 'Framework for Action: A Quality Education for All' strategy.

statement: Uphold Te Tiriti o Waitangi in the new resource management system
why: This party says that shared-decision making between the Government and tangata whenua is important to uphold Te Tiriti o Waitangi, and that this has been taken out of environmental laws.
how: This party would secure the role of Te Tiriti in the resource management system and affirm the role of tangata whenua as shared decision-makers and kaitiaki (guardians). The party will also implement strong evidence-based limits for ecosystem health.

statement: Improve endometriosis treatment
why: This party says that that women face disparities in healthcare, especially for pelvic pain conditions and endometriosis.
how: This party would work towards diagnosing and treating endometriosis faster. It would develop formal clinical guidelines for diagnosing and treating endometriosis, and fund specialist clinics for endometriosis across NZ.

statement: Create wrap-around services for new parents
why: This party says that that single mothers are vulnerable to hardship and need more support.
how: This party would fund a one-stop-shop service for new parents, providing pā harakeke wrap-around suppport for whānau during pregnancy, after birth, in early childhood, and throughout parenthood.  This is in addition to its policy to extent paid parental leave.

statement: Amend the definition of consent to be free and voluntary
why: This party says that that gender-based violence is increasing and women and gender minorities should be safe, respected and valued.
how: This party would amend the Crimes Act to amend the definition of consent and affirm that consent must be free and voluntary, and can be withdrawn at any time.

statement: Criminalise coercive control
why: This party says that that gender-based violence is increasing and women and gender minorities should be safe, respected and valued.
how: This party would amend the Crimes Act to criminalise coercive control.

statement: Extend paid parental leave to 15 months
why: This party says that women and families deserve to be safe and supported. Women deserve to get paid for their work, and compensated for time at home carrying out the essential work of caregiving.
how: This party would increase paid parental leave to 15 months for the primary caregiver, and have additional ring-fenced leave for partners. This party would also increase payments.

statement: Fill empty stores by changing retail lease rules and addressing vacant buildings
why: This party says that towns and cities need help to keep their centres vibrant. Empty shops are apparent on most main streets because of high rents set when the market was stronger. Many commercial leases don't allow for a rent review below the level set.
how:
This party would ensure market rent reviews can lower rents as well as raise them. This will apply to both new and existing leases for businesses with a turnover of under $30m. 
It would also give councils the power to auction leases on shops that have been empty for more than a year, and a low-cost tribunal will be established for commercial lease disputes.

statement: Recognise Palestine as a state and sanction Israel
why: This party says that that NZ should be an independent voice against global atrocities, authoritarians, and imperialist ambitions. This party says most United Nations member states have already recognised Palestinian statehood.
how: This party would recognise Palestine as a state and pass a bill drafted by this party to sanction Israel.

statement: Rewrite foreign policy to oppose imperialism
why: This party says that war and authoritarianism is rising globally, and NZ should be an independent voice for peace, freedom, democracy, and should speak out against nuclear weapons and American militarism. This party says foreign policy should challenge imperialism that creates chaos and hardship, and should always support countries facing conflicts and human rights abuses.
how: This party would withdraw NZ from the Five Eyes security alliance and decline to participate in AUKUS, as part of efforts to step away from military and security frameworks with the United States. This party would rewrite NZ's foreign policy to stand against human rights abuses and focus on upholding peace and justice, and would have the Defence Force focus on climate change, humanitarian responses and environmental monitoring.

statement: Support sovereignty and independence in the Asia-Pacific
why: This party says that that NZ should work with Pacific neighbours to create a greener, safer, and more just world. This party says NZ should be a world leader on issues of climate action, protection of nature and indigenous and human rights, and should work to uphold the international rule of law and collective obligations towards issues like climate change.
how: This party would support Pacific sovereignty, independence, and oppose militarisation in the Pacific. This party would also support decolonisation and democracy movements globally, including those of indigenous peoples in Asia-Pacific region and work to urgently progress climate change initiatives through international institutions. It would support calls for West Papua to be independent of Indonesia, and for French-ruled Polynesian islands to be independent and call for an indigenous-led human rights investigation and a visit from the UN's Special Rapporteur on the Rights of Indigenous People

statement: Increase democratic scrutiny of trade agreements
why: This party says that that NZ should have an independent approach to foreign affairs and trade that focuses on climate action, nature protection, indigenous and human rights.
how: This party would implement a suite of measures including increased democratic scrutiny of trade agreements, and enforceable recognition of Te Tiriti o Waitangi obligations, workers’ rights, human rights and climate commitments in trade agreements.

statement: Decriminalise cannabis for personal use
why: This party says that harmful drug use must be treated first as a health issue, rather than a criminal justice issue. While there can be adverse consequences from drug use, not all drug use is abusive or problematic, and evidence indicates making substance use illegal makes it harder for people to seek help. In terms of drugs, cannabis causes far less harm than alcohol, methamphetamine, cocaine, or tobacco.
how:
This party would regulate cannabis for legal personal use, with a legal age limit. Previous criminal convictions for these offences are removed from all records. Cultivation for personal use would generally be no longer illegal, and an evidence-based approach would be taken on which regulatory model best minimises harm. This includes improving drug-driving laws and providing education on the harmful effects of heavy or prolonged cannabis use.
Medicinal cannabis would be accessible and affordable for patients.

statement: Increase free public health services
why: This party says that everyone should have reliable access to public healthcare, including during and after civil emergencies. This party says hospitals and GP clinics are stretched and over-capacity, and suffering from under-investment from successive Governments. It says private provider costs in healthcare are preventing people from seeking help early, causing health issues to escalate.
how: This party would work towards free public primary healthcare and dental care, that can be accessed by everyone. They would increase focus on prevention and early screening, early diagnosis and treatment of non-communicable diseases, such as kidney disease, cancers, diabetes, cardiovascular and respiratory diseases. This party would fund the creation of mobile clinics for health care, mental health, diagnostic services and dental vans, for rural communities and during and after civil emergencies, including by-Māori, for-Māori community clinics. This party would also increase funding for data an

statement: Improve wages and staffing for health providers
why: This party says that that under-investment in health services has led to an understaffed hospital workforce and GP clinics that can't accept new enrollments. They say there are unsafe conditions for health workers and lengthy wait times. This party says everyone should be able to access timely healthcare from a supported workforce
how: This party would ensure all health workers have fair wages. They would fund pay parity for primary care and hauora providers. This party would set safe staffing levels, to improve worker wellbeing and quality of care.

statement: Increase funding for Pharmac
why: This party says that that Pharmac should invest in new health care devices and medicines so that treatment and quality of life for patients improves.
how: This party would increase sustained funding for Pharmac.

statement: Expand the conditions that pharmacies can treat
why: This party says that that pharmacists should help treat common health issues and should be encouraged to give appropriate medical advice. This party says they should be compensated fairly to do so.
how: This party would Expand the Minor Health Conditions Service to help pharmacies treat common health issues, and update the Integrated community pharmacy services agreement to compensate pharmacists fairly.

statement: Support migrant workers to residency
why: This party says that that people coming to NZ for work should have fair and achievable pathways to residence. The party says that migrant workers are not disposable, yet they face exploitation, are denied basic rights and are unfairly targeted by immigration compliance officers.
how: This party would create new residency pathways for migrants who have settled in NZ long-term, including those whose visas have expired. This party would also allow migrant work visa holders to switch employers and would end the 12-month stand-down period requiring workers to leave the country between visas.

statement: Abolish acceptable standards of health requirements for migrants and refugees
why: This party says that says that migrants and refugees with health conditions or disabilities are discriminated against by the acceptable standards of health requirements.
how: This party would abolish the Acceptable Standards of Health requirements for visa applicants.

statement: Support families of migrants and refugees to get visas
why: This party says that says that nobody should be unfairly separated from their families or communities. This party says people who flee war or persecution to seek asylum in New Zealand should be supported and treated with dignity.
how: This party would clear the backlog for refugee family reunification, including resourcing Immigration New Zealand to clear the backlog of tier 1 and 2 family reunification categories and process asylum claims quickly. This party would restore birthright citizenship, expand work rights for partners, remove income barriers to supporting a parent visa, and stop detention and electronic monitoring of asylum seekers.

statement: Increase the refugee quota
why: This party says that that people who fear for their life in their country, should be supported to seek a better life in NZ. They say people escaping war or persecution should be supported to rebuild their lives as part of our communities.
how: This party would progressively increase the refugee quota to 5,000 by 2029. This party would also increase funding for refugee resettlement programmes and create a new humanitarian visa for family of New Zealanders in conflict zones.

statement: Create an immigration system based on Te Tiriti o Waitangi
why: This party says migrants and refugees should be supported to rebuild their lives in NZ.
how: This party would implement Māori aspirations for an immigration system based on Te Tiriti o Waitangi. It would develop resources and decision-making with iwi and hapū to strengthen traditional whanaungatanga connections. This party would also provide Te Tiriti education to new migrants and refugees.

statement: Increase benefit payments and improve standards for beneficaries
why: This party says that everyone has a right to a liveable income that guarantees enough for food, safe housing and good quality of life. This party says the cost of living has got worse, and thousands of children go to bed hungry and families are struggling to pay rent or mortgages.
how: This party would increase benefits to liveable rates and individualise benefit entitlements. This party would also abolish benefit sanctions. The party would reform the Social Security Act to uphold dignity of people seeking support and ensure everyone has a secure income, and implement a high-trust working model at work and income. This party would also overhaul recoverable assistance grants, write off existing debt to MSD and ban attachment orders against beneficiaries.

statement: Introduce a tax for net wealth over $10m
why: This party says a wealth tax is part of a fairer tax system, that can reduce income inequality and ensure everyone has enough to live. This party says multi-millionaires pay $9 in tax for every $100 they make, while teachers pay $22 in tax for every $100 they make. This party says a wealth tax makes super-rich New Zealanders pay a fair share.
how: This party would introduce a 2.5 percent tax on net wealth worth over $10m, with an exemption for the family home.

statement: Expand ACC to cover income support and treatment
why: This party says that that everyone deserves a livable income if they are unemployed, disabled, sick or a caregiver.
how: This party would extend ACC to cover income support and treatment for injuries, disability and illness, regardless of origin.

statement: Strengthen working for families
why: This party says that that families are struggling to pay rent or mortgages, to feed their children, or to warm their homes, as the cost of living has worsened. This party says that families should be looked after at every stage of life.
how: This party would increase the working for families rate, reduce abatements and extend tax credits to families who are unemployed.

statement: Prioritise rehabilitation for convicted offenders
why: This party says that rehabilitation is important to keep communities safe. It says current approaches to justice neglect rehabilitation, which causes more harm and hardship for communities.
how: This party would resource evidence-based rehabilitation for anyone convicted of an offence. Tikanga based and restorative justice solutions, like Te Pae Oranga, would be available to anyone to access. This party would also improve community re-integration support for offenders leaving the criminal justice system, and would increase the Steps to Freedom grant to cover at least 30 years of inflation.

statement: Increase accountability in policing
why: This party says that the justice system should be safe, equitable and fair. This party aims to meet the basic needs of communities in order to prevent crime happening in the first place.
how: This party would require body cameras for frontline police and strengthen the powers of the Independent Police Conduct Authority. The party would also deliver de-escalation and trauma training for police, and increase resourcing for Māori Wardens and Pacific Wardens.

statement: End military-style academies for young offenders
why: This party says that says the justice system should be fair and equitable. This party says people should not be punished for being poor, and communities are safer when young people have access to food, healthcare, education and have a safe home environment.
how: This party would end military-style academies for young people and raise the age of criminal responsibility. This party would also ban young people being detained alongside adults. This party would expand access to specialist youth courts, including the Rangatahi and Pasifika Courts, Alcohol and Other Drug Treatment Court, and New Beginnings Court, so young people across NZ could access them.

statement: Improve accessibility to justice and legal assistance
why: This party says that the justice system should be fair and equitable, and communities should be supported to prevent crime happening in the first place.
how: This party would expand the district court initiative, Te Ao Marama, to all courts in New Zealand. This party would also extend legal aid and duty lawyers, better resource community law centres and make applications for protection and parenting orders free.

statement: Extend hate speech laws
why: This party says that that everyone deserves to live free from violence, harm and discrimination.
how: This party would extend hate speech laws to cover religion, gender, disability and rainbow communities. This party would implement this alongside other recommendations of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into the Terrorist Attack on Christchurch Mosques on 15 March 2019.

statement: Implement the recommendations of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into the Terrorist Attack on Christchurch Mosques on 15 March 2019
why: This party says that that everyone deserves to live free from violence, harm and discrimination.
how: This party would implement all recommendations from the royal commission of inquiry, including passing hate speech laws, and continuing to oppose possession of military-style semi-automatic firearms.

statement: Implement recommendations of Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care
why: This party says that that the Royal Commission of Inquiry into abuse in care was a harrowing account of how society and the Government failed, and must change. The party says survivors have called for all 138 recommendations to be implemented.
how: This party would implement all recommendations of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care, in consultation with people with lived experience of abuse in care.

statement: Ban alcohol advertising and sponsorship
why: This party says that says it is important to take an evidenced, harm-reduction approach to alcohol and drugs.
how: This party would would phase out all alcohol advertising and sponsorship, including at sporting and cultural events, and use funding from the alcohol levy to establish a national harm-reduction campaign.

statement: Enable licensing for psychedelic treatment
why: This party says that the 'war on drugs' approach from 50 years ago has increased harm and addictions, and diverts money away from public health services. This party supports an evidence-based approach that prioritises people's health.
how: This party would enable a licensing system for psychedelic treatment, and recognise taonga status of our native psylocibin (magic mushroom) species.

statement: Reduce nicotine availability and fund culturally responsive services to quit smoking and vaping
why: This party says that that funding for addiction services should be increased, and NZ should take a harm-reduction approach to alcohol and drugs. This party believes young people should be protected from nicotine by stronger regulations for retailers.
how: This party would phase out nicotine availability and fund culturally responsive vaping and smoking cessation services. This party would also implement stronger regulation and enforcement for nicotine retailers.

statement: Restore pay equity and negotiate a settlement for care workers
why: This party says that the previous pay equity law better protected care and support workers who look after disabled people, older people and some of the most vulnerable people in New Zealand every day. However, this law was changed in 2025, and since then, these workers have been undervalued. This party believes a carer's pay should reflect the skill and responsibility their jobs demand.
how: This party would restore the pay equity law to its pre-previous-government form. The party would also fund the settlement for the approximately 65,000 care and support workers whose claim was stopped after those changes were made to the law by passing legislation to settle the claim. The final settlement would be agreed through bargaining with the workers and their unions. This party estimates that this policy would cost $1.1 billion a year.

statement: Make public transport free for children and other specified people and cap fares at $2 for adults
why: This party says that New Zealanders deserve a fast, convenient and affordable transport system. It believes that years of underinvestment in public transport have left our cities harder to get around without a car. However, it says our cities have the potential to be accessible, vibrant and connected for locals and visitors. This will make it easier and more affordable for people to get where they need to go using cleaner modes of transport, also helping to cut greenhouse gas emissions.
how: This party would make bus and train fares free for children, teenagers, students, apprentices, Community Service Card holders, and Total Mobility Users, and cap bus and train fares at $2 for adults.

statement: Create improved public transport services between regions
why: This party says that the fuel crisis is costing ordinary people every time they travel. We need transport alternatives that are more affordable, fast, frequent, and reliable. It says communities are currently designed to prioritise working best for cars, when they should be designed to work best for people.
how: This party would fund up to 150 new regional bus services to supplement existing services, extend the Te Huia train to Tauranga with track and tunnel improvements and pilot an overnight passenger train service between Wellington and Auckland. It would also bring back the Southerner train connection between Christchurch and Dunedin.

statement: Improve public transport within cities
why: This party says that New Zealanders spend too much time and money sitting in traffic, filling up the car, and waiting for trains and buses. This party says there needs to be more affordable and accessible alternatives to driving a car.
how: This party would deliver immediate improvements to bus routes along the planned Mass Rapid Transit routes in Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch and plan and deliver light rail or bus rapid transit in line with the Infrastructure Commission’s preferred option. The party would also fund Wellington’s critical rail renewal work needed to fix broken-down track assets and infrastructure. It would lastly work with Auckland Transport to fund and deliver level crossing removals to allow for more frequent trains, fewer delays, and better safety outcomes.

statement: Fund public transport for the regions
why: This party says that regions are often left behind when it comes to public transport infrastructure upgrades, with the focus on major cities. It says that communities living in smaller towns also deserve the opportunity to access affordable and accessible public transport.
how: This party would fund the planned bus improvements in smaller cities and towns in the Waikato, Bay of Plenty, Taranaki, Horowhenua, and Otago. It would also work to revitalise town and city centres and increase safe walking and biking infrastructure.

statement: Fund and deliver level crossing removals in Auckland
why: This party says that over the last 10 years, there have been almost 70 crashes and hundreds of near-misses at level crossings across Auckland. Removing them will allow for better safety outcomes, more frequent trains and fewer delays.
how: This party would work with the Auckland Council to identify the best options to fund and deliver level crossing removals.

statement: Guarantee every 16-to 24-year-old who has been out of work for six months a pathway into education, training, or a new job
why: This party says that youth unemployment is at nearly 15 per cent, roughly three times that of the wider working-age population, which is at an 11-year high. Yet there is so much work to be done in New Zealand. This party says it does not make sense, with nearly 100,000 young people not in employment, training or education. A long period without a job at the start of a working life also lowers a person’s wages for years afterwards.
how: This party would establish the Jobs for Young People pilot programme, based on the successful Jobs for Nature model, to support new jobs in businesses, councils, iwi, non-profits or the public sector. It would also scale up funding of the Mayor's Taskforce for Jobs for all 67 councils, connecting young people with local businesses, community organisations, iwi and hapū. Lastly, it would make sure there is a national workforce strategy plan for young people.

statement: Ensure AI does not replace human judgement or democratic decision-making
why: This party says that artificial intelligence should support human judgement, not replace it. Decisions that affect people's rights, welfare, health, education, employment, or access to public services must remain subject to meaningful human oversight and appeal.
how: This party would require public registers of AI systems used by government agencies with full transparency around AI use, including where in policy processes it has been used, and where or how it has been used to inform decisions. The party would ensure people are held accountable for AI decisions and that everyone has a right to challenge AI-assisted decisions, and to opt out of being subject to AI-assisted decision- making.

statement: Refrain from purchasing or deploying autonomous weapons
why: This party says that Artificial intelligence should support human judgement, not replace it, especially when it concerns warfare and the implications of that for the life and wellbeing of humans.
how: This party would refuse to purchase or deploy autonomous weapons systems and support an international ban on these, in the same way the international community has banned chemical and biological weapons.

statement: Protect data sovereignty
why: This party says that data is a taonga (treasure). The party believes that New Zealanders, iwi, hapū, communities, and creators should retain meaningful control over how data about them is used. Language in particular is crucial to identity and culture, and must be protected from AI.
how: This party would enforce explicit consent standards for AI training data, where appropriate remuneration must be provided for any Intellectual property used for training AI models. The party would ensure there are fines for any breaches, with the Privacy Commissioner given more power to enforce NZ's privacy laws. Government AI systems would be transparent, and there would be specific regulations requiring co-governance and co-development of Māori data and IP to protect Māori data sovereignty. Lastly, private information provided to the government and classified government will not be sent to t

statement: Place limits on AI data centres' use of water and electricity
why: This party says that while AI seems like a virtual technology, it actually consumes large amounts of resources, taking up land, using water to cool servers and requiring electricity to power data centres. This party says that any data centres based in New Zealand would need to follow strict regulations to protect the environment.
how: This party would require AI data centres to report on their environmental impact before being built. New facilities would be required to provide new renewable energy to cover their electricity use and their would be community consultation during the consenting process. To increase transparency, this party would require data centres to report their water use publicly.

statement: Ensure news companies are paid by AI companies for their use of AI
why: This party says that AI carries many risks, and can impact how information is understood. It says that news companies generate information and should be compensated by digital AI companies for how much information journalists generate ends up in AI summaries or responses.
how: This party would update and pass the Fair Digital News Bargaining Bill, requiring AI companies pay local media outlets for data used in their AI summaries.

statement: Encourage the adoption of multiple types of AI
why: This party says that AI companies can concentrate economic power, leading to bad outcomes for workers and individuals. These risks should be regulated by government.
how: This party would encourage the use of public-interest and open-source AI models wherever possible, and mandate the use of multiple and interchangeable AI models to prevent vendor lock-in. It would encourage the use of NZ-based and NZ-focussed large language models, rather than relying on AI tools from overseas companies.

statement: Protect children and worker's rights in the use of AI
why: This party says that AI can concentrate economic power and impact individuals and communities. Power should not be concentrated, and the use of AI should not be at the expense of children and worker's rights.
how: This party would ensure children are not forced to use AI, especially at school, and broadly make sure that AI use around kids is in line with the UNCRC’s Joint Statement on Artificial Intelligence and the Rights of the Child. It would also require that workers are consulted about AI use in their workplace.

statement: Create an AI office and require transparent AI use
why: This party says that people have a right to know when they are interacting with AI and how it is being used. AI content should always be clearly labelled so that people understand when they are using an AI model.
how: This party would create labelling requirements for artificial intelligence, and audit algorithms for high-risk AI systems, so there is monitoring of AI use in the public sector. It would create an AI office within the department of prime minister and cabinet (DPMC) and aim to eventually establish an AI commission with independent powers to conduct audits assurance and education regarding AI use. This party would also collaborate with international best practice like the EU AI Act and build on NZ's work in the Christchurch Call to cooperate with like-minded countries regarding AI regulation and

statement: Resource evidence-based rehabilitation for anyone convicted of an offence, and ensure tikanga-based and restorative justice solutions (such as Te Pae Oranga) are available to anyone who wishes to access these.
why: Justice and Community Safety — Keeping communities safe through prevention and rehabilitation.

statement: Expand Te Ao Mārama to all courts in Aotearoa, and ensure specialist youth courts including the Rangatahi and Pasifika Courts, Alcohol and Other Drug Treatment Court, and New Beginnings Court are available to all who wish to access them.
why: Justice and Community Safety — Keeping communities safe through prevention and rehabilitation.

statement: End military-style academies, raise the age of criminal responsibility and ban the detention of young people in the company of adults in all circumstances.
why: Justice and Community Safety — Keeping communities safe through prevention and rehabilitation.

statement: Require body cameras for frontline police, strengthen powers for the Independent Police Conduct Authority, deliver de-escalation and trauma training for police, and increase resourcing for Māori Wardens and Pacific Wardens.
why: Justice and Community Safety — Keeping communities safe through prevention and rehabilitation.

statement: Improve community reintegration support for people leaving the criminal justice system, including housing, and increase the Steps to Freedom Grant to cover at least 30 years of inflation.
why: Justice and Community Safety — Keeping communities safe through prevention and rehabilitation.

statement: Extend legal aid and duty lawyers, better resource community law centres and make applications for protection and parenting orders free.
why: Justice and Community Safety — Keeping communities safe through prevention and rehabilitation.

statement: Implement the recommendations of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into the Terrorist Attack on Christchurch Mosques on 15 March 2019. Extend hate speech laws to cover religion, gender, disability and rainbow communities. Continue to oppose possession of military-style semi-automatic firearms.
why: Justice and Community Safety — Keeping communities safe through prevention and rehabilitation.

statement: Implement all recommendations of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care, in consultation with people with lived experience.
why: Justice and Community Safety — Keeping communities safe through prevention and rehabilitation.

statement: Strengthen local electoral democracy by transferring administration of local government elections to the Electoral Commission, enabling 16-year-olds to vote and requiring the use of a single transferable voting system.
why: Local Government — Empowering local democracy.

statement: Reinforce councils’ responsibility to give effect to Te Tiriti o Waitangi by making the role of local government as a Te Tiriti partner explicit, and reinstate their ability to keep Māori wards for their districts.
why: Local Government — Empowering local democracy.

statement: Reject the proposed rates cap and enable a range of new funding and financing tools, such as a bed levy, congestion charging and GST from rates and growth.
why: Local Government — Empowering local democracy.

statement: Ensure that the ‘four wellbeings’ (social, economic, environmental and cultural) are core to the purpose of local government and empower councils by devolving further responsibilities from central government, with appropriate resourcing.
why: Local Government — Empowering local democracy.

statement: Enable greater use of community-based decision-making processes — such as citizens’ assemblies — including greater community input in the process for local government reorganisation.
why: Local Government — Empowering local democracy.

statement: Devolve power and redistribute resources back to tangata whenua in recognition that Māori are the decision-makers and facilitators of the destiny of their own whānau, hapū and iwi.
why: Māori Centred — By Māori, for Māori.

statement: Invest in outcomes that minimise the disparities and inequities tangata whenua face across the majority of social and economic outcomes.
why: Māori Centred — By Māori, for Māori.

statement: Resource marae through a Marae Resilience Fund for Māori to lead initiatives for their people, wāhi tapu (sacred sites) and whenua in accordance with their own tikanga. Create ongoing funding for provisions for civil emergencies in recognition of being consistent community lifelines.
why: Māori Centred — By Māori, for Māori.

statement: End perpetual leases on whenua Māori and amend the Public Works Act to prevent the acquisition of Māori freehold land, Māori customary land and lands within a reasonable proximity to marae, urupā and wāhi tapu.
why: Māori Centred — By Māori, for Māori.

statement: Expand the learning, speaking and promotion of te reo Māori in both formal and informal settings to encourage the widespread use of the language across the nation.
why: Māori Centred — By Māori, for Māori.

statement: Expand free mental health services to all communities so everyone can access support when they need it. This includes expanding youth services like Piki, Mana Ake and Youth One Stop Shops throughout Aotearoa, Asian Family Services and dedicated support for postnatal mental health.
why: Mental Health — A safe, supportive and accessible care system.

statement: Implement community care models and ensure mental health facilities are resourced adequately to enable phasing out the use of seclusion (solitary confinement) entirely, and increase the availability of early intervention to reduce the use of compulsory care.
why: Mental Health — A safe, supportive and accessible care system.

statement: Link primary health and secondary mental health services with clear referral pathways in every health region and focus on areas which have disproportionate need.
why: Mental Health — A safe, supportive and accessible care system.

statement: Protect at least 30% of New Zealand’s ocean territory by 2030 through reforming marine protected areas legislation to ensure it is fit for purpose and enables both tikanga-led tools consistent with Te Tiriti, and approaches to improve ocean health outcomes.
why: Oceans and Fisheries — Abundant oceans teeming with kaimoana.

statement: Phase out damaging fishing methods, starting by banning bottom trawling on seamounts, and banning set netting and dredging.
why: Oceans and Fisheries — Abundant oceans teeming with kaimoana.

statement: Ban seabed mining in the coastal marine area and the exclusive economic zone and maintain pressure for a moratorium on seabed mining in international waters.
why: Oceans and Fisheries — Abundant oceans teeming with kaimoana.

statement: Embed kaitiakitanga Māori in marine policy and operational management. Resource iwi and hapū to lead oceans protection and implement mātauranga- and tikanga-based projects for ocean conservation.
why: Oceans and Fisheries — Abundant oceans teeming with kaimoana.

statement: Reduce fisheries bycatch of protected species by ensuring cameras are rolled out on the entire fishing fleet and by setting fisheries-related mortality limits.
why: Oceans and Fisheries — Abundant oceans teeming with kaimoana.

statement: Review the Quota Management System and move towards an ecosystem-based fisheries management model, in line with the Māori fisheries settlements.
why: Oceans and Fisheries — Abundant oceans teeming with kaimoana.

statement: Enable a tikanga-based pathway for people who whakapapa Māori to establish Aotearoa citizenship, regardless of country of residence or birth.
why: Overseas New Zealanders — Cultivating Kiwi connections around the world.

statement: Reduce and re-balance student loan repayments and interest rates for overseas student loan borrowers, extend the repayment holiday for overseas borrowers, and abolish border arrests for student loan repayment violations.
why: Overseas New Zealanders — Cultivating Kiwi connections around the world.

statement: Extend the time that overseas New Zealanders can spend outside Aotearoa without losing voting eligibility.
why: Overseas New Zealanders — Cultivating Kiwi connections around the world.

statement: Restore the 10-year period for time spent in Aotearoa New Zealand to be eligible for superannuation.
why: Overseas New Zealanders — Cultivating Kiwi connections around the world.

statement: Pursue reciprocal health care, welfare support and visa waiver arrangements with other countries, and widen existing agreements to include temporary visitors.
why: Overseas New Zealanders — Cultivating Kiwi connections around the world.

statement: Extend visa-free travel to Aotearoa for visitors from the Pacific Islands.
why: Pacific Peoples — Deepening connections and uplifting communities.

statement: Restore and increase the international climate aid funding Aotearoa contributes. Affirm and support calls by Pacific Island nations for stronger climate action in international negotiations.
why: Pacific Peoples — Deepening connections and uplifting communities.

statement: Resource tangata moana leadership on climate action within Aotearoa.
why: Pacific Peoples — Deepening connections and uplifting communities.

statement: Replace the Recognised Seasonal Employer Scheme with an alternative that gives Pacific workers access to fair wages, housing and essential services, and provides for open work rights and residency pathways rather than being tied to a single employer.
why: Pacific Peoples — Deepening connections and uplifting communities.

statement: Support the independence of West Papua and French-occupied Polynesia. Call for an Indigenous-led human rights investigation and a visit from the Special Rapporteur on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples.
why: Pacific Peoples — Deepening connections and uplifting communities.

statement: Support Pacific Island states with their marine protection initiatives, including by increasing funding support for the South Pacific Regional Environment Programme and supporting marine protected areas in the Pacific Ocean under the High Seas Treaty.
why: Pacific Peoples — Deepening connections and uplifting communities.

statement: Uphold Te Tiriti throughout the work of the public service, and fund Māori organisations, iwi, hapū and marae to run community and environmental initiatives that meet the needs and aspirations unique to their rohe (region).
why: Public Services — Strong essential services accessible to everyone.

statement: Fund public services adequately to ensure that they are able to work in service of the public good, and that public services (and state-owned enterprises) remain in public hands.
why: Public Services — Strong essential services accessible to everyone.

statement: Reform the public finance system to ensure that the fiscal management approach supports New Zealand’s long-term resilience, the productive capacity of our economy, and an ensures the health and well-being of everyone.
why: Public Services — Strong essential services accessible to everyone.

statement: Affirm the importance of advocacy and monitoring done by independent commissions with expertise in an area, starting with restoring the monitoring role of the Children’s Commissioner alongside its advocacy function.
why: Public Services — Strong essential services accessible to everyone.

statement: Introduce standardised career progression, pay, community secondment opportunities and training across the public sector to improve staff retention and skills development, and ensure equal pay for equivalent roles.
why: Public Services — Strong essential services accessible to everyone.

statement: Provide secure, flexible and full funding arrangements for the community sector, recognising the value of the work, and ensuring independence within a supportive legislative framework.
why: Public Services — Strong essential services accessible to everyone.

statement: Improve training in Te Tiriti and te reo Māori for all public servants, resulting in consistency across all agencies.
why: Public Services — Strong essential services accessible to everyone.

statement: Ensure that the public service is a leader in disability-responsive employment, including by providing resources and training to meet access needs and counter ableism.
why: Public Services — Strong essential services accessible to everyone.

statement: Work with the different rainbow communities to develop appropriate health care services and strategies built cultural values and holistic models of care and wellbeing.
why: Rainbow Communities — Rainbow communities thriving with freedom, equality and respect.

statement: Increase resourcing for rainbow organisations, including dedicated support for Māori and Pasifika-led organisations, to support the development and delivery of services that reflect the diverse needs, values, and strengths of rainbow communities.
why: Rainbow Communities — Rainbow communities thriving with freedom, equality and respect.

statement: Resource clear pathways for timely, free, non-discriminatory access to all forms of gender-affirming health care based on informed consent and self-determination, including reversal of the ban on puberty blockers.
why: Rainbow Communities — Rainbow communities thriving with freedom, equality and respect.

statement: Promote the human rights of takatāpui, intersex and rainbow people, amending the Human Rights Act to clarify that all forms of sexual orientation, gender identity and variations in sex characteristics, are prohibited grounds of discrimination, and implement the Law Commission’s Ia Tangata report recommendations.
why: Rainbow Communities — Rainbow communities thriving with freedom, equality and respect.

statement: Prohibit all non-consensual and medically unnecessary surgeries or medical interventions on intersex people.
why: Rainbow Communities — Rainbow communities thriving with freedom, equality and respect.

statement: Reform laws and policies so rainbow asylum seekers, refugees and migrants can access legal gender recognition, partnership recognition, family reunification, and resettlement support.
why: Rainbow Communities — Rainbow communities thriving with freedom, equality and respect.

statement: Launch a dedicated long-term strategy for the needs of an ageing population which encompasses the holistic wellbeing of kaumātua, elder abuse prevention, ensuring income is equitably accessed and sufficient to live comfortably, and the establishment of a state-owned, not-for-profit retirement village scheme.
why: Seniors — Happy, healthy and supported.

statement: Increase funding for community spaces and the establishment of facilities, programmes, education and volunteering opportunities that are accessible to seniors.
why: Seniors — Happy, healthy and supported.

statement: Expanding housing options by building more papakāinga, prioritising kaumātua on social housing waitlists, and ensuring housing designs are suitable for their needs — single-level and warm, with mobility features and room for intergenerational living.
why: Seniors — Happy, healthy and supported.

statement: Ensure support services are grounded in cultural values, and that home and community care workers are well trained, supported and paid equitably and fairly by including travel time.
why: Seniors — Happy, healthy and supported.

statement: Resource Māori, Pacific and migrant organisations to provide kaumātua care that is aligned with their values, cultural practices and tikanga.
why: Seniors — Happy, healthy and supported.

statement: Revitalise ‘Buy Kiwi Made’ and expand country of origin labelling so it’s easier to support local businesses.
why: Small Business — Championing small, local enterprise.

statement: Commit government departments to buying more goods and services from Aotearoa businesses.
why: Small Business — Championing small, local enterprise.

statement: Foster sustainable, low-carbon jobs in the information and communication technology sector by expanding access to grants and rebates for smaller sized firms.
why: Small Business — Championing small, local enterprise.

statement: Continue to invest in community-led regional development with a focus on sustainable building, regenerative agriculture and horticulture, improving low-carbon infrastructure, and iwi- and hapū-led economic activity.
why: Small Business — Championing small, local enterprise.

statement: Reform competition laws to create a fairer playing field for small businesses and to benefit consumers. Increase the resources and powers of regulatory agencies to investigate anti-competitive practice.
why: Small Business — Championing small, local enterprise.

statement: Amend the Treaty of Waitangi Act to recognise that Te Tiriti is the authoritative text and that Te Tiriti works in conjunction with He Whakaputanga o te Rangatiratanga o Nu Tireni.
why: Te Tiriti o Waitangi — Advancing an Aotearoa that embraces Te Tiriti.

statement: Implement genuine Te Tiriti-based decision-making models across government and resource iwi and hapū to participate as partners rather than as advisors.
why: Te Tiriti o Waitangi — Advancing an Aotearoa that embraces Te Tiriti.

statement: Reform the Treaty Settlements process by amending the settlement policy guide for negotiators to enable fair negotiations and just reparations without ceding sovereignty, removing any clauses that refer to ‘Full and Final settlement’, ending the ‘large natural grouping’ approach to Treaty settlements, and validating hapū rangatiratanga.
why: Te Tiriti o Waitangi — Advancing an Aotearoa that embraces Te Tiriti.

statement: Increase resourcing for the Waitangi Tribunal, providing them with the power to make binding recommendations for the return of Crown and Private land to iwi, whānau and hapū.
why: Te Tiriti o Waitangi — Advancing an Aotearoa that embraces Te Tiriti.

statement: Facilitate the return of whenua outside of Treaty Settlements that was wrongfully alienated from tangata whenua, including through exploring a right-of-first-refusal process that enables the return of private land to iwi, hapū and whānau at point of sale.
why: Te Tiriti o Waitangi — Advancing an Aotearoa that embraces Te Tiriti.

statement: Support students with a universal student income, including at postgraduate level, and ensure courses that require work placements pay students at least the living wage.
why: Tertiary Education — Opportunities for everyone to learn and grow.

statement: Overhaul funding for the tertiary sector to ensure it delivers rigorous research, a wide range of course options, quality teaching, comprehensive student services, decent pay and conditions for staff, and full participation of disabled students.
why: Tertiary Education — Opportunities for everyone to learn and grow.

statement: Empower polytechnics with adequate funding and strong local control to meet workforce and community needs, and protect courses, campuses and staff from cuts.
why: Tertiary Education — Opportunities for everyone to learn and grow.

statement: Expand free apprenticeship programmes, reduce student loan repayments and work towards fees-free tertiary education and a student debt write-off.
why: Tertiary Education — Opportunities for everyone to learn and grow.

statement: Return to default student union membership and develop a governance model for tertiary organisations in which staff, students, communities and tangata whenua govern together.
why: Tertiary Education — Opportunities for everyone to learn and grow.

statement: Transform public transport networks, including building mass rapid transit in Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch, and providing comprehensive bus lanes in all cities.
why: Transport — Easy, sustainable ways to get around.

statement: Invest in nationwide rapid rail for passengers and freight to connect regions and major cities and contribute to economic development and decarbonisation.
why: Transport — Easy, sustainable ways to get around.

statement: Introduce targeted subsidies for e-cargo bikes. Introduce e-bike sharing schemes in community hubs, to allow more families to save on transport costs.
why: Transport — Easy, sustainable ways to get around.

statement: Fund affordable, reliable, interregional rural bus services, and on-demand public transport, including by-Māori for-Māori public transport to serve kōhanga reo and rural schools.
why: Transport — Easy, sustainable ways to get around.

statement: Extend Community Connect to provide free fares for students and apprentices, community service card holders, everyone under 18, and all Total Mobility card holders.
why: Transport — Easy, sustainable ways to get around.

statement: Enable the provision of transport services publicly instead of for profit by replacing the Public Transport Operating Model.
why: Transport — Easy, sustainable ways to get around.

statement: Create safe walking and biking routes to all community hubs including schools through building more bike lanes and safe crossings, and lowering speed limits near schools.
why: Transport — Easy, sustainable ways to get around.

statement: Implement a phase-out date for the import of fossil-fuel powered vehicles, build more EV (electric vehicle) charging stations, remove regulatory barriers to EV car-sharing and re-introduce incentives for EV uptake.
why: Transport — Easy, sustainable ways to get around.

statement: Prioritise violence responses and prevention by improving workforce and broader public understanding of the drivers and signs of violence, and how to respond in ways that enhance safety and healing.
why: Violence Prevention — Keeping whānau and communities safe.

statement: Restore relationship and sexuality teaching guidelines — including education on healthy relationships, diverse identities and sexualities, and affirmative consent — in all schools.
why: Violence Prevention — Keeping whānau and communities safe.

statement: Increase funding for counselling and mental health support for victims, whānau, witnesses, defendants and legal professionals engaging in the justice system.
why: Violence Prevention — Keeping whānau and communities safe.

statement: Create a new Commissioner for Animals to independently monitor and advocate for the rights of animals, and an independent ministry.
why: Welfare of Animals — Caring for all animals that call Aotearoa home.

statement: Phase out harmful activities including debeaking of hens, intensive winter grazing, factory farming, octopus farming, farrowing crates and rodeo.
why: Welfare of Animals — Caring for all animals that call Aotearoa home.

statement: Require that imported products meet the animal welfare standards of Aotearoa, including for cosmetics.
why: Welfare of Animals — Caring for all animals that call Aotearoa home.

statement: Introduce consistent, clear and enforceable standards for manufacturing claims about animal welfare and ingredients (such as ‘free range’, ‘cruelty free’ and ‘vegan’).
why: Welfare of Animals — Caring for all animals that call Aotearoa home.

statement: Retain the ban on live exports of farmed animals by sea and extend the ban to include live exports of farmed animals by air and wild-caught animals such as endangered tuna longfin eels.
why: Welfare of Animals — Caring for all animals that call Aotearoa home.

statement: Strengthen worker bargaining power by changing employment law to default union membership. This means people automatically join a union when they start a new job, but can opt out later.
why: Workforce rights — Employment protections and decent pay for all workers.

statement: Expand the right to strike, including for breaches of collective agreements and political and solidarity reasons.
why: Workforce rights — Employment protections and decent pay for all workers.

statement: Strengthen employment law to protect all workers’ free time with a right to disconnect. Ensure protection from unwanted contact or surveillance out of working hours.
why: Workforce rights — Employment protections and decent pay for all workers.

statement: Explore legislating to put workers’ representatives on boards of publicly listed companies.
why: Workforce rights — Employment protections and decent pay for all workers.

statement: Guarantee annual minimum wage increases that at least keep up with inflation. Pay all publicly funded roles a living wage. Work towards matching the minimum wage to the living wage.
why: Workforce rights — Employment protections and decent pay for all workers.

statement: Protect platform and gig-economy workers by strengthening the test for whether a worker is a contractor.
why: Workforce rights — Employment protections and decent pay for all workers.

statement: Establish strong product policy measures, including mandatory product stewardship, a beverage container return scheme, phase-outs of problematic products and comprehensive right-to-repair.
why: Zero Waste — Building a sustainable circular economy.

statement: Direct revenue from the waste disposal levy into waste minimisation initiatives and stop diverting the local government portion to other purposes. Increase the levy to match international best practice and apply a consistent rate across all landfill classes.
why: Zero Waste — Building a sustainable circular economy.

statement: Introduce a moratorium on waste-to-energy plants and explore energy generation from biogas associated with animal and plant wastes.
why: Zero Waste — Building a sustainable circular economy.

statement: Build on proposed reforms of the Waste Minimisation Act to implement timely, binding, measurable and ambitious waste reduction targets. Ensure legislation gives effect to Te Tiriti o Waitangi. Introduce comprehensive duty-of-care systems for the waste and resource recovery sector covering all waste streams, including hazardous waste.
why: Zero Waste — Building a sustainable circular economy.

statement: Make greater use of discarded soil. Divert soil from landfills, where safe and appropriate to do so.
why: Zero Waste — Building a sustainable circular economy.

statement: Prioritise local, mana whenua and community-driven solutions to resource recovery, implementation of national zero-waste strategies, and organic waste reduction, diversion and processing.
why: Zero Waste — Building a sustainable circular economy.

statement: Easy Read version of the 2026 manifesto
how: An Easy Read (plain-language, illustrated) summary of the 2026 manifesto published in August 2026 for disabled people and others who prefer simplified text. It points readers to the full manifesto online.

statement: 'Drink Swim Fish' freshwater and oceans policy
how: A 4-page water policy (announced 6 July 2026) aimed at safe drinking water, swimmable rivers and healthier oceans: science-based national freshwater limits including lower nitrate limits, stronger wastewater-discharge rules, phasing out synthetic nitrogen fertiliser, phasing out bottom trawling and other destructive fishing, protecting at least 30% of oceans, and reviewing the fisheries quota system.

statement: Te Waonui a Tāne: an ongoing, protected funding source for marae
how: An 11-page policy (announced 9 August 2026) to recognise and resource marae as social and cultural infrastructure. It proposes a Rangatiratanga Trust with a $2.44 billion Crown funding input, including a $2 billion intergenerational fund (Te Tōtara Haemata) and annual restoration funding for marae, governed with regional marae representation.

statement: Youth Jobs Guarantee: a job or training pathway for every 16-24-year-old out of work for six months
how: A 7-page jobs policy (published October 2026) guaranteeing every 16-to-24-year-old who has been out of work for six months a pathway into a locally based job or training, delivered with councils and building on the Mayors Taskforce for Jobs. The document's indicative costings rise from $604m in the first year to $1,631m in the fourth.

statement: 'Safe, sovereign AI': regulate artificial intelligence for the public good
how: An 8-page AI plan (announced 12 October 2026). It proposes rules so that AI does not replace human or democratic decision-making (no fully automated decisions with substantive effects in public services), protects data sovereignty, privacy and creators' work, operates within environmental limits (including controls on data centres), shares benefits rather than concentrating them, and is transparent and accountable.

statement: Paid placements for trainee nurses, teachers and social workers; abolish the training wage for apprentices
how: A 4-page workforce policy (16-17 October 2026): a universal weekly payment for students during compulsory practical placements (nursing, teaching, social work and similar), relocation support, abolition of the training-wage exemption so apprentices get at least the minimum wage, a grant for apprentices' tools, and more pastoral support. Indicative costs are about $75-80m and $117m a year for the two parts.

statement: Bill to remove ring-net fishing exemption from Hauraki Gulf high protection areas
how: A 6-page draft member's bill (released 6 October 2026) amending the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection Act 2025 to remove the exemption that allows ring-net fishing in high protection areas, and to allow further management actions, developed with iwi, where protection objectives are not being met.

statement: Standing policy: Agriculture Policy
how: Standing party policy on farming: support farmers to reduce environmental harm and emissions, uphold Te Tiriti in sector governance, fair prices for producers, better data, and treat farm animals as sentient.

statement: Standing policy: Animal Welfare Policy
how: Standing party policy to align animal-welfare law with animals' needs (nutrition, environment, health, behaviour, mental state), strengthen oversight, reduce systemic exploitation of animals and recognise Māori kaitiaki relationships with animals.

statement: Standing policy: Arts, Culture and Heritage Policy
how: Standing party policy to resource the arts and heritage sector, protect traditional and contemporary Māori art, and expand arts education and platforms in schools and communities.

statement: Standing policy: Biodiversity and Environmental Regeneration Policy
