how: Standing party policy on conservation: protect threatened indigenous species from pests, disease and human activity, take a holistic approach to restoring ecosystems, and support tangata whenua as kaitiaki.

statement: Standing policy: Business Policy
how: Standing party policy on business: reform regulators, require accessibility, support the Māori economy and new business models, promote local business and co-invest in skills and research.

statement: Standing policy: Children’s Policy
how: Standing party policy on children: reform social support, extend paid parental leave, reform Working for Families and lift minimum entitlements with the aim of eliminating child poverty, and improve cross-government child protection.

statement: Standing policy: Climate Change Policy
how: Standing party climate policy: Te Tiriti-based solutions, energy efficiency and democratisation, low-carbon transport, a rapid fossil-fuel phase-out, more plant-based and resilient farming, an economy that does not rely on growth, and adaptation planning that prioritises the most vulnerable.

statement: Standing policy: Communities of Colour Policy
how: Standing party policy on working in partnership with people of colour and ethnic communities to meet their needs and aspirations and tackle racism.

statement: Standing policy: Community in the Economy Policy
how: Standing party policy on regional development, local economies and procurement, and on government relationships with, and funding of, the community and voluntary sector.

statement: Standing policy: Digital Policy
how: Standing party policy on equitable access to digital technology and data, with a harm-based approach to social media, AI and quantum computing, Te Tiriti and privacy/online-safety protections.

statement: Standing policy: Drug Policy
how: Standing party policy taking a harm-minimisation, health-based approach to alcohol and other drugs instead of criminal prohibition: accessible addiction treatment, a legal regulated cannabis market and drug-checking/education.

statement: Standing policy: Emergency Management Policy
how: Standing party policy on civil defence: resource agencies and communities to prepare for and respond to emergencies, strengthen infrastructure resilience, use local and Māori knowledge, prioritise vulnerable people and fund managed retreat from high-risk areas.

statement: Standing policy: Energy Policy
how: Standing party energy policy: reform electricity markets, support community energy ownership, legislate fossil-fuel reductions, electrify transport and heat, and expand efficiency and renewable supply.

statement: Standing policy: Food Policy
how: Standing party policy on the right to safe, affordable food, including Māori food practices, and a national food-system strategy for local resilience, less waste and lower emissions.

statement: Standing policy: Freshwater Policy
how: Standing party freshwater policy: Te Tiriti-centred, holistic protection and restoration of rivers, lakes, aquifers and wetlands.

statement: Standing policy: Global Affairs Policy
how: Standing party foreign-policy statement supporting an international rules-based order, human rights, environmental protection, disarmament and non-violent conflict resolution.

statement: Standing policy: Government in the Economy Policy
how: Standing party economic policy: a fairer tax system, universal public services and infrastructure, living within planetary limits, Māori economic justice and more public ownership and direct service provision.

statement: Standing policy: Housing and Sustainable Communities Policy
how: Standing party housing policy: a large government-run public housing programme, more Māori housing, accessible housing for disabled people, lower building emissions and regenerative urban development; housing treated as a right.

statement: Standing policy: Human Rights Policy
how: Standing party human-rights policy: strengthen tangata whenua rights, protect future generations, extend human-rights law and treaty commitments, and give courts and human-rights bodies more power.

statement: Standing policy: Immigration Policy
how: Standing party immigration policy: fair, flexible selection, dignity and fair employment for migrants, family reunification, and a firm commitment to refugees and asylum seekers.

statement: Standing policy: Justice Policy
how: Standing party justice policy: a system grounded in Te Tiriti and tikanga, prioritising restorative justice, rehabilitation, prevention and mental-health responses, tackling bias and improving access to justice.

statement: Standing policy: Land Use and Soils Policy
how: Standing party policy on land use: manage land under Te Tiriti, protect and regenerate soils, and minimise the impacts of mining.

statement: Standing policy: Livelihoods Policy
how: Standing party policy on income support: an adequate, accessible and dignified welfare system recognising unpaid work, regulation of lenders and debt help for low-income households.

statement: Standing policy: Marine Policy
how: Standing party oceans policy: Te Tiriti-based marine governance, precautionary ecosystem-based management, and protection and regeneration of marine ecosystems.

statement: Standing policy: Media Policy
how: Standing party media policy: support independent and community media, publicly owned broadcasting and funding for local content, prioritising under-served audiences including Māori and children.

statement: Standing policy: Overseas New Zealanders Policy
how: Standing party policy on the New Zealand diaspora: services and rights for New Zealanders abroad, connection with home and participation (including voting).

statement: Standing policy: Rainbow Policy
how: Standing party Rainbow policy built on the Te Whare Takatāpui framework, addressing discrimination and health and wellbeing for people of diverse genders, sexualities and sex characteristics.

statement: Standing policy: Recreation and Sport Policy
how: Standing party policy on equitable, publicly funded access to sport and recreation, and regulation of harmful activities including gambling.

statement: Standing policy: Rural Communities Policy
how: Standing party policy on rural communities: locally led solutions and access to public services that support rural wellbeing and ecosystems.

statement: Standing policy: Security and Defence Policy
how: Standing party defence and security policy: an independent, Pacific-oriented, non-violent approach; democratic oversight of security and intelligence agencies; and a defence force focused on peacekeeping, disaster relief, humanitarian work and environmental monitoring.

statement: Standing policy: Seniors Policy
how: Standing party policy on older people: independence, connection, respect, equitable services and protection of cultural values for frail or dependent seniors.

statement: Standing policy: Tagata Moana Policy
how: Standing party policy on Pacific peoples (Tagata Moana): community and cultural connections and support for decolonising and reindigenising Pacific identities.

statement: Standing policy: Te Tiriti o Waitangi Policy
how: Standing party policy on honouring Te Tiriti o Waitangi, upholding Māori rights and supporting Māori development and constitutional transformation.

statement: Standing policy: Tourism Policy
how: Standing party tourism policy: sustainable, low-emission, community-benefiting tourism and Māori cultural tourism under tikanga and tino rangatiratanga.

statement: Standing policy: Trade and Foreign Investment Policy
how: Standing party trade policy: a global trade regime within ecological limits, enforceable human-rights and environmental protections, and democratic, transparent economic decision-making.

statement: Standing policy: Waste and Hazardous Substances Policy
how: Standing party policy to move all sectors to a circular economy, eliminate unnecessary waste and hazardous substances, and manage the rest safely through reuse and recycling.

statement: Standing policy: Women’s Policy
how: Standing party women's policy: gender equity in leadership (including wāhine Māori), and protecting women and girls from harm at home, at work, in the community and online.

statement: Standing policy: Workforce Policy
how: Standing party workforce policy: a just transition to a low-emissions economy, training and upskilling, workers' rights to secure income, safety and collective organising, and better work-life balance.

statement: Standing policy: Youth Policy
how: Standing party youth policy on the rights, participation and wellbeing of young people.

statement: Member's bill to entrench the Māori electorate seats
how: 23 Jan 2026: a member's bill in Hūhana Lyndon's name to entrench the Māori seats in electoral law, as the general electorate seats already are.

statement: Member's bill to recognise whales (tohorā) as legal persons
how: 9 Feb 2026: Teanau Tuiono's member's bill to give whales legal personhood with rights including freedom of movement and a healthy environment.

statement: 'A Home for Everybody' campaign: end homelessness, strengthen renters' rights
how: 26 Mar 2026: launch of the party's 'A Home for Everybody' housing campaign calling for an end to homelessness, stronger renters' rights and a large public-housing build.

statement: Announcement of the 2026 tax policy
how: 21 Jun 2026: release of 'A tax system for all of us' (wealth tax, capital acquisitions tax, higher tax on the biggest companies, bank levy, income tax cut for 96% of earners).

statement: Announcement of the 'Drink Swim Fish' water policy
how: 6 Jul 2026: launch of the Drink Swim Fish policy programme on drinking water, swimmable rivers and healthy oceans.

statement: Make union membership the default for new employees
how: 16 Jul 2026: the party backed an Automatic Union Membership member's bill amending the Employment Relations Act so new employees are union members by default, and said it would take the policy into the election.

statement: Require big supermarkets to donate edible surplus food (food waste bill)
how: 23 Jul 2026: Kahu Carter's Waste Minimisation (Food Waste) Amendment Bill, modelled on France's Garot law, would require large supermarkets to minimise food waste and partner with food-rescue groups.

statement: One-year moratorium on consenting new AI data centres
how: 26 Jul 2026: call for a one-year pause on new AI data centre consents while rules on water, energy and community benefit are developed.

statement: Campaign slogan 'For all of us' and campaign priorities
how: 26 Jul 2026: at the party AGM the co-leaders launched the slogan 'For all of us' and the manifesto; the release also discusses a Buy Kiwi Made-style approach to government purchasing.

statement: Presumptive ACC cover for firefighters with occupational cancers
how: 27 Jul 2026: a member's bill to give eligible career and volunteer FENZ firefighters automatic ACC cover for cancers likely caused by their work.

statement: Announcement of Te Waonui a Tāne marae funding policy
how: 9 Aug 2026: launch of the Te Waonui a Tāne policy for ongoing, protected marae funding.

statement: Member's bill to ban grocery price gouging
how: 17 Aug 2026: the Commerce (Excessive Pricing in Retail Grocery Industry) Amendment Bill would make it unlawful for supermarkets to charge unreasonable prices for groceries.

statement: Restore, extend and permanently fund Ka Ora, Ka Ako free school lunches
how: 20 Aug 2026: commitment to restore the original Ka Ora, Ka Ako school lunch model, extend it and fund it permanently, with locally prepared food.

statement: No AI or automated decisions on welfare payments or sanctions
how: 11 Sep 2026: pledge that in government AI and automated decision-making would not be used to cancel, suspend or reduce benefits or impose sanctions.

statement: $200 million for te reo Māori
how: 14 Sep 2026: commitment of $200m for te reo Māori initiatives in homes, schools and communities, including through Te Taura Whiri i te Reo Māori and Te Mātāwai.

statement: Fairer commercial rent reviews and council auctions of long-empty shop leases
how: 20 Sep 2026: plan to let market rent reviews lower as well as raise rents and to let councils auction leases of shops empty for over a year.

statement: Cap political donations at $30,000, ban corporate donations, create a lobbyist register
how: 22 Sep 2026: a package of electoral-finance reforms including a $30,000 donation cap, a ban on company donations and a public register of lobbyists.

statement: Restore pre-2025 pay equity law and fund a care-worker settlement (~$1.1bn a year)
how: 1 Oct 2026: commitment to restore pay-equity law to its pre-2025 form and set aside about $1.1 billion a year to settle the claim of around 65,000 care and support workers.

statement: Intercity passenger rail: overnight Auckland-Wellington, Christchurch-Dunedin, Te Huia to Tauranga
how: 3 Oct 2026: plan for intercity passenger rail including an overnight Auckland-Wellington service, Christchurch-Dunedin trains and an improved, electrified Te Huia extended to Tauranga.

statement: 'Connect: Aotearoa' transport plan: free fares for some groups, $2 fare cap, bus lanes and rapid transit
how: 4 Oct 2026: transport plan with free public transport for children, students, Community Service Card holders and Total Mobility users, a $2 fare cap for everyone else, bus lanes in the three main cities and mass rapid transit.

statement: Implement all 138 Royal Commission (Abuse in Care) recommendations
how: 12 Nov 2025: the party called for all 138 recommendations of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care to be implemented and for boot camps to stop.

statement: Recognise the State of Palestine immediately
how: 11 Aug 2025: the party called on the government to recognise Palestinian statehood immediately and take further action on Gaza.

statement: Commercial leasing reforms applied to Christchurch's empty shops
how: 28 Sep 2026: Christchurch-focused release on the commercial leasing policy (council tools for long-empty shops, rent rules for small businesses).

statement: Fund and deliver Auckland level-crossing removals
how: 5 Oct 2026: commitment to work with Auckland Council to fund and remove level crossings on the Western Line to unlock City Rail Link capacity.

statement: Hauraki Gulf protection: close commercial-fishing carve-outs, phase out bottom trawling, protect 30% by 2030
how: 6 Oct 2026: plan to close the ring-net exemption in Hauraki Gulf high protection areas (draft bill attached), phase out bottom trawling and protect 30% of the Gulf by 2030.

statement: Announcement of the 'Safe, sovereign AI' policy
how: 12 Oct 2026: release of the AI regulation policy (human decision-making, data sovereignty, environmental limits, shared benefits, transparency).

statement: Economic development plan: rescope Investment Boost toward R&D (3% of GDP target)
how: 13 Oct 2026: economic development plan that the party says would create 284,000 jobs over four years (64,000 attributed to its policies on top of Treasury's forecast, per independent modelling it cites); it includes rescoping the Investment Boost tax incentive to drive research and development toward 3% of GDP.

statement: Cancel the $2.4bn of planned public service cuts
how: 15 Oct 2026: commitment to cancel the public-service savings slated in Budget 2026 (stated as $2.39bn over 2026/27-2029/30; $3.17bn to cancel over 2027/28-2030/31).

statement: Universal weekly payment for students on practical placements
how: 16 Oct 2026: a universal weekly payment for students during practical training for nursing, teaching, social work and similar roles, plus relocation support.

statement: Abolish the training wage; more support for apprentices
how: 17 Oct 2026: commitment to remove the training-wage exemption so apprentices are paid at least the minimum wage, with more support for apprentices.

statement: Remove $5 charge for prescriptions
why: This party says that that last year, 155,000 New Zealanders didn't collect medicine they had been prescribed because they couldn't afford it. Not receiving treatments mean that health problems are exacerbated, and research shows that people who skip medication are more likely to end up in hospital. Making prescriptions free is an upfront cost for the government which removes pressure on the health system.
how: This party would remove the $5 fee for prescriptions of funded medication. This would apply to anyone who is entitled to free healthcare in New Zealand, instead of just people under age 14 and over age 65 and those with Community Services Cards. This would cost $74.5m a year, funded by a capital gains tax. This party estimates that this policy would cost $74.5 m a year.

statement: Create a 28% capital gains tax on commercial and residential properties, excluding family homes
why: This party says that NZ is one of the few countries in the world without some form of capital gains tax. Much of New Zealand's wealth is held in property rather than enabling economic growth. A capital gains tax would increase New Zealand's productivity and make housing more affordable. Money raised from the tax would be invested in healthcare.
how: This party would introduce a 28% tax on commercial properties and residential investment properties. Family farms, homes, KiwiSaver, shares, business assets, inheritances, gifts, and personal items would be exempt. The tax would only apply to people who own multiple properties or commercial properties, and only to profits made after 1 June 2027.

statement: Introduce a $20 weekly fare cap on public transport
why: This party says that a cap on public transport fares will help address the everyday struggles New Zealanders face as a result of a high cost of living.
how: This party would introduce a weekly fare cap of $20 on public transport in Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch. Everywhere else in New Zealand would see a weekly fare cap of $10. This would begin on 1 July 2027. Once the caps are reached, the rest of that week's trips would be free. There would be no sign-up required; transport users would use their public transport card or payment method as usual for public buses and trains and some ferries.

statement: Create a fund to invest in infrastructure and businesses
why: This party says record numbers of New Zealanders are moving overseas in search of better opportunities. This fund would invest in infrastructure and back innovative NZ businesses. It would create secure, well-paid jobs, enticing people to stay and build their lives in NZ, in turn, growing the economy.
how: This party would establish the fund with a foundation of existing government assets and an initial capital contribution, sitting alongside but separate from the New Zealand Super Fund. It would be independently governed by the Guardians of the Super Fund, with the Minister of Finance as sole shareholder. Some assets would be protected in law to remain under continual public ownership. Other assets would require Ministerial approval before being sold.

statement: Provide loans to support local GPs to buy into practices
why: This party says that doctors cannot always afford to buy their own practice. Yet private family doctors form the bulk of general practitioners in the health system. If more GPs can afford to open a practice in their local community, it will lower waiting times to see doctors and ease the pressure on busy hospitals.
how: This party would introduce a Family Doctor Loan Scheme providing up to 90% of the cost of buying into a practice. This would cap at $500,000 and would be interest-free for the first two years. A 3 percent annual interest rate would apply after that, with 10 years allowed to repay. Up to 50 loans would be available per year for owner-operated general practices. Funding would be supplied through the existing Small Business Cashflow Loan Scheme. This party estimates that this policy would cost $25 million a year if fully subscribed.

statement: Increase funding for people undertaking apprenticeships in the trades
why: This party says that youth unemployment continues to rise, with many New Zealanders choosing to move overseas in search of better job opportunities. It believes that expanding the Apprenticeship Boost will provide tradies and young people with greater support as they learn and build their careers in NZ.
how: This party would extend employer payments from one year to two years at $500 a month from 1 July 2028. It would also provide a $1000 toolbox grant to help new apprentices cover the cost of tools, kit, uniform and course materials from 1 July 2027. Eligibility for the Apprenticeship Boost would also be extended to include five new trades; road construction, water and sanitary engineering, personal services, sales and marketing, and sports and recreation, with a structured mentoring programme piloted, also from July next year. This party estimates that this policy would cost $56.5m a year over f

statement: Introduce legislation to pay small business owners within 15 days of their invoice
why: This party says that small business owners spend too much time chasing overdue invoices. Owners work hard to grow their businesses, and risk their own money along the way. Small businesses deserve to be paid on time.
how: This party would introduce legislation enforcing big companies to pay small businesses within 15 days for invoices under $25,000. The party would also restore the disclosure requirements in the Business Payment Practices Act 2023 so companies must publish how quickly they pay. This would be introduced within the first 100 days of taking office, and is part of a $1.56bn small business package over four years.

statement: Set a target for 15 percent of government contracts to go to NZ small businesses and start-ups
why: This party says that small businesses make up 97 percent of all New Zealand businesses. If they have more opportunities, the NZ economy will benefit as a whole.
how: This party would break up large contracts for government work into smaller jobs, making it more accessible to bid for work. It would also investigate how government agencies can safely share information between each other so small business owners can concentrate on running their business rather than providing details they have already submitted.

statement: Offer up to $10,000 in tax credits for small businesses purchasing equipment
why: This party says that tax credits for equipment will improve cash flow for small businesses so they can continue to grow. It will also mean small businesses can replace essential equipment sooner rather than having to wait for the adequate finances they need.
how: This party would lift the low-value asset write-off threshold from $1,000 to $10,000 for businesses with annual revenue below $10 million, from 1 July 2027. This means investments up to $10,000 would be wiped off from the tax bills of small businesses. This party estimates that this policy would cost $1.56bn over four years.

statement: Increase compulsory GST registration for businesses to $80,000
why: This party says that that reaching the current $60,000 threshold for GST registration adds an extra 15% on prices that small businesses charge their customers. Lifting the threshold means that businesses don't have to worry about losing customers due to higher costs, or spend time filing GST returns.
how: This party would lift the GST registration threshold from $60,000 to $80,000 from 1 July 2028.

statement: Reduce New Zealand's debt levels to around 20 percent of GDP
why: This party says that the country’s debt burden should not be shouldered by future generations, making it vital to invest in infrastructure and productive capacity.
how: This party would aim to reduce net debt to around 20 percent of GDP (gross domestic product) over time. It says net debt gives a better picture of the government’s overall fiscal position because it recognises that the government owns financial assets as well as has liabilities. At the same time, it would still prioritise investment to support economic growth.

statement: Create a GDP target for core Crown spending and revenue
why: This party says that New Zealand should be investing now for a more productive future by reducing the future debt burden and investing in key capital projects like ferries, hospitals and schools.
how: This party would hold core Crown expenditure and revenue at around 33% of GDP (gross domestic product) when a capital gains tax is fully implemented.

statement: Restore the Reserve Bank's mandate around prices and employment
why: This party says that monetary policy should be consistent with two objectives: maintaining stable prices over the medium term and maximum sustainable employment. It says keeping inflation in the target band is critical to household budgets, business planning and investment, and prolonged unemployment stops the economy from reaching its full potential.
how: This party would restore the Reserve Bank's dual mandate of price stability and maximum sustainable employment.

statement: Restore wellbeing reporting to the Public Finance Act
why: This party says that a government cannot measure its success without considering whether it results in poorer outcomes for New Zealanders’ lives.
how: This party would restore wellbeing reporting to the Public Finance Act, to take into account the social as well as fiscal impact of its decisions. These wellbeing measures would be used alongside traditional economic measures.

statement: Support a social media ban for under-16s to go through to select committee
why: This party says that it is important to help parents keep their children safe from online harm, but any law would need to be fit for purpose.
how: This party would support the bill through its first reading and see it go to select committee before the election.

statement: Guarantee jobs for NZ-trained graduate nurses
why: This party says that graduate nurses are being trained here, but because of a lack of job openings, too many are being forced to look overseas instead of starting their careers in New Zealand. The pressure on the health system from the shortage of nurses spills over into patient healthcare.
how: This party would guarantee a job for every eligible New Zealand-trained nursing graduate, affecting about 2400 nurses. It would also address pressure on primary care because of the nursing shortage by doubling the funding available through the current recruitment subsidy. The current rate for rural nurses would be lifted from $20,000 to $40,000 and it would rise from $15,000 to $30,000 for nurses in urban areas. This party estimates that this policy would cost $525m.

statement: Stop running youth offender boot camps
why: This party says that strongly opposes the Government’s proposal for permanent youth "boot camps," military-style academies run by Oranga Tamariki for serious young offenders. A 12-month pilot finished in July and the party says harmful behaviour has prompted some participants to leave and serve their sentence in mainstream youth justice facilities. The party notes this will not be an option for future young offenders, and also that the majority of participants reoffended within a year.
how: This party would reject a bill currently before Parliament allowing the military-style academies for serious young offenders to continue.

statement: Remove rough sleepers from "Move On" bill
why: This party says that the current 'Move On' bill criminalises people for sleeping rough when they have no other option. The bill, introduced as a means of maintaining public order, would require disruptive individuals to leave an area for up to 24 hours or risk a fine or prison. The party says while the bill has been somewhat amended, it still does nothing to fix homelessness, which is only fixed with stable housing.
how: This party would push to amend the bill at committee stage to remove rough sleeping and begging from the legislation entirely.

statement: Review the Emissions Trading Scheme
why: This party says that the Emissions Trading Scheme is broken, due to the carbon price being too low to drive meaningful emissions reductions. The current ETS also makes it cheaper to plant exotic forests than to grow food.
how: This party would review the ETS so it maintains a genuine price on emissions. It will stand by the Paris Agreement and aim to restore certainty to the carbon market. It will focus on changes that incentivise genuine reductions rather than relying on offsets, reconsider the role of forestry and develop new rules to prevent whole-farm conversions. New forestry registrations in the ETS will be paused while the work is done.

statement: Create an office to help safely guide the use of AI
why: This party says that AI holds great potential to increase productivity but also carries risks in the form of job losses, harmful content, or a lack of accountability around intellectual property. There is also the risk of data centres driving up energy costs.
how: This party would introduce a number of measures including an Office of AI, which would sit within the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, with a senior minister attached. As well as co-ordinating AI policy across government, the office would develop standards for responsible AI use and create a long-term workforce plan. It would also look at government procurement, emerging risks and opportunities and copyright protection from AI. An online safety regulator within the Department for Internal Affairs would be set up.

statement: Launch AI support for small businesses and schools
why: This party says that AI holds great potential to increase productivity but also carries risks in the form of job losses, harmful content, energy use by data centres, and a lack of accountability around intellectual property. People, small businesses, schools and communities must be able to access and share in the benefits of AI.
how: This party would launch a $2 million a year fund to help small businesses and community organisations adopt AI safely. It would also boost AI adoption and extend MBIE's AI Advisory pilot to $3 million a year, as part of a wider AI policy. A team would be created to help schools adapt to AI.

statement: Set rules for data centres around resource use
why: This party says that AI holds great potential to increase productivity but also carries risks in the form of job losses, harmful content, or a lack of accountability around intellectual property. The party says data centres must pay their own way without additional costs on households or businesses.
how: This party would ensure data centres are responsible for their own connection costs and finding their own renewable energy supply. Centres would also have to use water efficiently and reduce electricity demand during peak periods, to ensure they don't drive up costs for households and businesses. These measures are part of a wider policy aimed at harnessing the benefits of AI while still ensuring safely and accountability.

statement: Create a workforce plan to ensure people benefit from AI
why: This party says that AI holds great potential to increase productivity but also carries risks in the form of job losses, harmful content, and a lack of accountability around intellectual property. Small businesses, schools and communities must be able to access and share in the benefits of AI.
how: This party would create a long-term workforce plan and work with businesses, experts and unions to ensure productivity gains from AI show up in wages and conditions rather than job losses alone. The plan would review the skills people need, and provide backing for accessible training, including micro-credentials. This is part of a wider AI policy.

statement: Strengthen protections over data and copyrighted material
why: This party says that protecting NZ's data sovereignty in the age of AI is a huge challenge, but New Zealanders should have a say over how their data, and data collected here, is stored, governed and used. Creative people must be able to retain control over work used by AI, and be paid for it.
how: This party would strengthen control over NZ data, and would work with iwi and hapū on how Māori data is collected, owned, governed and used. A copyright framework would be developed with creators, publishers and tech companies so creators control and are paid for work used by AI.

statement: Establish a citizenship pathway for migrants' children born in NZ
why: This party says that immigration should be planned around what New Zealand needs, in a way that's fair to everyone here and everyone who comes. It should attract the skills and talent our country needs, while protecting migrants from exploitation and supporting their arrival.
how: This party would set up a citizenship pathway for children born in NZ. It would also protect humanitarian appeals against deportation and review parent visa, health, and English-language rules. This is part of a wider immigration policy which aims to treat migrants with decency and make NZ an attractive place for talent, while reflecting the country's workforce, housing and infrastructure needs.

statement: Allow migrants to move between accredited employers
why: This party says that immigration is a balance between the country's needs and the need to attract talent and skills. To do this, NZ should protect migrants from exploitation and support their arrival, while ensuring that our immigration settings consider NZ's workforce, housing and infrastructure needs.
how: This party would protect migrants from exploitation by enabling them to move between accredited employers after three months, rather than tying their visa to one employer. By strengthening the Accredited Employer Work Visa scheme, and improving support in their communities, migrants would be less vulnerable,

statement: Extend permanent residence eligibility to four years
why: This party says that NZ's immigration policies are a balance between the country's needs and making NZ a place that is attractive to skilled migrants and where they can have confidence in the system. Migrants should be encouraged to put down roots by increasing the length of time they must stay before applying for permanent residence.
how: This party would encourage a longer stay by extending the eligibility period for permanent residence from two years to four. This would be supported by a programme of NZ orientation and civic education, to strengthen social cohesion.

statement: Create an immigration statement that reflects NZ's needs
why: This party says that immigration should be planned around what New Zealand needs, in a way that's fair to everyone here and everyone who comes. Migrants bring much-needed energy and skills but they need clear and predictable rules to attract them, and protection from exploitation, while ensuring NZ has the capacity for them.
how: This party would introduce a set of measures including the setting of immigration goals through a Government Policy Statement that reflects the country's workforce, housing and infrastructure needs. The wider policy includes extending the length of time needed for permanent residence, allowing migrants to move more easily between accredited employers, and offering better community support.

statement: Introduce powers to protect consumers against price gouging
why: This party says that New Zealanders are paying too much for basic items such as food. It believes a crackdown is needed on big companies who charge excessive prices for essential goods or services. It notes that there is no legal test for excessive or unfair pricing in NZ.
how: This party would adjust legislation to address price gouging and give the Commerce Commission to new powers investigate what dominant companies are charging and take them to court. The legislation would only include industries that supply essentials such as food and groceries, banking and insurance, telecommunications, energy, fuel and investment. The law will apply where a company has enough market power that customers can't realistically switch, suppliers have nowhere else to go, or new competitors struggle to enter a market. Companies found to have overcharged consumers will face penalties

statement: Introduce corporate homicide as an offence
why: This party says that negligent employers need to be held accountable for workplace deaths. New Zealand has one of the highest workplace death rates in the developed world and yet employers cannot be held accountable for corporate homicide. Making this an offence would serve as a stronger incentive to take workplace safety seriously.
how: This party would hold introducing an offence for corporate homicide to encourage industries and employers to put in place adequate safety systems.

statement: Separate wholesale food businesses from the retail supermarket sector
why: This party says that New Zealanders are not paying a fair price for groceries. The country needs a more competitive supermarket sector, which is currently dominated by two players who favour their own retail stores at the disadvantage of smaller players.
how: This party would would make Woolworths and Foodstuffs run their­­ wholesale supply businesses independently from their retail stores. It would also give Kiwi grocers the right to buy their stock from any wholesaler they choose, and free up small players to void anti-competitive arrangements that keep their prices high. Rebate and data deals would be made more transparent.

statement: Increase foreign aid to 0.7 percent of GDP
why: This party says that NZ needs to have an independent foreign policy, focused on Pacific partners. The country needs friendship and allies with close partners, particularly in Australia and the Pacific, in uncertain times.
how: This party would progressively increase international aid to 0.7 percent of GDP, as fiscal limitations allow. There is no specific time limit for this policy.

statement: Work towards a Pacific agreement on climate mitigation
why: This party says that the Pacific is NZ's neighbourhood, and NZ is a Pacific country. These relationships are especially important as NZ is going to host the Pacific Islands Forum in 2027. Climate change and economic development are major challenges in this region, and NZ needs to support neighbouring countries with these challenges.
how: This party would work towards a Pacific agreement on climate mitigation, adaptation and displacement. It would specifically focus on Tuvalu and Kiribati on long-term plans for climate adaptation and possible resettlement.

statement: Recognise the state of Palestine
why: This party says that NZ has a reputation as an honest and independent country which defends international law. When human rights abuses and war create genocide and ethnic cleansing, NZ must have the moral clarity to speak up, specifically regarding the situation in Palestine.
how: This party would recognise the state of Palestine at the UN and place economic sanctions on Israel. It would ensure that the ACC and NZ Super Funds are divested from holdings in the Palestinian occupied territories, according to the list prepared by the UN. It would support South Africa at its case at the International Court of Justice, saying that Israel is breaching the Genocide Convention.

statement: Develop new trade markets around the world
why: This party says that the world is more uncertain and more competitive than at any time in recent memory, and old alliances and assumptions are under real strain. It is possible to trade as well as disagree with a country. Public support for globalisations is decreasing, but the answer is agreements with other markets, not tariffs.
how: This party would continue to pursue trade agreements, especially with new markets in Africa and South America. It would prioritise relationships with ASEAN countries, the EU and Canada. It would make it easier to move money and data across the Pacific.

statement: Continue support for the Paris Agreement, Antarctic Treaty and other international institutions
why: This party says that climate change, conflict and migration do not stop at borders, and NZ has a responsibility to the world. While institutions like the UN, WTO, International Court of Justice and International Criminal Court are imperfect, they need continued support to be reformed rather than abandoned. As a small country, NZ needs to do its part to work on goals like the Paris agreement and the care of Antarctica.
how: This party would support and retain membership of the UN, World Trade Organisation, International Court of Justice and International Criminal Court. It would continue to fulfil the responsibilities and requirements of the Paris Agreement and Antarctic Treaty and advocate for international scientific cooperation. It would support the country of Ukraine in its war against Russia.

statement: Deliver a health strategy for the rainbow community
why: This party says that the rainbow community deserves a health system that understands their needs, with a strategy that ensures they are represented in health system planning. Access to healthcare shouldn't depend on who you are.
how: This party would work with the rainbow community to deliver a Rainbow Pae Ora health strategy, which would ensure their needs are embedded in the health system. It would include identifying barriers to access, and culturally competent care that respects their identities and needs.

statement: Add at least 6000 more social housing places over the next 4 years
why: This party says that NZ has a backlog of construction work. Homes need building, schools need improving and hospitals need fixing. Government investment will get this pipeline underway, helping to reduce high unemployment and opportunities for businesses to win work.
how: This party would provide more social housing - at least 6,000 additional social housing places over four years. As part of this policy, more people will be helped into the trades by expanding the Apprenticeship Boost and Māori Trades Training scheme. This party would budget $2.9bn to spend on Kainga Ora over four years.

statement: Make improvements at 2000-plus schools
why: This party says that NZ has a backlog of construction work. Homes need building, schools need improving and hospitals need fixing. Government investment will get this pipeline underway, helping to reduce high unemployment and create more opportunities for businesses to win work.
how: This party would make improvements at more than 2,000 state schools and integrated schools, aided by expanding the Apprenticeship Boost and Māori Trades Training scheme. This party's whole education policy is costed at $400m.

statement: Spend more on hospital maintenance and repairs
why: This party says that NZ has a backlog of construction work. Homes need building, schools need improving and hospitals need fixing. Government investment will get this pipeline underway, helping to reduce high unemployment and opportunities for businesses to win work.
how: This party would tackle long-overdue repairs at hospitals so they are safe, reliable and fit for purpose. As part of this policy, more people will be helped into the trades by expanding the Apprenticeship Boost and Māori Trades Training scheme. This plan is costed at $200m.

statement: Remove 10% of student loan balance from certain graduates
why: This party says that student debt can hang over people for years, making it harder to save for a home, start a family or plan for the future. In launching this policy, this party hopes to encourage students to stay and work in NZ, rather than going overseas.
how: This party would write off 10% of eligible student loan balances. Students already finished and repaying their loan from 1 April 2027, and to current or future students three years after their studies, as long as they spent those years in NZ, would be eligible for the write-off. Eligible people would have to be up-to-date with their payments and have not received the now-defunct Fees Free incentive. Smaller loans of $2000 or less would be fully written off after the three years. This party estimates that this policy would cost nearly $40m a year once fully running in 2031.

statement: Restore pay equity deals
why: This party says that recent changes to the Equal Pay Act have stripped workers in low-paid female-dominated workforces of the right to pursue pay equity claims. These changes have raised the threshold for workers to prove their work had been historically undervalued, affecting nurses, teachers, carers and others.
how: This party would reverse changes to pay equity laws within the first 100 days of government, with care and support workers the first in the queue.

statement: Set stricter consumer rules for warranties and subscriptions
why: This party says that Kiwi consumers are being hit by hidden fees and trapped into contracts and subscriptions which are easy to join but hard to exit. These include gym memberships or phone and internet contracts with unclear pricing, excessive notice periods or auto-renewals.
how: This party would firm up contract rules, banning unfair exit fees on telecom contracts, and ensuring full prices are clear and auto-renewals or excessive notice periods are obvious. It would also address extended warranties on whiteware and electronics at checkouts, ban "junk care insurances"; and make subscription services and gym memberships easy to cancel.

statement: Allow 16 and 17 year olds to vote at local body elections
why: This party says that democracy should be accessible to everyone that is old enough to make their own decisions. It notes that a Supreme Court ruling in 2022 said that not letting 16 and 17-year-olds vote in New Zealand breached the Bill of Rights. Allowing older teens to vote in local body elections is a good way to increase interest, and does not require a Parliamentary majority.
how: This party would back lowering the voting age for 16 and 17 year olds at local body elections, something was previously introduced as a bill but was interrupted by a change of government.

statement: Restore same-day enrolment at general elections
why: This party says that recent changes to dismantle same-day enrolment at general elections will make it harder for people to exercise their democratic right. It says about 110,000 people would have missed out on voting at the last election under such changes.
how: This party would restore same day voter enrolment, allowing eligible NZers to enrol and vote simultaneously.

statement: Make it easier for independent car mechanics to access tools to fix cars
why: This party says the cost of fixing a car is not as competitive as it could be. It argues consumers are not able to use any mechanic because they don't have always access to the tools or information dealers have to make the repair. Similar moves in Australia mean car repairs by independent mechanics are 25% cheaper than dealerships.
how: This party would enable independent mechanics and petrol stations to access manuals, software and tools to fix modern cars. This effectively gives drivers the right of repair. This is part of a wider policy on market competition, which includes giving the Commerce Commission the power to investigate fuel prices, and freezing fuel excise taxes for three years.

statement: Increase competitive scrutiny of the fuel market
why: This party says that the fuel market needs to be opened up further to increase competition and ensure prices are fair.
how: This party would put the wholesale and retail fuel markets under greater scrutiny by the Commerce Commission, which would report weekly on fuel prices and investigate if changes in wholesale fuel prices do not follow through to the pump. Independent petrol stations would also gain greater access to fuel supplies, and NZTA would be required to look at making surplus land available for independent unmanned petrol stations and EV chargers. This party has committed to freezing fuel excise tax for three years.

statement: Give all care and support workers a pay rise
why: This party says that care and support workers deserve immediate and practical support for the hardship they have experienced with cancelled pay equity claims. This party says the work of caregivers has been unfairly undervalued because it has predominantly done by women.
how: This party would give an immediate pay rise of $4 an hour to 65,000 care and support workers through its pay parity policy. The change will take effect from the start of 2027.

statement: Expand visa-waiver access for Pacific Island Forum nations
why: This party says that it often falls on Pasifika families in NZ to sponsor a visit from loved ones from the islands, but for cost or other reasons, they may be unable to secure a visa. This party says NZ values its Pacific community and should reduce the barriers for them to connect with family.
how: This party would expand visa-waiver access to citizens from the Pacific Islands Forum nations.

statement: Repeal and replace the Disability Support Services Bill
why: This party says that the Disability Support Services Bill attacks the rights and independence of disabled people and carers. It says the bill ignores the reality many families face, ignores complex circumstances that may include abusive situations and gives the Minister powers to cut disability support without proper safeguards or consultation.
how: This party would repeal the Government’s Disability Support Services Bill, replacing it with legislation developed alongside disabled people.

statement: Increase transparency and consumer protection in the airline industry
why: This party says that passengers need clearer pricing and more rights when they fly. Increasing consumer protections and opening up the industry to more competition should help to make flying cheaper and more accountable.
how: This party would require airlines to show the real price of airfares up front for price comparison. It would also increase transparency by requiring airlines to publicly report on profits and performance data, such as delays. Automatic refunds would kick in when flights are cancelled or significantly changed, and customers would have to be compensated or reimbursed when checked baggage is significantly delayed.

statement: Increase access to airports for smaller airlines
why: This party says that flying is expensive, and on many regional routes there is little or no competition. Opening up opportunities for smaller airlines should lead to more choice and potentially lower airfares.
how: This party would open up fair access to essential airport infrastructure for smaller airlines, and work with the industry to retain regional flights. Airports would be able to borrow more cheaply so infrastructure upgrades don't unduly increase fares.

statement: Share payment information in the banking and insurance sector
why: This party says that NZ has four major banks - BNZ, Westpac, ASB and ANZ - and these banks take up most of the market, around 80-90%. This decreases competition and makes the focus for lending individuals rather than small businesses, who pay as much as 4.5% more than big businesses. It should be easier for alternative banks and payment systems to compete with the big banks. It should also be easier for individuals to switch banks and insurance providers.
how: This party would require that major banks give smaller competitors access to payments platforms and data so they can compete more effectively. A government-verified ID could be used to join a bank, minimising paperwork and the difficulty of changing provider. Open insurance information would make it easier to change insurer also

statement: Support new financial technology companies
why: This party says that NZ "fintech" companies have strict regulations which make it harder for new entrants to the market to compete if they aren't a full bank. It should be easier for new companies to enter the banking and payments market, and regulation should reflect this. These companies should also have the option to grow into full digital banks.
how: This party would create specific regulations for payment financial technology companies, so it is easier for these businesses to start and attract customers. There would be a pathway for payments businesses to develop into digital banks. A secure system would be used so that real-time payments could be delivered 24/7 for fintechs by 2030.

statement: Retain NZ ownership of Kiwibank
why: This party says that Kiwibank was created as an alternative to the big four banks (ASB, ANZ, BNZ and Westpac), who have between 80-90% of the banking market. The Kiwibank company should challenge these companies and offer a NZ-owned alternative. It should remain in NZ ownership.
how: This party would retain 100% ownership of Kiwibank in New Zealand.

statement: Increase the minimum wage every year
why: This party says that people are struggling with low wages and inflation. Other parties have pledged to freeze the minimum wage for the next three years, leaving young and lowest paid workers to fall behind.
how: This party would not freeze the minimum wage; instead, it would increase it every year.

statement: Ensure schools provide locally-made lunches
why: This party says that school costs add up and a school lunch is one less meal to provide as well as being a job-creator for the community.
how: This party would improve the cut-back school lunch programme so meals are fresh and locally-made.

statement: Decrease the number of branded items required in school uniforms
why: This party says that families are struggling with rising school costs. Lowering the number of branded items is one way that ensures schools can maintain their identity without making parents pay a premium for school uniforms.
how: This party would will limit the number of compulsory branded items in a school uniform and allow parents to buy non-branded alternatives for the rest. Schools will have to consider affordability, and uniform costs will be tracked and published to ensure they are getting cheaper.

statement: Allocate 5% of government procurement contracts to help stimulate the Māori economy
why: This party says that Māori unemployment has increased to nearly 11% and the Māori economy has gone backwards. However, Māori businesses have demonstrated that they can deliver. Overseas, indigenous minority-owned businesses have risen significantly and this has improved socio-economic conditions for targeted groups.
how: This party would reinstate its Progressive Procurement policy, which would initially allocate 5% of government procurement contracts to Māori businesses.. This has proven sustainable in the past and would equate to about $900m worth of contracts, injecting capital into Māori businesses and supporting wider growth.

statement: Tighten digital regulation, especially around deepfakes, children and social media
why: This party says that smart phones are one of the parenting challenges of our time. Tech companies have too much power over what we see and fake images are harder to spot. Many parents worry about what their children are seeing or if they are being bullied. More responsibility should be placed on the companies making money from these platforms.
how: This party would introduce more digital regulation to Parliament within the first 100 days, including no social media accounts for under-16s. Social media companies would be legally responsible for policing this, and a new digital duty of care will be introduced with stronger privacy and other protections for those under 18. Other action would include more control for users over their feeds, and stronger rules around deepfakes and non-consensual sexual images. An independent digital regulator will be created, with powers to take action against companies that break the rules.

statement: Provide more support for children's sports and hobbies
why: This party says that parents and schools need help to keep kids safer online, keep them active and prevent screen addiction. Technology has its place, but at present it's a dominant force in children's lives while sport, hobbies and other after-school activities are out of reach for many families.
how: This party would boost funding for after school sport and activities with an extra $4m for Tū Manawa Active Aotearoa and $12m over four years for the Active Me - Kia Tū programme which supports families with sports registration, uniforms and equipment. This is part of a wider set of policies around AI and digital use which includes clear expectations around screentime in school and a continuation of the ban on mobile phones in class.

statement: Provide support and clear expectations for schools around digital use
why: This party says that that parents and schools need help to keep kids safer online, keep them active and prevent screen addiction. Technology has its place but children need help to regulate their consumption and to protect themselves against online harm.
how: This party would provide more support for schools with digital technology. This includes clear expectations on screentime and a continuation of the ban on mobile phones at school. Schools and parents would be helped to find and use online-safety tools, including an education AI app. This is part of a wider policy on AI use, tighter social media regulation and a ban on social media accounts for under-16-year-olds.

statement: Create an Independent Pricing Authority to set GP funding
how: An Independent Pricing Authority, modelled on Australia's Independent Health and Aged Care Pricing Authority, would set an evidence-based national funding rate for general practice by July 2028; Health NZ would have to fund any increase the following year, and money now collected as co-payments would be added to practice funding.

statement: More emergency care outside hospital (paramedics, telehealth, pharmacists, early discharge teams)
how: Part of the ED Recovery Plan: more extended-care paramedics, a clinical telehealth service, longer emergency medicine supplies from pharmacists, and early supported discharge teams in every region.

statement: Stronger ECE oversight and restored network planning
how: Unannounced checks, clearer financial reporting and a better complaints process for ECE providers; restored network planning that supports community-based, smaller and parent-led providers; and better information about providers for parents.

statement: Require a small-business impact check before new laws and rules
how: Under Small Business First, ministers and agencies would have to consider the impact on small businesses before new laws, regulations and procurement rules are approved.

statement: Limit parliamentary urgency
how: Urgency would be restricted to genuine emergencies, fixing urgent errors, Budgets and a 100-day plan signposted before the election, and rushed laws would be sent back to select committee.

statement: Donation disclosure for third-party campaigners
how: Third-party campaigners in local and national elections would have to disclose donations on the same terms as political parties.

statement: Landlords to provide curtains or window coverings (member's bill)
how: Helen White's member's bill would extend the healthy homes standards so landlords must provide insulated curtains or window coverings in rentals.

statement: Energy performance standards for office buildings (member's bill)
how: Rachel Brooking's Building (Energy Efficient Office Buildings) Amendment Bill would require office buildings to meet energy performance standards.

statement: Advertised ticket prices to include all mandatory fees
how: Under the Fair Go Law the advertised price of tickets (and other goods) would have to include all mandatory fees, with no surprise checkout charges, and introductory-offer pricing would have to be clear.

statement: Require disclosure of international money transfer fees (member's bill)
how: Arena Williams's member's bill would amend the Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013 to require full disclosure of fees, commissions and exchange rates before an international money transfer is made; it passed its first reading in April 2026.

statement: Make possession, cultivation and use of cannabis free from prosecution
why: The ALCP says cannabis prohibition is unworkable and discriminatory, wastes public money and fuels the black market.
how: Part of the party's 'Policy Minimum Programme': no prosecution for possessing, growing or using cannabis and cannabis/hemp products.

statement: Create regulated R18 cannabis commerce like alcohol and tobacco, but with no promotion
why: The ALCP says cannabis prohibition is unworkable and discriminatory, wastes public money and fuels the black market.
how: Legal adult-only sales with no advertising or promotional aspects, with details fine-tuned by a policy council.

statement: Provide for medicinal cannabis, including home-grown medicine and prescribed preparations
why: The party says legal access would promote safer modes of use such as vaporisation and mouth sprays.
how: Establish therapeutic applications of cannabis, allowing both home-grown medicinal cannabis and prescribed preparations.

statement: Enable full-scale hemp production, prioritising local low-cost biofuel, fibre and hurd
why: The party says hemp would create jobs (especially in depressed regions), cut emissions and pollution, save forests and improve soils.
how: Allow full-scale cannabis-hemp farming and use, with priority for localised biofuel production and fibre and hurd for building materials, paper, plastics and textiles; hemp seed as food.

statement: Expunge all cannabis convictions and apologise for prohibition
why: The party says up to 20,000 people a year are convicted of cannabis offences and that Māori are four to five times more likely to be convicted.
how: Wipe all cannabis convictions; the 2020 addendum adds that apologies must be made for the injustices of prohibition.

statement: Hold a prohibition 'truth and reconciliation' commission
why: The party says Parliament has a duty to challenge injustice and break down prejudice.
how: A full commission on prohibition 'in the interests of accountability'.

statement: Set up a tobacco, alcohol and cannabis authority (Drugs Policy Council) to regulate recreational substances
why: The party says credible, harm-reduction drug education is impossible under current 'double standards'.
how: A single regulator to develop the regulatory framework for recreational substances, with 'adults only' enforcement and honest drug education in schools funded from prohibition savings.

statement: Redirect prohibition enforcement money to health, education, community and serious crime
why: The party says police would be freed up for 'real crime' and public trust in the law would improve.
how: Shift funds currently spent enforcing cannabis laws into health, education, community and employment, and more police and court resources for serious crime.

statement: Stop overseas cannabis offences being a barrier to immigrating to New Zealand
why: The party says it has no other immigration position beyond inclusiveness and tolerance.
how: Cannabis offences in other jurisdictions should not bar migrants.

statement: Reallocate drug-war resources to border security and civil defence
why: The party says the international war on drugs aids organised crime and terrorism.
how: Resources freed by ending the cannabis 'drug war' would strengthen border security and civil defence.

statement: Allow at least five cannabis plants per household and affordable micro-licences for small growers
why: Part of the party's 2020 'cottage industry' ideas, which it says are still under discussion.
how: A 'bare minimum' five-plant home-grow allowance, affordable micro-licences for existing growers, Kiwi seed strains, safe edibles, quality-controlled retail products and protection against racially loaded enforcement; an age limit more consistent with alcohol and tobacco.

statement: Start a national conversation about governing without political parties ('Exit politics')
why: NAP says parties force voters into 'package deals' and the system is 'better at producing political careers than producing good decisions'.
how: Experiment with citizens' assemblies, deliberative democracy, local decision-making, participatory budgeting, digital consultation and rotating civic representation, with New Zealand as 'a laboratory for innovation in governance'.

statement: Move peacefully to a society based on voluntary cooperation, guided by principles of self-sovereignty and self-government
how: Its listed principles: self-sovereignty, self-government, self-ownership, self-reliance, self-defence, self-control, self-respect, self-help, solidarity and 'safer communities together'.

statement: Invest $50m in roads and rail lines to create a transport hub in Rolleston
why: This party says that Rolleston is a well-placed hub for moving goods around, as it is on State Highway 1, the main southern train line, and connected by road and rail to the West Coast. Because many agricultural goods are moved through this area, making it easier to move goods between trains and trucks will increase efficiency and economic opportunity for producers in this area.
how: This party would invest $50m in a road and rail "intermodal hub" in Rolleston. This funding would be dependent on the result of a business case, where private freight companies and customers would also invest in the hub. It would only go ahead with a mix of public and private funding. This party estimates that this policy would cost $50m.

statement: Improve transport links in the South Island, especially state highway bridges
why: This party says that the South Island is particularly vulnerable to failures in transport networks, particularly given its reliance on several bridges. Earthquakes, flooding, spread-out communities, big rivers and mountains all mean roads and bridges can easily be damaged and communities could face long detours or have no way to get around. Focusing government money on improving the most at-risk parts of the network could make the South Island transport network more resilient.
how: This party would use the next government policy statement on transport to prioritise the South Island road network's most important points, especially state highway bridges.

statement: Change the policy settings for farmers leasing high country land from the Crown
why: This party says that the Crown owns 1.2 million hectares of land through the South Island, which is leased to farmers for pastoral grazing. Much of this land is at higher elevations. Farmers need certainty about which kinds of activities they can do on this land without requiring consent. Giving farmers other income sources on this land, like beekeeping or horticulture, would provide farmers with the confidence to invest and diversify.
how: This party would pass a law implementing changed policy settings for the kinds of activity to be carried out on Crown pastoral land, and for when farmers need approval or consent for activities.

statement: Charge international visitors to access locations like Milford Sound, Aoraki, Cathedral Cove and the Tongariro Crossing
why: This party says that international tourists are key parts of the economy, especially those who want to see natural attractions. These are managed by the Department of Conservation, and while New Zealanders could continue accessing them for free, tourists should pay some costs towards the upkeep. This money would be invested into tourist infrastructure at these locations.
how: This party would charge international visitors for access to a handful of key NZ attractions from 2027. This money would be largely reinvested in tourist infrastructure and conservation efforts in these areas. This is expected to raise $60 million per year.

statement: Create standard planning rules for small towns
why: This party says that smaller towns which receive a lot of visitors can have planning rules which make it hard for new businesses to set up. Changing planning rules for town centres would make it easier to convert spaces into new businesses or accommodation. This would especially help places where businesses want to cater to a growing tourist sector.
how: This party would create standardised zoning and planning provisions in small towns, aimed at increasing mixed-use buildings and growth in town centres.

statement: Create timeframes and regional performance metrics for businesses on conservation land
why: This party says that tourism on conservation land is important to the New Zealand economy. More businesses should be able to receive concessions for operations on conservation land, and these concessions should be faster and simpler. This will create jobs and encourage tourists. Currently, around 1,600 businesses operate on conservation land, with revenue around $5.3m each year.
how: This party would remove some rules around concessions on conservation land, so 30-40 percent of applications could be processed automatically. Regional performance metrics would calculate how these concessions are granted and how long it takes.

statement: Approve data centres only when they are accompanied by more power production
why: This party says that data centres are a growing industry well-suited to setting up in NZ, especially the South Island with its cool climate. However, data centres also use a lot of electricity, which could drive up prices for households and businesses. Making sure that data centres are only built when new electricity generation will also be built would give data centres and electricity generators security without making power prices more expensive.
how: This party would only approve new data centres when these are accompanied by new, firm generation.

statement: Complete construction of Tower Three at Christchurch Hospital
why: This party says that public money should be saved for what is most important, including health infrastructure. Christchurch has the South Island's largest hospital, and the area is growing, so the hospital needs to be larger to meet demand.
how: This party would pay for finishing the fit-out of the new wing of Christchurch Hospital. The 96 beds the wing has capacity would be finished and ready for patients, which is estimated to cost $70m.

statement: Deliver 98 new teaching spaces in the South Island
why: This party says that parts of the South Island are rapidly increasing in population, like Selwyn district and Queenstown. Other places have schools with aging buildings that need to be replaced, like Invercargill and Twizel.
how: This party would deliver on 98 new teaching spaces (in addition to 224 already funded), and nearly 100 more classrooms promised for the South Island.

statement: Add 240 beds to Christchurch Men's Prison
why: This party says that the offenders need to face consequences, and building more beds in Christchurch Prison is required so more people face consequences in prison.
how: This party would complete the already-agreed redevelopment of Christchurch Men's Prison, increasing the number of beds from 926 to 1166. A health centre and 52 specialist mental health beds are included as part of the plan. This policy would be paid for by a public-private partnership. The first phase would be completed in mid-2030 and is expected to cost $700m-$800m. This party estimates that this policy would cost $700m-$800m..

statement: Create an ID card for service dogs to access public places
why: This party says that trained and certified service dogs support people with disabilities including blindness and low vision, epilepsy and hearing loss. These animals have the right to access all public places but are sometimes turned away because they are assumed to be pets. An ID card for these animals will ensure that the dogs and their owners can show they have the right to access public places.
how: This party would issue a standardised national card for all owners of certified service dogs. This would make it clear to businesses and other operators that these animals and their owners have the right to be in public places, and would distinguish them from other animals and pets which do not have the same rights.

statement: Make the Game Council and Fish and Game responsible for managing introduced animals
why: This party says that the Game Council and Fish and Game are run by hunters and anglers, who should take the lead in managing introduced species in their areas. These organisations need a clearly defined role for managing Herds of Special Interest and coordinating access for hunters on conservation land
how: This party would make the Game Council the statutory manager of introduced game animals in NZ. It would also be responsible for managing access for hunting on conservation land and negotiating between the needs of different users. The legislation for Fish and Game New Zealand would be reformed, directing more resources to habitats, accountability for licence holders and simplifying administration.

statement: Promote hunting-related jobs and tourism
why: This party says that hunting can contribute to the economy. People want to come to New Zealand to hunt animals like tahr which cannot be hunted elsewhere. Jobs like taxidermy, guides and helicopters are supported by people hunting. Increasing the number of people coming to New Zealand to hunt will be good for the economy.
how: This party would promote tourism for guided hunting in overseas markets. It would simplify the process of shipping a taxidermied trophy animal outside of the country, including working on customs processes and veterinary certification. It would develop further rules around different types of hunting: recreational, commercial, guided, and aerial.

statement: Pursue trade deals with European, South American, Asian and African countries
why: This party says that NZ should grow its exports to reach the goal of doubling exports by 2034. The first seven countries identified for trade deals currently only receive $1.8bn of exports from New Zealand, which shows potential for growth.
how: This party would pursue trade deals with Brazil, Switzerland, Argentina, Bangladesh, Nigeria, Uruguay and the European Free Trade Association (Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway). Negotiations with these countries would begin in the next five years. When deals were signed, a second set of deals with South Africa, Turkey, Colombia, Morocco, Sri Lanka and Mauritius would be the next focus.

statement: Double NZ's export earnings by 2034
why: This party says that exports help grow NZ's economy, increasing jobs and wages. If businesses are selling more outside of NZ, more money will return to local communities. Exports have increased from $94.4bn to $114.1bn over the current term of government, and that trajectory should continue.
how: This party would continue to support a goal of doubling NZ's export earnings by 2034. This would be done by carrying out at least 23 trade missions in the next term of government, procuring deals with 13 countries identified as candidates for trade agreements, and by securing agreements for supplying essential goods like oil. Digital customs and trade processes would eliminate barriers to trade, and New Zealand Trade and Enterprise would have a sharper mandate to develop export growth.

statement: Increase funding for rural doctors and nurses to train in skills for urgent care
why: This party says that people who live in rural NZ should be able to access health care without travelling a long way. Ultrasounds are useful diagnostic tools, and giving rural-based clinicians the ability to use them will make it easier to decide whether they can be treated locally or need hospital care. Currently, 29% of rural clinicians are paying for PRIME emergency response training themselves; government funding for this program could make it easier for rural health professionals to respond to emergencies.
how: This party would invest $2.5m in a ultrasound training programmed called POCUS, aimed at rural doctors and nurses who carry out after-hours care and provide additional funding for rural clinicians to receive PRIME emergency response training. This would train 140 health professionals in ultrasounds and 150 people in emergency response. To increase the workforce in rural health practices, a $6m investment would help rural general practices to get more staff. This party estimates that this policy would cost $8.5m.

statement: Increase paid parental leave to 30 weeks by 2029
why: This party says that parents need more flexibility for taking leave, including taking paid leave at the same time as their partner, so they can receive more support if needed. Current arrangements create financial penalties for people who take time off work to care for their children. Both parents should have the opportunity to access parental leave if they choose.
how: This party would increase parental leave to 27 weeks in the 2027 budget, with further increases in 2028 and 2029. This leave could be split between parents or shared in overlapping periods. After returning to work, pay for annual leave would be calculated based on yearly salaries, rather than average pay for parents who have earned less due to taking parental leave. This party would also continue contributing to a parent's Kiwisaver while they take paid parental leave. Eventually, this party would aim to increase paid parental leave to 40 weeks.

statement: Fund a detailed business case investigating another route across of the Waitematā Harbour
why: This party says that the existing Harbour Bridge in Auckland is a busy corridor, which is needed for $1b of economic activity. This is projected to increase to $3.9b by 2051. Making it easier to get to central Auckland from the north would be good for productivity and increase economic activity. Bridges and tunnels have both been proposed, but detailed information about this project is needed before the government spends billions of dollars on it.
how: This party would fund an independent detailed business case of the second Waitematā crossing, led by someone who reports to the ministers for finance, transport, Auckland and cabinet as a whole. Consultation with other major parties will ensure that funding for this project can endure across terms of government.

statement: Review policies allowing "plug-in" and small-scale solar panels for renters and apartments
why: This party says that in contexts like apartments or for renters it isn't possible to install traditional solar panels, but small solar set-ups on balconies are an option. After a review found that these systems are safe, this party says that making the regulations for small solar set-ups in NZ simpler will improve reliability and affordability for people. Countries like Germany already have similar rules, which this party says is proof they will work in New Zealand.
how: This party would follow the recommendations in the solar regulatory review, to reduce the number of approvals needed for new solar set-ups. It would allow more installers to carry out inspections and making approval times for lines companies shorter, and estimates that the net benefits would be between $28 million and $50 million over 10 years. This party estimates that this policy would cost $28 million and $50 million over 10 years.

statement: Create a government surplus by 2028/29
why: This party says that limiting government spending and debt is good for the economy and for people. Having clear rules that governments follow when making decisions about spending is a way to protect the NZ economy from global economic effects.
