how: This party would commit to returning the government to surplus, where revenue is more than debt, by the 2028/29 financial year. Over time, this would reduce the ratio of debt to GDP.

statement: Keep government debt below 40 percent of GDP
why: This party says that high debt levels limit what governments can do while in power. Lower debt levels give the government, and the economy, more options if oil prices increase or natural disasters occur.
how: This party would reduce the proportion of debt to less than 40% of GDP and commit to keeping it that low.

statement: Keep Crown expenditure close to 30 per cent of GDP
why: This party says that if the government spends too much, it can cause inflation and increase interest rates. Ensuring the government is a smaller percentage of NZ's overall GDP would reduce the amount spent on debt servicing and improve economic conditions.
how: This party would reduce Crown expenditure to around 30 per cent of GDP. This principle would be applied when determining the government budget.

statement: Introduce no new taxes in the next term of government
why: This party says that that it is focused on growing the economy and do not want to introduce new taxes. It does not want to make commitments that would involving adding or increasing taxes for any New Zealanders. It says it can invest in government services without changing any parameters on the tax system.
how: This party would not introduce any new taxes, including an accomodation levy or "bed tax" for councils receiving a lot of tourists. It would not introduce any specific tax on banks either.

statement: Enrol New Zealand citizens in Kiwisaver at birth
why: This party says that Kiwisaver is a way for people to build up money for themselves during retirement, and everyone who is working should be part of it. The money in Kiwisaver is also important for providing capital for investments in New Zealand's future, like major projects or infrastructure. Contributions from the government for babies who are automatically enrolled will help the investment grow over time.
how: This party would make Kiwisaver compulsory from July 2028 and life combined contribution rates (individuals and employers) to 12% by 2032. For babies, it would contribute a $1500 "Baby Boost" payment to all New Zealanders at birth, automatically enrolling them in Kiwisaver. It would also make other changes to Kiwisaver, including government contributions through paid parental leave and requiring employers to maintain payments for people over the age of 65 who are still working.

statement: Reform the development contributions system to pay for infrastructure associated with housing projects
why: This party says that NZ needs to grow its housing stock and infrastructure, and the Fast-track planning laws have made it easier for new housing to be built. However, some councils are concerned that there is not appropriate infrastructure, like roads and water systems, to support these new developments. To make it easier for councils, the costs of this new infrastructure should be easy to recover when a new project is approved.
how: This party would allow councils to amend their "Development Contribution" policies to recover costs from new developments, including in the six months after an application is granted, rather than costs being locked in at the time of application. For projects in multiple council areas, there would be a mechanism to calculate costs for different territorial authorities. Over time, this system would be replaced with "Development Levies" which would be in place by 2029.

statement: Increase public access to conservation land and shooting ranges
why: This party says that hunting is an important part of managing introduced species, and hunters need access to firearms ranges for practicing and information about public land so they can pursue species there. Information from the Outdoor Access Commission will make it easier for hunters to do important work in the areas where they are needed.
how: This party would establish a pre-existing right to operate for shooting ranges. It would include the Outdoor Access Commission's maps in a new government environmental management system and work with community organisation and DOC to enhance access to conservation land for hunting.

statement: Reduce the student loan repayment rate to 10 percent
why: This party says that New Zealanders should keep more money, rather than paying taxes, to save money for their own future. Taking home more pay and repaying a student loan over a longer period will give graduates more options for how to spend their money. People who have been educated in New Zealand and are staying to work here should have more money available while starting their careers.
how: This party would reduce the annual repayment rate for student loans to 10 percent, from the current rate of 12 percent. Student loans for people in NZ would remain interest-free. People could continue to make additional repayments if they wished. Currently, there are $16.8bn of student loans owed to the government. Because of a slower rate of repayment, this party would write off $283m of student loans in the 2026/27 financial year to make up the loss in value from the interest-free loans.

statement: Fund further enforcement and create harsher penalties for overseas-based student loan holders
why: This party says that many New Zealanders receive a heavily subsidised education, but do not use their skills in NZ. To support people to stay in New Zealand, overseas-based student loan holders who are not making repayments need to be penalised. The Inland Revenue Department (IRD) already has some tools, like charging interest to overseas-based loan holders and monitoring the border for people who have not paid their student loans. More penalties and limits for people who are not paying their student loans would recover more money.
how: This party would add another 1 percent of interest for overseas student loan holders. For overseas-based New Zealanders withdrawing their Kiwisaver under the "permanent migration" category, money from Kiwisaver would clear the remaining student loan debt first. IRD would receive $10m of additional funding for student loan recovery and be allowed to register a charge for recovery in another country without getting a court order. As is already the case in Australia, this party would set up an information-sharing agreement to share details of student loan holders with the UK. If elected, this par

statement: Ban under-16 year olds from social media
why: This party says that 1 in 3 children between the ages of 13-17 spends more than 5 hours on social media every day. Parents should not be responsible for monitoring what children are seeing alone; social media companies also have a responsibility to make sure kids are safe. Restricting social media use will give parents and teachers more options to look after teenagers and create positive behavioural shifts.
how: This party would pass a bill requiring that companies including Instagram, TikTok, Facebook and Snapchat check the age of all users to make sure they are not under 16. These companies would be required to regularly report on risks to children on their platforms, and an online safety regulator would monitor compliance. AI companies and other new technologies would be included in the framework, and platforms which fail to take these measures will be fined, based on a percentage of their annual global revenue.

statement: Instruct councils to keep annual rate increases between 2 and 4 percent
why: This party says that median increases of rate around the country have been as much as 14.2 percent in the last year. Paying for rates adds financial pressure to households and limiting the amount that rates can increase by would mean that councils prioritise roads, water systems, rubbish and parks rather than other services.
how: This party would limit council rate rises to between 2 and 4 percent per year. Every 6 years, this target range would be reviewed and adapted if necessary. In exceptional circumstances, councils could apply for an exemption by demonstrating their financial management or to recover from an unpredictable event like a natural disaster. An independent regulator would monitor and advise councils and the government on the rates target. The caps would take effect from 1 July 2029.

statement: Allow Kiwisaver to be used by farm workers buying homes or farms
why: This party says that that the Kiwisaver policy was designed with urban housing in mind. Farm workers may be living in provided housing, and not able to access Kiwisaver for a house, as they are not living in the home. This means that people working on farms have to wait longer to buy property. Similarly, Kiwisaver withdrawals cannot be used for purchasing a farm through a company. This change will allow people to buy their first farms with less debt.
how: This party would amend the Kiwisaver legislation to allow people working on farms in provided housing to use their Kiwisaver balance for their first house, even if they are not living in it. If they are buying a farm where they are the majority owner, and will be living on the farm, regardless of whether the ownership structure is a partnership, a trust, a company or individuals, they will be eligible to withdraw their Kiwisaver for this purchase too.

statement: Distribute money from the international visitor levy directly to councils
why: This party says that councils create the infrastructure tourists use and deserve a direct financial benefit for hosting visitors, who also put pressure on local resources. Distributing the international visitor levy money not committed to the Department of Conservation and a tourism growth fund to councils is an alternative to a bed tax, which would disproportionately affect domestic tourists in New Zealand. This would also give councils money sooner than the time it would take to set up a bed fee. This is an alternative to raising taxes, which this party opposes.
how: This party would distribute $100m of the International Visitor Levy to DOC and $50m to a Tourism Priorities fund each year. The rest of the money, an estimated $385m over the first four years, would be distributed to councils, determined as a share of how many international visitors spend the night in their areas. This party would also commit to keeping the levy at the current amount for the next three years, to provide certainty to the tourism industry. As tourist numbers grow, the amount given to councils is expected to increase.

statement: Raise the income threshold for people who can pay a lower deposit for their first home
why: This party says that a home is an essential way for New Zealanders to build wealth. The First Home Loan scheme has operated since 2003, allowing people to purchase their first homes with a 5% deposit, instead of a standard 20% deposit. However, some people who are struggling to afford the deposit on their first home fall above the income cap of $95,000 for a person buying alone and $150,000 for two people buying together (both with no dependents). Raising the eligibility criteria will mean more people can buy homes with low deposits. Raising and simplifying the eligibility will allow more peop
how: This party would raise the eligibility so anyone earning less than $300,000 per year, whether single or a couple, could access the 5% deposit of the First Home Loan scheme. These lower deposits would only apply to people purchasing their first property. The loans would be approved by banks, as already happens, meaning no-one would be issued with a loan they cannot afford. The fiscal impact of this policy is expected to be between $4m-$6m.

statement: Offer government backed long-term loans for home batteries and solar installations
why: This party says that home energy tools like solar power and batteries lower household power bills and provide resilience in the energy system. Electrification and renewable energy is a good investment, and a government backed fund will make it easier for people to add these developments to their homes or businesses. With a high cost of living, this would help people finding it hard to pay power bills.
how: This party would launch the Home Energy Fund, jointly owned by central government and participating councils. The fund would pay a approved installer to add batteries or solar panels to a home and then property owner would repay the fund at low interest rates over a ten-year period. The loans would be secured against the value of the property, and available to ratepayers with at least 20% equity in their property. The loans could be used for solar installation, batteries, heat pumps, insulation and other developments to make homes more efficient.

statement: Allow rooftop solar and battery installation without a consent
why: This party says that energy security should be a priority for NZ, and it should be easy for businesses, households and farms to electrify. Changing planning processes to make it possible to install solar panels and batteries increases independence and resilience in the energy system and reduces power bills.
how: This party would allow property owners to install rooftop solar without a consent, regardless of regulations around height limits or landscape overlays. Battery installation not enclosed by an existing building would also be allowed as a property right, and there would be standard rules to govern any safety issues or other concerns about this. This would be part of other changes in the replacement for the current Resource Management Act.

statement: Create standard rules for on-site small solar and hydro energy projects
why: This party says that small battery, solar and hydro projects have confusing regulations, making it hard for users like farmers to use natural resources on their own land. From the perspective of energy resilience and affordability, there should be standard and predictable rules so that it is easier for more people to build energy projects on their property. Small-scale renewables are a huge opportunity which New Zealanders should be able to take advantage of.
how: This party would permit on-farm mounted solar panels with clear and consistent rules around the country, including safeguards to protect environmentally important land and manage other effects. Small run-of-river hydro projects would be allowed for generating energy used on site, as long as the project is below a certain size and has acomadations for fish passage, water flow and other river users.

statement: Specify that an active "yes" is required in laws around sexual consent
why: This party says that NZ law does not define what consent is, but instead says what consent is not. This means that for legal purposes, the absence of a person saying "no" can be considered consent, depending on the circumstance. To create a better system for the victims of sexual offending, and to be in line with other jurisdictions, the definition of consent should be specified in the law.
how: This party would amend the Crimes Act to specify that consent must be actively given, whether through words or actions. Consent is also not permanent; consent given at one point in time, for one action, is not consent for all future actions. The prosecution would still need to prove beyond reasonable doubt that consent wasn't given, and that the defendant didn't believe, on reasonable grounds, that it was.

statement: Prevent "good character" from being a mitigating factor in sentencing for sexual offending
why: This party says that crime should have real consequences. A "good character" assessment can be a factor in receiving sentencing discounts for sexual offending.
how: This party would prohibit judges from using "good character" assessments as a mitigating factor for any sexual offending.

statement: Create a dedicated police team for Auckland public transport
why: This party says that as Aucklanders get used to the City Rail Link, more people will be using public transport. Visible police officers help prevent offending. Taking public transport should feel safe, and having a police unit dedicated to Auckland's trains and buses will be good for all travellers.
how: This party would create an Auckland Transport Police Team, which would operate across Auckland's public transport network, on vehicles as well as at transport stations and hubs. This would require an addition 50 sworn officers, and would be funded with an additional $7m to the police in the 2027 Budget. This party estimates that this policy would cost $7m from 2027.

statement: Separate the Foodstuffs business into two nationwide cooperatives
why: This party says that Foodstuffs owns three grocery brands, limiting competition on prices in NZ. Previous attempts to reform the sector have suggested targeting both Woolworths and Foodstuffs, but a cost-benefit analysis says only focusing on Foodstuffs is the better option. Instead of Foodstuffs being divided into North and South Island branches, the company should be divided into New World and Four Square and Pak 'n' Save, creating greater competition.
how: This party would amend the Grocery Industry Competition Act in its first 100 days in government, asking the Commerce Commission to develop an implementation plan for separating the businesses in a way that is good for consumers. Owner-operators of supermarkets would retain their roles, but with a different overarching company structure to get support from. Restructuring Foodstuffs is a faster way to reach three competitors in the New Zealand market, rather than the time it would take for another player to develop operations around the country.

statement: Create a dedicated Building Consent Authority for large commercial buildings
why: This party says that it should be easier for large commercial projects to be built in New Zealand without needing a council inspection. Councils do not always have the capacity or expertise to sign off on large and complex projects, creating delays. Making it possible for engineers to sign off on parts of projects will reduce council inspections for parts of construction. Council capacity could be dedicated to consents and management of housing, and mean large projects could be built more quickly and cheaply.
how: This party would allow qualified engineers to sign off on building work by clarifying the role of producer statements in the Building Act, giving these descriptions a standard role in consent processes. It would also create a dedicated dedicated Building Consent Authority for large commercial projects, with specialist expertise and a nationally consistent pathway for consents. Developers could choose to use this BCA or get approval from their local council.

statement: Limit the use of screens in school for primary-aged and younger children
why: This party says that evidence says there needs to be caution around screen use in young children. For early childhood education, there should be no screen use at all, while the use of digital technology in the first three years of primary school should be strictly limited. Technology should only be used to enhance education, rather than being the main way that kids learn. Instead, the focus should be on hands-on learning and interaction.
how: This party would end all screen use and individual device use in early childhood education settings. Screen use in Years 1 to 3 would be strictly limited, and age-appropriate restrictions would be placed on screen use for older primary aged students.

statement: Use a checklist in early childhood settings to assess school readiness
why: This party says children need to be ready for school, and parents and teachers need to be aware of developmental milestones. Skills like toilet training, holding pencils and scissors, and eating independently are important for kids to thrive as they start school. A checklist of expectations for starting school will help teachers and parents know when a child might need extra support to be prepared for being at school all day. This would formalise a process many ECE centres already have.
how: This party would create a "School Start Check" for use by ECE centres and parents. The expectations for transitioning to primary school would be clear, and kids struggling to meet these expectations would be given extra support. The checklist would not be a "pass/fail" test, and not completing the checklist would not prevent a child from starting school.

statement: Require primary school writing assessments to be completed on paper
why: This party says that primary-age education should be focused on books, handwriting, conversation and in-person interaction, not digital technology and screens. Evidence shows that writing by hand when learning to write and read helps children retain information.
how: This party would require that students complete the writing component of twice-yearly primary school assessments on paper, by hand, rather than on computers.

statement: Require retirement villages to pay out house sales within nine months
why: This party says that older New Zealanders need the balance in relationships with retirement village companies to shift more towards residents. Residents and families need certainty about when money will arrive when they no longer occupy a unit. While some have called for a three month repayment deadline, it says that modelling shows that this would add up to about $118,000 to the cost of entering a village if all expenses were passed to residents.
how: This party would require retirement villages to pay residents or their families 10 percent of their net termination proceeds within four weeks of when they leave a unit. The maximum amount of time that villages could take to repay residents or families would be shortened to nine months. It would retain the current "hardship pathway" and current exit protections for residents, like stopping weekly fees when a occupation agreement ends. The 10 percent upfront payment requirement will not apply to villages with fewer than 50 units.

statement: Change the structure of Fire and Emergency New Zealand
why: This party says that firefighters fulfil a vital role in the community, but are stymied by organisational structures, unreliable equipment and lack of support for volunteers. The FENZ board is a Crown agent and reports to the Internal Affairs minister; with concerns about the organisational structure and gaps in training, it says reform in needed urgently.
how: This party would remove the FENZ board and reorganise it as a government agency, directly accountable to the minister for emergeny management. FENZ would be required to write the turnaround plan and cover costs from existing baselines.

statement: Increase funding for volunteers and frontline work at Fire and Emergency NZ
why: This party says that firefighters fill a vital role serving the public, despite faulty appliances. Volunteers work in fire response around the country, but though this is risky work and requires extensive training, these volunteers need more support, beyond what is already covered by ACC. It says that for volunteer and professional firefighters alike, investment in equipment will make their work safer and more effective, as currently many of their tools are not fit for purpose.
how: This party would require FENZ to provide private insurance covering mental injury and gradual process injuries for operational volunteers. It would direct FENZ to create a fleet management plan which could be used to secure production slots in advance for equipment that needs replacement. It would also ask for a plan that would allow all recruits to get experience on live fires during training, modernise axle mass rules, ensure all Type 3, 5 and 6 appliances are delivered, accepted, and put into operational use and prioritise capability over emissions profiles for frontline vehicles.

statement: Increase the threshold for shares to be declared due to foreign investment rules
why: This party says that financial investment is required for growth. It should be easier for businesses to invest across borders, especially as global fuel shocks push up prices.
how: This party would double the threshold for shares of overseas businesses to be required to follow the foreign investment fund rules.

statement: Open supplier panels for government procurement
why: This party says that businesses create wealth, not governments. Businesses need opportunities to grow, no matter what stage they are at. As well as reducing other regulations like resource management, businesses should be able to compete for government contracts. Currently, the government purchases more than $50bn of services and goods from businesses each year.
how: This party would open current supplier panels for government contracts so that more businesses can bid to be suppliers. It says that this would increase competition.

statement: Rewrite industry health and safety codes in simple language
why: This party says that the government should do everything it can to make it easier to build, invest, hire and export, and help businesses grow in general. Making it easier to comply with health and safety law will make it easier for businesses to succeed.
how: This party would rewrite health and safety codes in simple, plain language to make it easier for businesses to comply with these regulations.

statement: Coordinate regulation for new financial technology businesses
why: This party says that NZ needs to support new technologies and businesses that create new jobs. Complex systems of regulations and consents should be simplified so that there is less bureaucracy.
how: This party would co-ordinate regulations across the Reserve Bank, Financial Markets Authority and MBIE to remove barriers impacting the introduction of new financial technologies.

statement: Double the number of Trade Academy places by 2030
why: This party says that NZ's growth and prosperity depends on the knowledge and skills of young people. However, some employers have been struggling to find the skills they need.
how: This party would double the number of Trades Academy places so that 20,000 places are offered by 2030. It would also roll out 9 new vocational education pathways designed by industry.

statement: Replace NCEA with a different grading system
why: This party says that NZ's achievement in maths, reading and writing has decreased. Structured literacy and maths and a simple grading system and regular assessment is a way to create better outcomes. A new curriculum should be used at all year levels.
how: This party would replace the NCEA system with grades and regular exams. Grades would range from A+ to E, rather than the NCEA system. New curriculums would be fully embedded at all levels.

statement: Encourage Active Investor Plus visa holders to stay in New Zealand
why: This party says that NZ needs partners on the world stage to help businesses get ahead. People from other countries with money to spend should be encouraged to stay and invest in NZ with the Active Investor Plus visa categories. Investment fund settings and IRD rules should not prevent them from doing so.
how: This party would ensure that IRD rules and investment fund settings do not discourage Active Investor Plus visa holders. These visa holders must have at least $5m or $10m to invest in New Zealand to meet the visa rules.

statement: Require government infrastructure builds to use internationally cost benchmarks
why: This party says that NZ has an infrastructure deficit, and replacements are needed to key pieces of infrastructure like schools, roads and hospitals. This infrastructure should be built affordably without using an inappropriate amount of taxpayer's money. Infrastructure built by government and councils should be managed carefully with asset and capital plans.
how: This party would require the Infrastructure Commission to use international cost-benchmarks for government funded builds of infrastructure like schools, transport and hospitals. It would also legislate requirements for asset management and long-term capital plans.

statement: Trial digital-first "seamless" travel between NZ and Australia
why: This party says that NZ and Australia are two of the world's most closely connected economies. Citizens of both countries can already use "smart gates" to enter the country without interacting with a border agent. In 2028 NZ and Australia are jointly hosting the Cricket World Cup, which is an opportunity to trial a way to enter the country without needing a paper passport at all.
how: This party would introduce a "seamless" digital system for travelling between New Zealand and Australia, to be trialled before the 2028 World Cup. To do this, NZ and Australian officials would work together to design the system. It would use a smartphone, digital credentials and biometric technology to identify people at the border, rather than a physical passport.

statement: Legislate affordability as a concern of the Electricity Authority
why: This party says that secure energy is important for NZ to grow its economy. More power supply, competition and choice, as well as regulating the right areas, can make power cheaper for New Zealanders.
how: This party would change the law so that "affordability" is a key objective for the Electricity Authority in its role as the sector regulator. Affordability would be balanced with its other objectives of competition, reliability and efficiency.

statement: Make the cost of building transmission for new electricity generation consistent for public and private players
why: This party says that affordable and reliable power is essential for growing the economy. However, some of the areas with possibility for new development of wind, solar and geothermal power generation do not have enough transmission capacity. The system of treating transmission as an asset means that one party might pay for building transmission that benefits multiple power companies and developers.
how: This party would amend the Electricity Act and revise the Industry Participation Code so transmission pricing methodology can recover the costs of investments made by parties other than Transpower. Privately funded interconnection investments would be required to use the same pricing method as well. To encourage private investment, there would be a regulatory framework for connecting private transmission to the main grid operated by Transpower.

statement: Create a single accreditation scheme for power to new developments or houses
why: This party says that connecting a new new home, subdivision, farm, factory or business to the electricity network is often slow and expensive. Customers have little choice in the work, as it is set and priced by the network authority. This area of the electricity industry should be more competitive.
how: This party would establish a single accreditation scheme for connection contractors, which would be independently assessed. Accredited contractors would be allowed to work on any network in the country. People seeking a connection could get quotes for the work from multiple people. Networks would still be allowed to inspect finished work and approve designs, but would be given set timelines for doing so.

statement: Create a back-up power contract for dry years
why: This party says that NZ uses largely renewable electricity, which is cheap and abundant. However, this power, especially hydro power, can be unreliable when there is a dry spell and the hydro lakes are low. Back-up has historically been provided by gas, but gas stocks are decreasing. As well as a contract for daily peaks, the 4 big power generators should have a contract for covering gaps over the weeks or months of a dry period.
how: This party would require the Electricity Authority to publish a report about the "back-up gap" with the size and timing of generation that is not covered. Along with published data on contract values, lengths and price ranges, this would help electricity buyers, sellers and investors know what is happening. It would require the creation of a back-up contract so that back-up power can be bought by anyone from any retailer on standardised terms. There would be regular auctions for this contract.

statement: Review the system that sets electricity lines charges
why: This party says that network charges are responsible for 2/3 of the price increases in power over the past year. This is partially because lines companies charges are set by an independent regulator and the current cap was set in November 2024 when inflation was high. It was designed for a system before solar power, as houses and businesses can now generate as well as consume power.
how: This party would review part 4 of the Commerce Act regarding electricity distribution to see whether the current system is delivering enough value for money for consumers. It would require distribution businesses to approve residential and small business solar connection applications within two working days, with penalties for lateness.

statement: Allow people with solar generation to sell power to any buyer
why: This party says that the current rules in the electricity sector assumes that power comes from big generators. However, as more people put solar panels on their homes or businesses, the power sometimes flows the other way. Currently, those with solar panels are locked into selling any excess power to the grid to the same company they have an electricity contract with. If these rules were more flexible, people could get a better price for power they generate.
how: This party would give every household and. business the right to sell power to whichever retailer they choose. This would be achieved through a Government Policy Statement, and specific legislation if needed. Lines companies would be required to base any power export limits on the true capacity of their network, and not restrict exports beyond any genuine network constraint.

statement: Fund $800 million Christchurch Northern Motorway extension
why: This party says that Canterbury is the engine room of the South Island, with State Highway 1 already carrying 21,500 vehicles a day. This is predicted to grow to around 28,000 vehicles a day by 2048, with Woodend feeling the peak pressure, amid other safety concerns. This project will create a reliable and safe transport corridor for people and freight travelling and commuting each day.
how: This party would fully fund an extension to the Christchurch Northern Motorway for $800 million, which would be allocated in next year's budget. This incorporates the Belfast to Pegasus Motorway and Woodend Bypass.

statement: Increase funding for Pharmac's medicines budget
why: This party says that this funding boost will expand access to new cancer and other life-saving medicines so Kiwis can access world-class treatment here in New Zealand.
how: This party would deliver a further $604 million uplift in Pharmac’s medicines budget. This will be funded by reducing foreign aid spent outside the Pacific.

statement: Set a national target for clinical trials
why: This party says that a national clinical trials target will mean that Kiwis can access the newest treatments sooner, accessing life-saving care. This matters even more for people living with a rare disorder, where so few treatments are funded that a trial can be one of the only options available.
how: This party would set a national target that within ten years, 5 percent of New Zealanders being treated for cancer will have part of their care delivered through a clinical trial, where a trial is right for them and they want to take part, aligning with Australia. It would also set up a single national front door for clinical trials, so companies have one clear place to go and patients can be matched to trials more easily, including those with a rare disorder who often struggle to find a relevant study. Lastly, it would simplify and standardise the approvals process, so a trial approved once c

statement: Unlock CAR-T cell therapy for cancer patients by funding BioOra
why: This party says that New Zealanders who need this life-saving technology currently rely on their cells being sent overseas to be made. This comes with a huge expense, despite scientists and clinicians who know how to do this already living here in New Zealand.
how: This party would co-invest $25 million with the BioOra company to expand its cell therapy manufacturing, research, and clinical facilities in Christchurch, so Kiwis who need CAR-T can be treated at home rather than sent overseas. BioOra is a New Zealand-based commercial-stage biotechnology company.

statement: Lower the free bowel screening age to 50 by 2029
why: This party says that New Zealand's rate of bowel cancer is among the highest in the world, with more than 3300 people diagnosed every year and 1200 losing their lives to it. Early detection is the difference between survival and death. Those treated at an early stage have a 90 percent chance of long-term survival.
how: This party would extend free bowel screening by lowering the age by two years every year to reach 50 in the next term of Government, so bowel cancer is found earlier when it is most treatable. It would continue the roll out of free bowel cancer tests for people of any age with symptoms, so cancer is found sooner no matter how old a patient is. Lastly, it would deliver additional colonoscopies to increase system capacity and work with Bowel Cancer New Zealand to determine how the CHALLENGE exercise programme could be made available for bowel cancer patients.

statement: Extend free breast screening extension to age 74 by 2029
why: This party says that breast cancer is New Zealand’s most commonly diagnosed cancer in women, with nearly 3900 new cases a year, and the risk grows with age. Free mammograms currently stop at 69, leaving older women to pay for screening themselves or go without.
how: This party would complete the free breast screening extension to age 74 by 2029, ensuring older women have access to early detection and life-saving care.

statement: Launch a prostate cancer screening pilot in two high-demand districts
why: This party says that prostate cancer is the most common cancer among New Zealand men, with more than 4,000 diagnosed and more than 700 deaths each year, making it the second biggest cause of cancer death for men after lung cancer. Found early, more than 90 per cent of men survive at least five years, but that falls below 40 per cent once the cancer has spread. However, there is currently no organised screening programme for prostate cancer.
how: This party would launch a prostate cancer screening pilot in two high-demand districts, offering men aged 50 to 70 regular screening to evaluate what works for a potential nationwide programme. It would also gather evidence for a potential nationwide programme, based on a proposal from the Prostate Cancer Foundation.

statement: Deliver free cervical screening for all women aged 25 to 69
why: This party says that cervical cancer is among the most preventable cancers, because nearly every case is caused by HPV, a common virus that the screening test picks up well before any cancer develops. When it is caught early, around 91 percent of women survive, but that falls to around 19 percent once it has spread. Successive Parliamentary Reviews since 2018 have recommended making cervical screening free for every woman.
how: This party would deliver free cervical screening for all women aged 25 to 69 from March 2027.

statement: Offer active prescriptions through a new health programme
why: This party says that New Zealand is facing a chronic disease epidemic. The number of Kiwis with type 2 diabetes is set to nearly double by 2040, yet most cases are preventable with a healthy diet and exercise.
how: This party would establish the Healthy Kiwis Programme to deliver active prescriptions, with a target to double the number of people receiving them by 2030, helping more Kiwis get active, eat well, and avoid chronic diseases like diabetes.

statement: Deliver a lung cancer screening pilot in Bay of Plenty and Hawke’s Bay
why: This party says that lung cancer is New Zealand’s biggest cancer killer, claiming more than 1700 lives every year. However, most people are only diagnosed once the disease is advanced, and the chance of a cure is slim. Screening can change this. International trials have found that low-dose CT scans for people at high risk reduce lung cancer deaths by 20 to 25 per cent.
how: This party would deliver a lung cancer screening pilot in Bay of Plenty and Hawke’s Bay, offering low-dose CT scans to people at high risk, such as current and former smokers. The pilot will test the best way to find, invite, and screen those most at risk, catching more lung cancers early and building the evidence for a potential nationwide programme.

statement: Create a support package for new employers
why: This party says that small businesses make up around 97 percent of all New Zealand enterprises. These business owners are helping drive the New Zealand economy. They deserve support so their businesses can grow.
how: This party would introduce a First Employee Support Package with practical first-year guidance and reduced penalties for genuine administrative mistakes. This will deliver practical, dedicated advice for new employers through the first year of their first hire - including employment agreement tools, payroll guidance, and tax and ACC reminders.

statement: Simplify sharing core business information with the government
why: This party says that changing a business address or contact details should be straightforward. Owners should not have to waste their time working through a list of agencies updating the same information in different systems.
how: This party would deliver a 'Tell Government Once' service built around the New Zealand Business Number and existing government systems, including Inland Revenue, ACC, the Companies Office and relevant licensing bodies. This will mean core business information can be updated once and shared across participating agencies and councils. It would also explore integrating this service with Councils. There would be clear privacy rules and business control over the information shared.

statement: Provide targeted work support to 30,000 Jobseekers
why: This party says that Jobseeker benefits are not meant as long-term support. The current "invest to save" programme should be continued and extended, with work support targeted to people who have been receiving a benefit for a longer period of time. More intense case management and employment programmes should be used to target the problems preventing people from being employed, and younger people should particularly receive more help. This will help to balance the welfare system more effectively.
how: This party would target extra case management and employment programmes to people receiving Jobseeker benefits for over 12 months, who are deemed "job-ready". At least 5,000 of these places would be reserved for young people. An additional $12m would be given to youth work programme He Poutama Rangatahi above existing baselines. It is estimated that this programme would save $9m by 2031.

statement: Reduce benefit payments for people receiving support for more than 2 years
why: This party says that welfare support should always be temporary, and after a long time receiving a benefit it is hard for people to find work. While the welfare system should provide a safety net, it should not prevent people from seeking work. Decreasing payments for people who have been receiving benefits for more than two years will incentivise these people to seek work. Parents with dependent children would have their payments decreased less than those without children.
how: This party would reduce payments for people who have been receiving Jobseeker benefits for 2 of the last 3 years, even if these periods of support were not consecutive. From April 2028, this party would reduce the rate for single people to the rate for 20-24 year olds; reduce the rate for couples without children, and reduce the Jobseeker rate for parents with dependent children half as much as for those without. The exact reductions would be based on benefit rates in 2028, as the rate changes with inflation. The Supported Living payment would not change. This party estimates this would save $

statement: Introduce drug testing for people receiving benefits
why: This party says that the intention of Jobseeker benefits is to help people find work, not to provide long-term support. Many types of work require drug tests for workers, so people receiving Jobseeker benefits should also be tested for drugs, to show that they are ready to work. If drug use is a barrier to employment, it should be addressed.
how: This party would institute random drug tests for people on Jobseeker benefits, as part of MSD's broader employment programme. If drugs are detected, a person will be tested again; if drugs are detected again, MSD will conduct a mandatory assessment to see whether drug use is a barrier to employment and whether it should be addressed. If drug use if not addressed, it could result in benefit sanctions, so that payments are reduced or stopped. It is expected that this policy would cost $1.5m per year.

statement: Increase the stand-down period to 26 weeks after leaving a job
why: This party says that benefits are intended as temporary support until someone is employed again. If someone chooses to leave a job, the current stand-down period of 13 weeks means they cannot receive a benefit for job hunting until this time has passed. In line with the UK's benefit sanctions system, people who repeatedly leave jobs should have a longer stand-down period.
how: This party would increase the current non-entitlement period for people who leave a job from 13 weeks to 26 weeks. Someone who has left a job more than once would not receive a benefit until this time, about 6 months, had passed.

statement: Change entitlements for benefits for new NZ residents to 5 years
why: This party says that NZ's welfare system is funded by taxpayers to provide a safety net. Currently, NZ residents are entitled to benefits after 2 years of living in the country. However, this party says that new migrants to NZ should be expected to provide for themselves and their families by working rather than receiving benefits. This is in line with approaches to new residents in Australia and the UK.
how: This party would extend the minimum residency requirements for receiving benefits to 5 years, from the current minimum of 2 years. This would begin in 2028, and new legislation might be needed to enact the change. Refugees and other protected persons would be exempt from this requirement and MSD could still issue hardship grants to residents in emergencies. This party estimates that this would save $49m over 4 years.

statement: Increase transparency and enforcement of "prompt payment" norms for small businesses
why: This party says that small businesses need to be paid promptly for effective cashflow, especially when they are working for government. Building on current reforms, government agencies should be accountable for how quickly they pay invoices and digital invoicing should be used to make processes simpler. Lowering payment fees could help small businesses by reducing costs.
how: This party would hold Government agencies to account for delayed payment by publishing how quickly agencies pay invoices. It would monitor whether fee reductions reach businesses and expand the use of eInvoicing. Open banking and the Reserve Bank's payment modernisation programme would be completed and fair payment terms through supply chains would be enforced.

statement: Support small businesses to adopt artificial intelligence
why: This party says that small businesses could benefit from using AI but in many cases do not have the time to research or experiment with implementing it. 150 businesses have taken part in an AI Advisory pilot to help them figure out applications for AI in their contexts. This party would offer more places on this pilot programme.
how: This party would fund another 120 places in the AI Advisory pilot programme. It would continue to co-fund support for some small businesses to do AI courses and receive expert input.

statement: Make it easier for businesses to navigate export processes
why: This party says that many NZ small businesses want to export their goods but do not have the time or expertise to navigate complex export processes. It should be easier to export NZ products offshore, and AI tools and trade agreements can facilitate this.
how: This party would use AI tools to create an "export navigator" to cover tariffs, rules of origin and market-access requirements. It would expand "paperless" trade with real-time electronic certification when exporting to close trading partners like the UK. There would be a "trusted exporter" fast-lane through the Secure Exports Scheme for eligible businesses, reducing the need for duplicated documentation.

statement: Establish a programme to support high-growth potential export businesses
why: This party says that many NZ businesses have products and expertise to share with the world but do not have the knowledge to effectively navigate the export system. By identifying small and medium sized businesses which could grow into export-oriented businesses, this party wants to support business owners to understand practical next steps to export their goods.
how: This party would create a "Next 200" programme for exporters, where businesses would have a dedicated NZTE relationship manager, introductions to potential contacts, market intelligence and help with customs requirements. NZTE would have a defined role in identifying opportunities and connecting business owners with potential customers.

statement: Decrease duplication and processing times for building regulations
why: This party says that that it has reformed consent processes to make it easier to build homes. Making it easier for building companies to get consents helps housing to be built and reduces processing times for regulations. It says there should be more consolidation in regulations which impact consenting.
how: This party would cut project information memorandum processing times from 20 to 10 working days and require regulators to reuse engineering and geotechnical reports if they are still relevant and fit for purpose. It would expand the list of overseas-certified products which could be used in buildings in NZ. It would change building indemnity insurance so it is proportionate to the building and enable greater consolidation in the building-consent regime more broadly.

statement: Increase the use of digital systems in business practices
why: This party says that many businesses serve their customers online and requirements to use faxes or publish newspaper notices feel obsolete. Wherever possible, secure and consistent digital systems should be used instead of paper alternatives.
how: This party would remove unjustified "paper retention" policies and create guidelines for accepting paper alternatives. It would remove licence display requirements when there are accessible digital alternatives. This party would replace compulsory newspaper notices with a searchable online gazette and remove fax and telex requirements, which are obsolete.

statement: Simplify renewal systems for small businesses
why: This party says that that many small businesses spend too much time working on paperwork, and in many cases, renewal systems for licences can be simplified, and declarations can be organised by professionls a business is already in a trusted relationship with.
how: This party would align renewal dates for licences where possible and introduce automatic renewals for low-risk businesses with strong compliance records. As already announced, this party would simply applications and renewals for alcohol licences too. It would allow eligible chartered accountants to administer statutory declarations on behalf of business clients, and would publish clear guidance and templates for small businesses on fire evacuation requirements.

statement: Increase employee support requirements for collective bargaining
why: This party says that currently, unions can begin collective bargaining without a minimum number of employees supporting the action. There should be a minimum number or percentage of employees in support of bargaining for a collective agreement process to take place. It says this is in line with similar laws in the UK.
how: This party would require support from 10 employees or 20 percent of a workplace, whichever is lesser, before collective bargaining over wages or working conditions can take place. The minimum number of employees would be two.

statement: Develop a fast-track process for some Employment Relations Authority disputes
why: This party says that employment disputes can be expensive and time-consuming, even if a dispute is relatively minor. For the peace of mind, costs, and time involved for employer and employees, it should be easier, faster, and cheaper to go through an employment dispute. Changes should particularly focus on the Employment Relations Authority, and on mediation so cases do not reach the Authority and are resolved more easily.
how: This party would create a fast-track through the Employment Relations Authority for minor disputes, and allow a greater role for mediators, with binding agreements clearly explained to all parties. It would require Employment Relations Authority decisions within one month of final submissions. To increase transparency, this party would create a process for tracking a case through the Authority's system and require the Authority to record and reuse oral evidence when legal and suitable, to prevent multiple submissions of the same evidence. It would review the Employment Relations Authority’s en

statement: Clarify and consolidate overlapping employment laws
why: This party says that NZ employment law is spread across many different frameworks, laws, and statutes. This makes it particularly hard for small businesses to comply with a wide variety of rules. By consolidating different employment rules, this party says employment regulations would be easier to navigate.
how: This party would progress a Employment Relations Consolidation Bill in Parliament, with the focus of the legislation making the law easier to navigate with minimal cross-references. It would also clarify part of the Employment Relations Act to clarify when a contractor becomes an employee so that both parties know which laws apply before a dispute process begins.

statement: Review the compulsory GST threshold
why: This party says that the compulsory GST registration threshold has been $60,000 since 2009. Inflation has decreased the real value of this threshold, and GST registration increases costs and administration for a business. This party says the threshold should be reviewed to see if it is still appropriate.
how: This party would commission a review of the GST threshold, focused on barriers to compliance and considering the fiscal cost of any change.

statement: Create a standard process for repeat hiring of seasonal workers
why: This party says that agriculture and tourism businesses often hire the same workers every season. Workers and employers know each other well, but have to repeat the same process of paperwork to be hired. This party says there should be a specific process for hiring recurring workers for seasonal work.
how: This party would develop a standard recurring seasonal agreement and a short renewal process for seasonal employers to use, meaning dates have to be changed but less paperwork is required.

statement: Support apprenticeship employers with digital record-keeping
why: This party says that employers with apprentices should be focused on training and learning rather than paperwork. There are already some digital systems in use, and this party says that digital record keeping should be extended to increase efficiency.
how: This party would work with training providers to ensure approved digital competency records and electronic supervisor sign-off are consistently accepted across apprenticeships.

statement: Require students to finish Year 11 before leaving school
why: This party says that currently students are allowed to leave school once they are 16, which means that in many cases students do not complete Year 11. With curriculum updates requiring English and maths learning until the end of Year 11, it is important students complete the year and gain these useful skills before entering the workforce.
how: This party would require students to complete Year 11 or turn 16 before leaving school, whichever is later. This party would also use a Foundational Award in literacy and numeracy for students who finish the year. Students would still be able to apply for a leaving exemption earlier if they had found a job or were moving into further training.

statement: Align start and finish dates across different schools
why: This party says that it can be frustrating for parents at the beginning and end of the school year, when different children of different ages start school on different dates. Making the calendar consistent will require fewer parents to have to take extra days off work when some schools are open and others are not.
how: This party would work with schools to align the start and end dates of the school year to make these dates more consistent.

statement: Expand protected areas in the Hauraki Gulf
why: This party says that the Hauraki Gulf is a special area and "Auckland's playground". It believes that the waters of the Gulf are best used by people who fish, dive, swim, or collect kaimoana recreationally. Further protection for the Gulf will preserve these recreational uses.
how: This party would establish the Hākaimangō-Matiatia Marine Reserve off Waiheke Island as a 23 square km marine reserve, and expand the size of the existing Goat Island marine reserve. It would remove the exemption for ringnet fishing in the High Protection Areas of the Gulf. The current ban on collecting shellfish and other species from rockpools would be maintained and this party would impose higher penalties and enforce this ban more strictly. It would develop a Sustainable Fisheries Plan for the Hauraki Gulf by consulting with industry, including reviewing the current corridors where bottom

statement: Rule out a licence for recreational sea fishing
why: This party says that at least 600,000 New Zealanders go fishing occasionally, and recreational fish provides food and enjoyment, as well as supporting the business of charter boat tourism for fishing access. Fish stocks need to be maintained for recreational users, but fishing for food is a right and should not require a licence. This party says that honorary Fisheries Officers, who do enforcement work on a voluntary basis, could be doing more of the work of fisheries enforcement.
how: This party would ensure that no licence is required for sea fishing. It would ban the commercial sale of marlin, so hunting this fish can continue to be a sport. Enforcement and fines for people who do not obey catch limits would be increased, and part of this enforcement would be carried out by increasing the number of Honorary Fisheries Officers to 200 around the country. There would be some instant fines for people who catch more than the limit of fish.

statement: Create a $20m fund for fishing technology
why: This party says that the fishing industry is worth nearly $2bn and supports many jobs in NZ. Technology can increase the efficiency of the industry, for instance new designs that reduce how many seabirds are caught by boats. This party wants to support the seafood industry to invest by matching its investments in new technology.
how: This party would match investment in new technology from the seafood industry, up to a total of $10m, to create a $20m fund in total. The focus would be on equipment that reduces seabed contact and bycatch.

statement: Review and rewrite current fisheries law
why: This party says that NZ's fishery laws needs to be fit for purpose and a changing climate. A committee needs to examine and test all aspects of a proposed Fisheries Amendment to ensure reform is fair for all interest groups.
how: This party would balance commercial and recreational interests in any reforms to fisheries law. It says that improving the current Quota Management System would be a focus of reform and transparent data about fish stocks and how many fish are being taken would be prioritised too.

statement: Expedite work and visitor visas for the partners of NZ citizens
why: This party says that young New Zealanders who have moved overseas should have a reason to return, stay, and work and live in NZ. Within 100 days of being elected, this party would institute a range of policies aimed at New Zealanders thinking of returning. Particularly, it would focus on people who have met their partners overseas, so it is easy to return to NZ with their partners.
how: This party would prioritise and expedite work and visitor visas for partners of NZ citizens.

statement: Remove the ban on minimum car parking requirements for new housing
why: This party says that some people are concerned about housing growth impacting their streets, such as an increase in cars trying to park on the streets. Previously, the minimum requirement for the number of carparks in new housing was removed, but this party says the result has been roads clogged with cars and parking on berms and footpaths.
how: This party would remove the ban on having any minimum parking requirements set by councils for new house developments. Instead, it would allow councils to use minimum car parking requirements in suburban areas outside those identified for intensification, such as around rapid transit stops and city centres.

statement: Remove level crossings around Auckland
why: This party says that many Aucklanders spend too much time sitting in traffic or waiting for delayed trains. Removing level crossings in Auckland increases safety on the Auckland train network for trains and cars, and means the frequency of trains can be increased.
how: This party would progress with level crossing removals in South and East Auckland as part of rail network upgrades following the City Rail Link.

statement: Complete the Eastern Busway in Auckland
why: This party says that Aucklanders spend too much time sitting in traffic, which is bad for families and for businesses. The Eastern Busway is an already-underway project to increase the frequency of buses in East Auckland, so that public transport is faster and more reliable for people in this part of the city.
how: This party would complete the Eastern Busway bus route to Botany from Auckland's city centre.

statement: Create more school space in Auckland
why: This party says that parts of Auckland are growing rapidly, and require more space in classrooms as the school roll grows. This party says that there are 727 new classrooms funded across Auckland and these should be finished, as well as wanting to build a new school in Drury in the south of Auckland.
how: This party would deliver 499 approved classrooms across Auckland, 203 of which are under construction and 296 of which need to be completed. It would also progress the Drury Specialist School for high-needs kids, aiming to open by Term 1 in 2028. It would secure the Drury East primary school site for a future school in this area.

statement: Continue work on an approved hospital in Drury, south of Auckland
why: This party says that health services need to be planned as communities grow for the decades ahead. A site for a new hospital has been approved in Drury, a new housing development in the south of Auckland, and this party wants that hospital to be built.
how: This party would progress the building of a new hospital in Drury, south of Auckland. A 13 hectare site has already been secured for the hospital.

statement: Create a "Food and Fibre" subject at Years 12 and 13
why: This party says that NZ's agriculture workforce is getting older; the average farmer is now 58. There need to be more young people working in the agriculture sector, and providing more school options for people interested in these subjects is one way to create this outcome.
how: This party would introduce an industry led "food and fibre" subject into the curriculum, which students could take in Years 12 and 13. The subject would start in 2029.

statement: Expand Landcorp's apprenticeship and equity schemes
why: This party says that the average farmer is 58 years old, and the agriculture workforce is getting older. This party wants more young people to come into this industry, particularly emphasising how much of NZ's agriculture gets exported. Landcorp, the government-owned company which owns farms throughout NZ, already has schemes to encourage young people which this party wants to expand.
how: This party would expand Landcorp's apprenticeship scheme, which offers young people farming experience and qualifications while working. It would also grow Landcorp's farming equity schemes for dairy and livestock, which are a way for younger farmers to build equity while working towards owning their own farms. This party also supports an already-announced $10,000 scholarship for "future leaders" in agriculture and horticulture.

statement: Increase diagnostic capacity in regional NZ
why: This party says that a survey of 192 people working in regional health services said a lack of diagnostic tools and cardiac imaging was a major unmet need for delivering health services. This party wants to connect diagnostic tools in public and private hospitals and use mobile scanners so that people needing healthcare can get it more quickly.
how: This party would roll out mobile diagnostic services in rural areas of NZ. It would also link diagnostic tools in public and private hospitals so the tools that already exist can be used to their maximum capacity. It would report results and lengths of wait times so there is transparency about what is happening with this important issue.

statement: Increase penalties for biosecurity breaches at the NZ border
why: This party says that the arrival of H5N1, the very pathogenic avian influenza, is one example of how NZ agriculture is threatened by biosecurity breaches. This party wants to increase visitors to New Zealand and trade with other country, which also creates risks for biosecurity. It wants to pass new legislation to protect the agriculture industry from unwanted pests and diseases as much as possible.
how: This party would increase penalties for serious biosecurity breaches from $1000 to $2000 and grant biosecurity officers the right to refuse entry or deport people holding temporary visas. It would pass an amended Biosecurity Act and amendments to the Hazardous Substances and New Organisms Act to strengthen the biosecurity system and increase access to agricultural and horticultural products and veterinary medicines from overseas.

statement: Maintain the current position of agricultural emissions not being priced or offset through the ETS
why: This party says that it is a party of low tax, and pricing emissions through the Emissions Trading Scheme is a type of tax. While other industries must be part of the ETS, it says that NZ farmers should not have to follow this, and technological solutions should be able to reduce emissions rather than pricing systems. It says it supports the international Paris Agreement to reduce emissions, but that emissions reduction should not be achieved through pricing agricultural emissions.
how: This party would continue to exempt agricultural emissions, including methane, from the ETS. It also supports a different way of calculating methane emissions where current levels of emissions are maintained.

statement: Negotiate agreements with other countries to ensure continuous supply of fertiliser
why: This party says that NZ uses over 2 million tonnes of fertiliser every year. This fertiliser grows grass, which feeds cows and sheep, which are exported as meat and milk. Fertiliser is created from imported phosphate and processed in NZ, which makes NZ vulnerable to price changes in the international phosphate market. This party wants to use diplomatic efforts to ensure that NZ has a continuous supply of fertiliser.
how: This party would negotiate fertiliser security arrangements with key phosphate-supplying countries, modelled on an agreement with Singapore on essential supplies. It would also create a $10m "Critical Agri Inputs" fund to invest in fertiliser production and distribution, in partnership wit the industry. This money would come from the Primary Sector Growth Fund.

statement: Double the number of places on the voluntary vet bonding scheme
why: This party says that many of NZ's young vet's are moving to other countries, which is a problem for the agriculture industry. The number of places in Massey University's vet training programme is increasing by 15 students from 2027, and this party also wants to increase the number of students who can sign up for the voluntary bonding scheme, which provides a financial incentive to new vets who commit to working in rural areas for a time after graduating.
how: This party would double the vet bonding scheme to 70 places each year from the 2027 funding round. The scheme would also be open to NZ citizens and permanent residents who have trained in accredited Australian vet schools and are qualified to work in NZ. There would be reporting on results from the scheme each year, an a full review after three years. This party estimates that this would cost $2m each year once fully implemented, with the money coming from MPI baseline funding.

statement: Remove the "right to silence" in criminal cases where a child has been murdered
why: This party says that the "right to silence" is a fundamental part of the judicial system where people can choose not to speak in a court case if they do not wish to. However, citing high-profile examples of children who have been killed while adults who were present refused to give information to authorities, this party says it wants to penalise people who do not speak when there are investigations of the death of a child.
how: This party would impose a maximum penalty of 10 years imprisonment for people who choose not to give information regarding the death of a child. It would apply when a child under the age of 12 dies and it is unequivocal that an adult was present. This party would amend the Crimes Act, in consultation with legal experts, to create this change.

statement: Divide the "generation" and "retail" aspects of power companies
why: This party says that New Zealanders are paying too much for power, because four large companies generate 90 percent of NZ's power, controlling the supply and selling the power directly to customers. The party says that this situation results in high prices for households and industry, leading to companies closing down and job losses.
how: This party would replace the current system so that generation and retail are not done by the same companies. This would make sure that the most expensive generator would not set the price for the rest of the market.

statement: Guarantee fixed-price contracts for new electricity generation projects
why: This party says that prices for electricity are too high in NZ. Because of the structure of the market with four major companies, it is hard for competitors to enter the market. The "gentailer" companies can hold back supply, making electricity more expensive, instead of investing in more power generation.
how: This party would guarantee long-term, fixed-price contractions for building new electricity generation. The companies building this infrastructure would receive guarantees that their power would be the first to be used when needed. This would make it easier for investors to fund electricity generation projects, and increase New Zealand's energy security and resilience.

statement: Separate the Foodstuffs supermarket chain into two national cooperatives
why: This party says that food prices are too high in New Zealand, as a result of a supermarket duopoly controlling 80% of the grocery market. Food producers and households do not get a good deal from this system. Creating more competition will drive prices down.
how: This party would introduce legislation to split the Foodstuffs brands into two cooperatives; one for New World and Four Square and the other for Pak'n'Save. This would create more competition with Woolworths and result in lower prices and fairer deals for producers. This would create more certainty for major businesses like McCains and Heinz Watties, which have experienced job losses as a result of a poorly functioning system.

statement: Give the Commerce Commission and Grocery Commissioner more powers
why: This party says that the current Grocery Commissioner does not have the power to enforce the sector properly. The Commerce Commission cannot apply penalties as high as its counterpoint in Australia, investigations are often slow, and penalties are not enforced.
how: This party would increase the powers assigned to the Commerce Commission and Grocery Commissioner. The Commerce Commission would be able to apply penalties for serious breaches of up to $10 million, three times the gain, or 10 percent of turnover. Investigations would be faster and enforcement stricter. The Grocery Commissioner would have powers to investigate, make binding decisions and apply penalties directly.

statement: Make it easier for small food suppliers to compete on supermarket shelves
why: This party says that prices for food are too high in NZ, in part because supermarkets limit small food providers' access to customers. The supermarkets control suppliers' access to the market, favouring larger providers.
how: This party would introduce a new industry framework into the Commerce Act 1986 to fix competition issues quickly without waiting for legislative change. This would ensure producers are not pushed off supermarket shelves by larger players.

statement: Return at least 50 percent of mining project royalties to the region where mining took place
why: This party says that mining plays a vital role in NZ's economy and regions as one of the country's most productive sectors. The benefits of mining do not always stay in these regions, and communities should directly benefit from local mining projects. If mining expands, infrastructure and development in the regions must grow too.
how: This party would invest 50 percent of mining royalties in the region the resources were extracted from. This money would be spend on infrastructure like flood protection, energy generation transport and housing development and would be backed up by targeted regional investment. This money would also fund Mines Rescue capabilities.

statement: Survey all of NZ to look for minerals
why: This party says that NZ needs to gain the maximum benefit from its resources. Knowing which resources are available is a key step for making decisions about future mining projects. Investing in science, technology and the mining workforce will protect the benefits of mining into the future.
how: This party would invest in advanced core-scanning technology and pay for a modern geological survey to be done throughout NZ. It would also reopen the School of Mines to build the mining workforce and ensure that money made in the mining industry stays in NZ. Building on policies like Fast-track, this would make it easier for new mines to be created.

statement: Disestablish the Independent Māori Statutory Board from Auckland Council
why: This party says that this board is not accountable to ratepayers, yet influences decisions that are part of Auckland Council. The board is not elected and cost $3.5m last year. It says that Auckland Council can engage with Māori and recognise their interests but that this engagement should happen through people who are elected.
how: This party would introduce a members bill to disestablish the Independent Māori Statutory Board. All functions of the board would be returned to the main body of Auckland Council.

statement: Support new parents with a $5000 grant for the first three years of their child's life
why: This party says that New Zealand's birth rate is only 1.53 children per woman, when the replacement rate is 2.1 children per woman. If something is not done, this party says New Zealand may become entirely dependent on immigration in the future.
how: This party would offer all new parents (where at least one is a New Zealand citizen) a $5000 grant per year for the first three years of their child's life. This grant would apply to the first, second, and third children which the couple have. The grant would be tax free and not replace any current support.  This party estimates that this policy would cost $400 million per three-year-cycle.

statement: Increase the milk quantity guaranteed to NZ dairy manufacturing
why:
This party says that the present 50 million litres per year is too low to incentivise production at a large scale. The status-quo supports New Zealand-based dairy manufacturers, but does not support these firms to scale to size, which disincentives investment into Fonterra. 

Marketing ‘New Zealand Dairy’, this party sees this policy as a means of making NZ’s dairy manufacturing sector more competitive in export markets. It says it is important for the milk provision not to be a subsidy; dairy manufacturing firms would cover delivery and collection costs and pay farmers market rates.
how: This party would increase milk access from 50 million litres to 500 million litres per year over the first six years. From there, access would taper to 80 per cent, 60 per cent, 40 per cent and 20 per cent to encourage immediate investment. This would be done through changing the Dairy Industry Restructuring Act 2001.

statement: Establish a Special Economic Zone at Marsden Point
why: This party says Marsden Point should be allowed to operate under a lighter regulatory framework to support domestic energy production. The party argues that, with rising global tensions and increasing energy costs, New Zealand needs to better ensure itself against spikes in global fuel prices. Establishing a special economic zone (SEZ) will attract foreign investment.
how: This party would establish a Special Economic Zone, which would see a combination of tax breaks, wage subsidies, and reduced regulation to incentivise the development of energy and port operations. The party says that the principal benefits of the economic zone would be the bypassing of planning regulations and the RMA. If elected, this party would consider providing additional funding to help local councils run services in the SEZ, such as investment in physical, transport or communications infrastructure.

statement: Complete the reconstruction of Christchurch Cathedral
why: This party claims the rebuild is representative of Christchurch's earthquake recovery. Completing the rebuild would restore a symbol of the city's heritage and be a boost for local tourism and business in the city.
how:
The party has pledged $15m dollars to Christ Church Cathedral Reinstatement Ltd to complete the company's proposed pathway. The funding would be alongside money Christchurch City Council, not instead of.
