The additional government funding would help complete the first stage of the new rebuild project. This would re-open the Cathedral and remove the hoardings from the square during the first stage of full revitalisation.

 This party estimates that this policy would cost 15 million over one year.

statement: Ensure that only NZ citizens can vote
why: This party says that it is a problem that after two years of living in NZ, someone can claim permanent residency and vote. For visa holders who have no expiry date for their visa, they can technically vote after one year. It says that only those who are natural-born citizens and have sworn allegiance to NZ should be able to vote for who governs the country and in referendums that can change NZ.
how:
This party would restrict voting rights for all referenda and levels of government (including local government) to those with legal citizenship.

Permanent residents will still retain other rights such as the right to live, work, study, and access government support.

statement: Provide superannuation only to NZ citizens
why: The party says that New Zealanders who have worked since they were teenagers deserve security in retirement. As superannuation becomes harder to pay for as the population ages, it's unfair for people who have lived and worked in the country for a lot less time to receive the same payments.
how: The party would phase in the demand that one be a citizen to be eligible for superannuation over three years. It would amend the eligibility criteria to remove access to NZ Super for permanent residents.

statement: Reserve social housing for NZ citizens first
why: This party says that housing is becoming more expensive and that there's a greater need for social housing. The party claims that it is unjust not to distinguish between a citizen and someone yet to become a citizen when providing a scarce resource like social housing.
how: This party would amend legislation to prioritise NZ citizens in the allocation of social housing. Resident class visa holders will retain eligibility to be on the waitlist, but NZ citizens will be fast-tracked up the waitlist for social housing.

statement: Allow a two-year amnesty on overstayers if they self-deport
why: This party says that the illegal overstaying of visas by migrants is causing public distrust of the immigration system. However, people have built a life here and are discouraged by bans on re-entering the country if caught and deported.
how: This party would provide a 24-month/two-year amnesty whereby, if one chooses to self-deport by leaving the country, they will be eligible to apply to immigrate to NZ legally. Any overstayer caught thereafter will receive a permanent ban from applying. Pacific overstayers will be able to apply for a legal visa right away and stay in NZ.

statement: Remove automatic work rights from student visas
why: This party says that student visa holders compete in the competitive graduate job market and can take jobs from New Zealanders. It stays the intent of international education is for overseas economies to give money to NZ by paying for their education, not to provide automatic work rights and residence pathways. The party also cites broader concern with net numbers of migrants entering New Zealand and sees changes to student visas as a way of reducing net migration and its effect on infrastructure.
how: This party would have student visa holders lose their automatic right to work. To be allowed to work, student visa holders would have to fulfil strict conditions to ensure they are not doing work that could be done by NZ citizens. People who have been on student visas and want to transition to another visa would have to leave NZ and reapply for a new visa from overseas.

statement: Create a benefit stand-down period of ten years for migrants and lengthen residency and citizenship eligibility
why: This party says that benefit support comes with the rights and responsibilities of being a New Zealander. It wants to prevent the use of benefits by migrants yet to become citizens and to slow down net migration.
how: This party would implement a benefit stand-down period of ten years. This period would be in line with the additional changes to citizenship and permanent residency, where the required period to qualify for citizenship would double from five years to a minimum of ten years and from two years to five years for permanent residency.

statement: Expand criteria for deportation
why: This party says that that public trust in the immigration system requires trust that violent offenders would be deported. Immigration to NZ is a privilege, not a right.
how: This party would widen the criteria for deportation liability to cover any offence for which imprisonment is available as a sentence. Automatic deportation will be applied to those found guilty of violent or sexual crimes, fraud, participating in an organised criminal group, money laundering, or exploiting migrants.

statement: Raise citizenship and permanent residence application fees
why: This party says that application fees will be increased to fund the additional administrative burden of its other immigration reforms. Such increases should be accepted by applicants, as, according to the party, immigration to NZ is a privilege, not a right. The party claims that the application fee should be reflective of the value of becoming a New Zealander.
how: This party would increase citizenship and permanent residence application fees. The revenue gained from this will fund the additional administrative burden resulting from these stricter processes.

statement: Promote healthy eating as preventative healthcare
why: This party says that too large a share of NZ health spending goes towards caring for people once they're sick, as opposed to before. The party claims that 59% of health spending is spent treating chronic illness, and only 1.75% on the prevention of such conditions.
how: This party would promote nutrition from primary school to medical school, use health coaches in GP care, and require a full independent review of our dietary guidelines. It would fund research and development to better assess nutritional interventions for preventing and treating mental illness. It would fund development in agricultural tech and cut regulatory barriers to help grow markets for organic food items.  It would investigate how the use of vitamins in the delivery of healthcare can prevent people from getting sick again, including intravenous vitamin C pre- and post-surgery for preven

statement: Make health coaches an integrated part of primary care
why: This party says that the healthcare system responds to crises without dealing with the underlying causes, such as poor nutrition. It claims the incorporation of health coaches can help educate patients on how to better avoid underlying causes of illness.
how: This party would fund health coaches to be staffed at local general practices.

statement: Fund organic and nutrient-based health interventions
why: This party says that there is too little investment in preventive care. Poor nutrition is a driver of underlying conditions that lead people to need expensive healthcare.
how: This party would fund NZ scientists to assess nutritional interventions for preventing and treating mental illness. It would remove Medsafe/Pharmac barriers to recognising safe nutrients and invest in hospital trials that assess the effectiveness of intravenous vitamin C to treat infections. Farmers would be supported by to invest in the research of alternatives to potentially harmful agricultural sprays. It would fund development in agricultural tech and cut regulatory barriers to help grow markets for organic food items.

statement: Commission a full and independent review of NZ's nutritional guidelines and education
why: This party says that too large a share of NZ health spending goes towards caring for people once they're sick, as opposed to before. The party claims that 59% of health spending is spent treating chronic illness, and only 1.75% is spent on the prevention of such conditions. Better education and info can help inform people of how they can best make healthier decisions.
how: This party would launch an independent review that seeks to better understand metabolic health. It would promote nutrition from primary school to medical school. Such a review would look at current dietary guidelines.

statement: Increase autonomy and reduce administration for general practitioners
why: This party says that preventive care is underemphasised as part of the NZ health system. Regulatory barriers can increase costs for doctors, and professional standards are seen as too restrictive from the party's perspective.
how: This party would reduce the regulatory burden on doctors in primary care. It would also allow greater diversity of medical viewpoints in professional standards.

statement: Lower the corporate tax rate to 20% for small businesses
why: This party says that NZ firms need support for greater productivity and growth. The party argues that small businesses operating on thin margins need additional support to invest, develop, and start up.
how: This party would lower the corporate tax rate for all firms with turnover less than $30 million. The party claims the cost would initially be $1 billion and that additional growth would cover additional costs over time.

statement: Replace the Waitangi Tribunal with a Treaty of Waitangi Completion Commission
why: This party says that the Waitangi Tribunal, in its capacity to hear alleged ongoing breaches of the Treaty, is beginning to violate Parliament's sovereignty and voters' rights through its criticism of government policy.
how: This party would replace the Waitangi Tribunal with the Treaty of Waitangi Completion Commission, tasked with finalising all claims lodged before 2008.  It would implement this policy within the first hundred days of forming a government.

statement: Ban public sales of fireworks
why: This party says that the fireworks cause distress for pets, fires, and lead to increased use of emergency response resources. This leads to healthcare and ACC costs.
how: This party would introduce legislation that will stop the retail sale, manufacture, and importation of fireworks for public use. Fireworks would still be allowed for approved public displays.

statement: Increase In-Work-Family-Tax-Credit by $70 a week
why: This party says that working parents are struggling to get by and afford the essentials. The party cites the additional, but temporary, $50 added to the IWFTC by the government this year as needing to be increased and made permanent. The party says such changes will turn the temporary relief into a long-term pathway for parents in work to be able to plan for their families’ future.
how: This party would increase the IWFTC by $70 a week. The increase would not apply to the Family Tax Credit (FTC), which covers parents regardless of employment status. This party estimates that this policy would cost between $500m and $600m annually.

statement: Replace the Accredited Employer Work Visa with a shortage-led skilled work visa
why: This party says that NZ's immigration system should be used to manage genuine workforce shortages.  However, it says that instead the accredited employer work visa has too often been used as a means to simply find a preferable candidate and is a risk for the workers themselves, who can find themselves with less protection from exploitation.
how: This party would replace the Accredited Employer Work Visa with the shortage-led skilled work visa. Such a visa would be limited to shortages, requiring evidence of attempted NZ recruitment, transparency data, and a wage floor to protect domestic wages. The party also says the reforms should be targeted towards the most needed industries, which would restrict access for other industries that have a larger domestic workforce.

statement: Increase the funding for the NZ Coastguard
why: This party says that Coastguard, as an organisation, is funded only 40% by the government. 60% of its funding comes from public donations. The party argues that an essential service needs a more reliable funding model, so the organisation has greater certainty.
how: This party would increase Coastguard funding. The party would review the Coastguard’s funding arrangement to lift baseline funding and establish a contracting model to ensure that there's adequate access to capital for critical maintenance and capability investment, improved workforce capability, and volunteer support for training, wear and tear, and call-out support. This party estimates that this policy would cost $12 million a year.

statement: Add infrastructure and service capacity requirements to residential fast-track permissions
why: This party says that they support increasing housing supply, but do not want the increase in housing to come at the expense of the quality of public infrastructure or access to services for those who have already lived in affected communities.
how: This party would require fast-track housing developers to detail what infrastructure they need and demonstrate whether the present infrastructure can meet demand and has funding. Local authorities would also be required to provide advice on network capacity and delivery risks.

statement: Establish a combat sport commission
why: This party says that the coroner's report on the killing of Kain Parsons, in conjunction with concerns of illegal underground fight clubs involved in organised crime, requires expanded regulation of combat sports.
how: This party would establish a Combat Sports Commission. This organisation would focus on licensing events and promoters to ensure legality and safety. It would introduce minimum health and medical standards, such as pre-and post-fight medical examinations, attending medical practitioners at all events, mandatory stand-down periods between contests determined by medical professionals, and penalty systems for unsanctioned events. The Commission would partner with Sport NZ to to support legitimate promoters and athletes.

statement: Establish a 12-month trial for commuter rail in Canterbury and further south
why: This party says that traffic wait times are too great between Christchurch and the wider Canterbury region. The party says there are existing rail lines between Christchurch and Dunedin, which are owned by the government and should be delivering for the public.  The party wants the trial to determine a business case for permanent passenger rail.
how: This party would commence a 12-month trial of passenger rail across Canterbury, such as Christchurch city to Rolleston and Rangiora. It would also connected Canterbury to Otago with a Christchurch-to-Dunedin service.

statement: Withdraw New Zealand from the Paris Agreement
why: The party says meeting Paris commitments could send up to $22 billion of taxpayers' money offshore while New Zealand produces about 0.17% of global emissions.
how: This party would take New Zealand out of the Paris Agreement and says it will campaign on this at the election.

statement: Set mining zones, longer permits, reopen the School of Mines and refocus the Department of Conservation
why: The party says mining rules are duplicated, slow and inconsistent and are stopping investment and jobs.
how: As part of its mining package this party would identify mining zones with clearer rules, lengthen mining permits to cover the life of a mine including rehabilitation, reopen the School of Mines and fund trades training, fund Mines Rescue, invest in R&D for onshore value-add, refocus DOC on areas of high conservation value, review stewardship land, remove duplication including in the Wildlife Act, and make consultation time-bound.

statement: Allow 50% first-year depreciation on new plant and machinery for manufacturers and export sectors
why: The party says weak productivity and low business investment hold New Zealand back, and that front-loaded depreciation lifts investment and GDP.
how: This party would introduce a targeted 50% first-year depreciation rate for new plant, machinery and equipment in manufacturing and targeted export sectors (such as mining, aquaculture, forestry, farming and fishing). It says this is separate from the existing 20% Investment Boost.

statement: Expand the Game Development Sector Rebate and baseline funding for the Centre of Digital Excellence (CODE)
why: The party says the video-game industry is growing fast but local talent is being lost to Australia because of limits on the current rebate.
how: This party would raise the rebate rate from 20% to 40%, raise the per-studio cap from $3 million to $10 million, lift the annual appropriation from $40 million to $45 million by 2028, lower the claim threshold from $250,000 to $150,000, baseline CODE's $5 million budget and grow it to $7 million by 2028.

statement: 'Life means life': degrees of murder, whole-of-life sentences for first-degree murder and child rape
why: The party says the justice system too often fails to hold offenders to account and victims should come before offenders.
how: This party would create a formal 'degrees of murder' regime (1st degree: life without parole; 2nd degree: minimum non-parole period of 30 years; 3rd degree: minimum 10 years), increase sentences for attempted murder and wounding with intent from 14 to 25 years, and introduce life imprisonment for rape of children.

statement: More mandatory minimum sentences, tougher parole and limits on sentence discounts
why: The party says sentencing has not delivered justice for victims.
how: This party would increase the use of mandatory minimum sentences for serious violent and sexual offenders, cap non-guilty-plea discounts at 10% (guilty-plea discounts stay at 25%), raise parole eligibility to 75% of the sentence for long-term offenders, require murderers to be assessed as low risk before release, set an 8-year minimum non-parole period for 'coward punch' killings, treat home burglary like aggravated burglary, and oppose any extension of the Clean Slate law.

statement: Create a dedicated organised-crime agency and fold the Serious Fraud Office into Police
why: The party says transnational organised crime is growing and needs to be dismantled.
how: This party would establish a dedicated agency, with a responsible minister, to dismantle transnational criminal networks, ensure Police have the resources they need, and abolish the SFO, replacing it with a specialised division inside NZ Police.

statement: Strengthen self-defence protections, including investigating 'Castle Doctrine' laws
why: The party says people should be able to defend themselves and their property in their home or business.
how: This party would investigate 'Castle Doctrine' and 'Stand Your Ground' laws (no duty to retreat), change Police and Solicitor-General prosecution guidelines so people who 'excessively defend' themselves at home or work are treated as victims unless there is overwhelming contrary evidence, and require the Solicitor-General to review any such prosecution.

statement: State-funded immediate reparation for victims, faster publication of sentencing notes, less name suppression
why: The party says victims should come first and the courts should be more open.
how: This party would have the state pay immediate reparation to victims and then recover it from offenders, require District Courts to publish sentencing notes within 72 hours, limit final name suppression to extreme cases, and review traffic penalty regimes for consistency.

statement: Grant automatic citizenship at birth only to children of citizens
why: The party says permanent residence is easy to get and children of non-citizens currently become citizens automatically.
how: This party would change birthright citizenship so that only the children of New Zealand citizens are automatically citizens at birth (currently a parent with indefinite residence also qualifies).

statement: Make refugee/protected-person status temporary and tighten asylum rules
why: The party says asylum claims have risen and the system cannot distinguish genuine claims from people using it as another immigration pathway.
how: This party would give refugees and protected persons a renewable 24-month residence permit reviewed against conditions in their home country (modelled on Denmark), bar asylum claims from people in New Zealand on a 'working-class visa', and stop temporary work rights during assessment being used as a stepping-stone to another visa.

statement: Hold a referendum on a legislated cap of 20,000 resident visas a year
why: The party says population growth must not outpace infrastructure and New Zealanders should decide the size of the country.
how: This party would hold a referendum on a legislated annual cap of 20,000 resident visas, linked to infrastructure capacity and a 30-year Population Plan.

statement: Require student visa holders to leave New Zealand before applying for a different visa
why: The party says export education is being used as a route to work and residence.
how: This party would require student visa holders who want to switch to another visa to leave and reapply from abroad.

statement: Other 'Make NZ Healthy' commitments: informed consent, metabolic health, recognising nurses, vitamin D review, research on agricultural sprays
why: The party says the health system spends almost all its money treating illness rather than preventing it.
how: In its 15-point 'Make NZ Healthy' plan this party also commits to put prevention 'back at the heart of healthcare', focus on metabolic health, make informed consent a core part of care, recognise consumer choice, find better ways to acknowledge nurses, fund a review of vitamin D levels, fund hospital trials of intravenous vitamin C, and invest in agricultural innovation including alternatives to potentially harmful sprays.

statement: Hold a select committee inquiry into COVID-19 vaccine injuries
why: The party says the recent COVID-19 inquiry report did not go far enough on vaccine safety and who was affected.
how: This party would establish a select committee inquiry into injuries the vaccine 'may have caused', so that those affected can give evidence publicly and decision-makers can be held to account.

statement: Reform retirement village law without retrospective three-month buy-backs
why: The party says retirement villages are an important housing option for seniors but residents need more protection and choice.
how: The party backs the Retirement Villages Amendment Bill announced for introduction next term, says it will deliver reform that protects residents and keeps the sector sustainable, and opposes proposals for retrospective three-month buy-backs.

statement: Bring back the Southerner passenger train and make the Mainlander more frequent
why: The party says South Island cities and towns should be reconnected by rail.
how: This party would work with the operators of the Mainlander service to secure a commercially sound agreement that runs more trains between Christchurch, Dunedin and Invercargill.

statement: Regional infrastructure: new Matakana Island wharf and support for Sun Air's Bay of Plenty services
why: The party describes a 'Regional Infrastructure Plan' to back the provinces.
how: The party leader announced the party would help Sun Air maintain its Bay of Plenty services and build a new wharf at Matakana Island.

statement: Introduce a nationwide container return scheme
why: The party says billions of beverage containers end up as litter and ratepayers carry the cost.
how: This party has introduced a member's bill for a scheme that puts a small refundable deposit on beverage containers, with operational details set by regulation.

statement: Pause Waikato Regional Council's Plan Change 1 farm rules
why: The party says Plan Change 1 would force thousands of Waikato and Waipā farms into costly consents under a planning system that is being replaced.
how: This party calls for PC1 implementation to be paused until the replacement RMA system is in place, existing lawful farming is protected, and future freshwater rules pass a 'primary production viability test'.

statement: Make banks liable for preventable payment scams (Preventing Payment Scams bill)
why: The party says the banks' own code on scams is 'by banks for banks' and too weak.
how: This party's member's bill would impose a duty on both sending and receiving banks to protect consumers, require confirmation of payee, know-your-customer checks, urgent account freezing and information sharing, and make the default that losses are not borne by the consumer when a bank fails that duty.

statement: Set national accessibility standards (Accessibility Standards Bill)
why: The party says about 17% of New Zealanders are disabled and face avoidable barriers.
how: This party's member's bill would create a framework for practical accessibility standards, especially for new public buildings, transport, housing and digital services.

statement: Oppose the New Zealand–India free trade agreement
why: The party says the deal includes immigration and Paris Agreement clauses and investment commitments that are bad for New Zealand.
how: The party opposes the India FTA as signed and has used 'agree to disagree' provisions in government on it.

statement: Free, structured prostate cancer screening for at-risk men (member's bill)
why: The party lists this among its current members' bills.
how: The Health (Prostate Cancer Screening Services) Amendment Bill (Sept 2025) 'will provide free, structured screening for at-risk men, using PSA testing, MRI scans, and targeted biopsies where needed.'

statement: Require organisations to accept physical ID, not only digital ID (member's bill)
why: The party says physical identification must remain a valid and equal alternative to digital ID.
how: The Identification (Protection of Physical Identification Methods) Bill (Sept 2025) would require organisations to accept passports, driver licences, 18+ cards, school IDs and other prescribed physical documents whenever proof of age or identity is required.

statement: Legislate 'New Zealand' as the country's official name (member's bill)
why: The party says officials have been changing the country's name 'by stealth'.
how: The New Zealand (Name of State) Bill (Aug 2025) would state in law that 'New Zealand' is the official geographic name of the country.

statement: Protect the right to pay with cash (member's bill)
why: The party says cash must remain a private, accessible and reliable way to pay.
how: The Cash Transactions Protection Bill (July 2025) would provide for the enduring use of cash as a method of payment.

statement: Define 'woman' and 'man' biologically in law (member's bill)
why: The party says the law needs clarity and consistency.
how: The Legislation (Definitions of Woman and Man) Amendment Bill (April 2025) would define 'woman' as 'an adult human biological female' and 'man' as 'an adult human biological male' in the Legislation Act 2019.

statement: Repeal diversity and inclusion requirements in the public service (member's bill)
why: The party says public service employment should be based on merit, not DEI targets.
how: The Public Service (Repeal of Diversity and Inclusiveness Requirements) Amendment Bill (March 2025) would remove those requirements from the Public Service Act.

statement: Require national referendums before conscience-vote issues become law (member's bill)
why: The party says conscience issues should be decided by the people, not MPs' conscience votes.
how: The Conscience Acts Referendums Bill (March 2025) would require a mandatory national referendum before any conscience issue is passed into law.

statement: Return fluoridation decisions to local communities by referendum (member's bill)
why: The party says fluoridation decisions were centralised without community say.
how: The Fluoridation (Referendum) Legislation Bill (Feb 2025) would repeal the Health (Fluoridation of Drinking Water) Amendment Act 2021 and restore local decision-making through referendums.

statement: Only the official New Zealand flag on government buildings (member's bill)
why: The party says government premises should display only the national flag.
how: The Display of Flags (Government Premises) Bill (July 2025) would make it law that government buildings can only display the official flag of New Zealand.

statement: End New Zealand's participation in the UN, WEF and WHO
why: The party's stated aim is to 'take our country back from foreign interests'.
how: Listed on the party's website as quoted by RNZ; no further detail could be retrieved.

statement: End climate accords the party says are 'based on faulty science'
how: Listed on the party's website as quoted by RNZ; no further detail could be retrieved.

statement: Establish energy independence, including oil and gas
how: Listed on the party's website as quoted by RNZ; no further detail could be retrieved.

statement: Free farmers from 'restrictive regulations'
how: Listed on the party's website as quoted by RNZ; no further detail could be retrieved.

statement: Scrap the current tax system
how: Listed on the party's website as quoted by RNZ; no further detail could be retrieved. The replacement system is not described.

statement: Scrap all race-based policies
how: Listed on the party's website as quoted by RNZ; no further detail could be retrieved.

statement: Establish a New Zealand constitution
how: Listed on the party's website as quoted by RNZ; no further detail could be retrieved.

statement: 'Expose and eradicate propaganda' from news media
how: Listed on the party's website as quoted by RNZ; no further detail could be retrieved.

statement: Protect children from what the party calls 'corrupt sex and gender education'
how: Listed on the party's website as quoted by RNZ; no further detail could be retrieved.

statement: Decentralise government and 'return power to the people'
how: Listed on the party's website as quoted by RNZ; no further detail could be retrieved.

statement: Entrench the NZ Bill of Rights Act as supreme law
why: The party says Covid-era measures showed fundamental rights could be overridden by a simple parliamentary majority and that select-committee consultation is 'a toothless illusion'.
how: Make the Bill of Rights the constitutional bedrock so no government or emergency declaration can override rights such as free speech, movement, assembly and the right to refuse medical treatment.

statement: Introduce Swiss-style binding citizens' referendums: a citizens' veto on laws and citizen-initiated laws
why: The party says Covid-era measures showed fundamental rights could be overridden by a simple parliamentary majority and that select-committee consultation is 'a toothless illusion'.
how: Citizens could gather signatures to force a binding nationwide vote to strike down a law, or to put their own draft law on the ballot, with a lower signature threshold than the current 10% for non-binding referendums.

statement: Decentralise government under a 'subsidiarity' principle and let regions keep part of the GST and tax raised locally
why: The party says Covid-era measures showed fundamental rights could be overridden by a simple parliamentary majority and that select-committee consultation is 'a toothless illusion'.
how: Return decisions on local infrastructure, land management and regional development to communities, shrink central ministries and give regions financial autonomy.

statement: Withdraw from the Paris Agreement and focus on flood management and carbon-rich soils
why: The party says farm animals cannot release more carbon than they eat and that extreme weather is 'nature, not climate change'.
how: Exit Paris (it says staying would cost more than leaving), maintain river flows and channels to reduce flood risk, and support ecological agriculture with minimal synthetic inputs.

statement: Replace the EPA with an independent Health-Environment Protection Agency and apply the precautionary principle to new technology
how: New technologies and products only with full liability for the business introducing them; independent biosecurity at every entry point.

statement: Leave the CPTPP (TPPA) and RCEP and pursue 'fair trade' bilateral deals
how: Withdraw from agreements that limit New Zealand's ability to legislate, increase Pacific trade, strengthen anti-monopoly law and place a moratorium on sales of farmland, forestry, housing and infrastructure to non-tax-residents.

statement: Free up land and revise the RMA to speed house building, with a mix of public and private housing
why: The party says every citizen should have access to an affordable, warm, dry home.
how: Identify land for subdivision, sequence servicing and construction, and have the Ministry of Housing take a hands-on role.

statement: Require high standards for new homes (R5 insulation, rainwater and greywater systems, energy efficiency) and fund hempcrete building
how: Also solar or micro-generation, green space for gardens, recycling of building materials, lower consent costs for sustainable materials, and a funding scheme for hempcrete homes.

statement: Fully fund night shelters and low-cost living spaces for homeless people
how: Shelters would provide two nutritious meals a day and supplements; the party also wants to restore New Zealand's leadership in social housing.

statement: Adopt an 'Open Source First' rule for government software procurement
why: The party says dependence on multinational software vendors is a hidden import cost and a resilience risk.
how: Agencies must check for a suitable open-source option before buying proprietary software, compare whole-of-life costs, and use New Zealand providers for support.

statement: Decriminalise personal cannabis use and cultivation and support medicinal cannabis and hemp
how: No criminal offence for personal possession or growing; support home-grown medicinal cannabis and small NZ suppliers over 'Big Pharma', with lower licensing barriers; update law to support hemp products.

statement: Create a nationwide anti-bullying strategy treating bullying as a public-health issue
how: Awareness programmes in schools and communities, leadership training for teachers and managers, bullying questions in routine health screening, and treatment of psychological effects.

statement: Make one doctor's injury diagnosis final for ACC and abolish ACC's review and dispute machinery
why: The party says ACC 'expert shopping' is used to decline claims.
how: Disestablish ACC review specialists and investigators, cancel contracts with FairWay and ICRA, stop paying external consultants to contest diagnoses; it claims $61.5m a year savings to redirect to surgery, rehabilitation and disability support.

statement: Pursue Pfizer for breach of contract over Covid-19 vaccines and recover ACC vaccine-injury costs
how: Release the full NZ Pfizer contract, bring a Crown claim to recover the $16.8m ACC has paid for vaccine injuries, guarantee ACC compensation for long-term vaccine harm, give ACC a statutory right of recourse against manufacturers, and review ACC law to cover distress and loss of enjoyment of life.

statement: Make early childhood centres and primary schools Wi-Fi free, using wired connections
how: Minimise Wi-Fi in high schools too and work with Chorus on wired fibre connections.

statement: Replace the fisheries Quota Management System with a LegaSea-style system keeping fisheries in public ownership
why: The party says the QMS has depleted fish stocks, privatised a public resource and priced locals out.
how: Tendered commercial permits with no private sale of fishing rights, catches landed and processed in NZ, only NZ-owned operators, fleet separation in the territorial sea, and more recreational and customary inshore access.

statement: Replace DOC with a Department of Outdoors – Wildlife, Recreation & Nature (DOWRN)
why: The party says governments have undervalued New Zealanders' outdoors culture and access.
how: A department promoting access to all public land, coasts and rivers, poison-free conservation (trapping rather than poisons), food gathering on public land, and early public engagement on access decisions.

statement: Repeal the cap on donations eligible for a 33% tax credit
why: This party says that the $100,000 cap introduced on charitable donations in Budget 2026 will limit donations to the charitable sector and put crucial giving at risk. The cap will cost the public more through increased demand on public services. Removing the cap would also help the underfunded arts sector.
how: This party would remove the $100,000 cap on charitable donations and instruct the Law Commission to carry out a review of regulations in the charity sector in NZ.   At the same time, a comprehensive review and reform of the charitable sector is needed to mitigate concerns about donor-controlled charities and people receiving tax benefits without providing meaningful charitable services.

statement: Increase incentives to electrify houses, industries and transport
why: This party says New Zealand has solar, wind, hydro and geothermal resources but continues to rely too heavily on fossil fuels. It says increasing renewable energy and promoting the electrification household and industry electrification would have many benefits such as increased GDP, lower carbon emissions, smaller power bills and 5,000 new jobs over the next 30 years.
how: This party would incentivise the electrification of industries and housing. Low-interest loans and funding would be made available for households, community energy projects and public transport.  This would include an expansion of EECA’s Warmer Kiwi Homes subsidies ($80m annually) for household solar and electricity initiatives, and low-interest electrification loans via the national Ratepayer Assistance Scheme.

statement: Phase out inshore bottom-trawling by 2030 and make fishing more sustainable
why: This party says that our seas are hitting their ecological and economic limits. Fish species are being depleted under the current quota management system, and critical habitats are unprotected. Just 0.5% of NZ’s extensive ocean territory is protected as a marine reserve.
how:
This party would change the fisheries management system and make it more transparent. This includes the phasing out bottom trawling in all inshore areas by 2030 and installing cameras on commercial fishing boats. It would also move away from single-species quotas towards an ecosystem-based approach, and raise the baseline for sustainable fish stocks. 
In the short-term, the party says its wider oceans policy would cost no more than $100m a year, with some costs recovered from the commercial fishing industry.

statement: Introduce a land value tax of 1.75 percent
why: This party says that the current tax system is outdated and does not address the cost-of-living crisis, unaffordable housing, and the increasing pressure of the superannuation system. Under its tax plan, this party says incomes will increase for 70 percent of New Zealanders, and another 20% will see no change.
how:
An annual land value tax of 1.75 percent on urban land - and 0.5% on rural land - would be part of a wider tax reset aimed at incomes, house prices and retirement savings. The land value tax would lower house prices an estimated 10-15 percent and discourage land-banking and large property portfolios. There would be potential exemptions for farmers, retirees and other "land rich, cash poor" land owners. 
This tax would fund a universal citizen's income, with an extra $4bn for other uses. The tax system would also be simplified, with the number of tax brackets reduced to three - 28 percent, 34 p

statement: Create a lobbying register
why: This party says that trust in government is under pressure, and political integrity is important. It agrees with integrity groups that there needs to be more transparency around politics, lobbying and big party donations, if trust is to be rebuilt.
how: This party would regulate lobbying, including a one-year cooling off period for ministers becoming lobbyists, and a public register for lobbying groups. This would be part of a fuller political integrity package which would cost about $52m a year.

statement: Increase innovation by lifting science funding to 2 percent of GDP
why: This party says that economic growth is slowing and new ideas are needed in the areas of science and technology.
how: This party would increase innovation by lifting science funding to 2 percent of GDP. It would also turn polytechs into regional innovation hubs, offer incentives to invest in technology and beef up proven accelerator programmes. The wider innovation plan would cost an additional $1.33bn but create $4bn revenue annually.

statement: Establish citizens' assemblies for major decisions
why: This party says that Parliament has become gridlocked on many issues, at the expense of courage and long-term thinking. Political pendulum swings have resulted in projects being cancelled and reforms repealed. Citizens' assemblies, representative groups of ordinary people looking for consensus, would be backed by an independent parliamentary commissioner to amplify their decisions.
how:
This party would select, at random, groups of ordinary people who would serve for a year. The number of people would mirror the number of MPs. They would be compensated for their time and listen to experts, organisations and affected parties on topics that politicians have struggled to find consensus on. The assemblies would work to find common ground and set the policy direction for the politicians to respond to. 
This policy could cost $10-$15m a year, depending on how many assemblies are held.

statement: Make public transport free
why: This party says that the numbers stack up on universal free-to-ride public transport. This would provide immediate relief in terms of fuel demand and the cost of living, less traffic and increased productivity. More people taking public transport would ease congestion on our roads.
how: This party would make public transport universally free. It notes that the government already funds 90 percent of the cost of public transport from taxes and rates - fares only cover about 10 percent of operating costs. By scrapping ticketing systems, free public transport has an estimated net cost of about $150m per year.

statement: Support sectors and councils with climate change action
why: This party says that as the climate changes, we need to act urgently to mitigate and adapt to its negative impacts. The focus should be on preventing further heating, adapting to climate disruption and pushing for greater global efforts.
how: This party would focus on helping sectors to cut emissions and adapt to change. It would offer incentives to improve air quality and reward efforts to sequester carbon with biodiversity alternatives to pine trees. It would also support local government in finding nature-based solutions to flooding and heat stress; this policy would cost $5b. In addition, there would be subsidies for households and businesses to go electric or solar as part of its energy policy.

statement: Tighten rules on water quality
why: This party says that current economic models ignore the health of the ecosystems they rely on. This party believes native forests, wetlands and living soil should be funded as infrastructure. This means setting bottom lines to preserve rivers and protect biodiversity, and also supporting businesses that work to restore nature.
how: This party would improve water quality through stronger regulation and independent oversight. Water quality would also be impacted by increased conservation and biosecurity funding, with particular focus on wetlands, native reforestation and other biodiversity-rich projects.

statement: Support a circular plastics economy
why: This party says NZ's native forest, wetlands and living soil should be funded like the infrastructure they are. That includes supporting purpose-led businesses working to restore and protect nature.
how: This party would design a circular plastics economy aligned to the New Plastic Economy Roadmap. This plan, developed by the plastics industry and Scion, addresses the creation, use and reuse of plastics, treating it as a resource rather than waste.

statement: Restructure the electricity market to bring prices down
why: This party says that New Zealand has solar, wind, hydro and geothermal resources but continues to rely too heavily on fossil fuels. It says increasing renewable energy and promoting electrification would have many benefits such as increased GDP, lower carbon emissions, smaller power bills and 5,000 new jobs over the next 30 years.
how: This party would consolidate the energy industry, merging the four energy regulatory agencies into one, and shrink the number of energy distributors from 29 to no more than 8. It believes this policy would help make electricity more affordable. The party's full energy plan would be funded from about $500m in dividends from government stakes in electricity gentailers.

statement: Increase the energy grid up to 30GW by 2050
why: This party says New Zealand has solar, wind, hydro and geothermal resources but continues to rely too heavily on fossil fuels. Increasing renewable energy and promoting the electrification of households and industries would have many benefits such as increased GDP, lower carbon emissions, smaller power bills and 5,000 new jobs over the next 30 years.
how: This party would push for cross-party agreement to boost renewable energy by adding 19GW of new renewable generation capacity to the grid by 2050, bringing it up to 30GW. It would also launch a capacity investment scheme like Australia's to unlock capital and encourage industries to electrify their processes. The party's full energy policy would be funded through ringfenced government dividends from electricity generators.

statement: Create a political corruption watchdog
why: This party says that trust in government is under pressure. It believes there needs to be more transparency around politics, lobbying and big party donations, if trust is to be rebuilt.
how: This party would create an independent body to investigate political corruption and a party policy costing unit to verify policy claims. Other moves to strengthen political integrity include a ban on misleading election ads and strengthening the Official Information Act and whistleblowing laws. The anti-corruption body would cost $40m annually, part of a wider political integrity package which would cost around $52m a year.

statement: Cap political donations at $30,000 per donor
why: This party says that trust in government needs to improve. It believes there needs to be more transparency around politics, lobbying and big party donations if trust in politics is to be rebuilt.
how: This party would cap political donations at $30,000 per party per donor per election. Donations from companies and trusts would be banned, so only registered voters could donate. This is part of a political integrity package which would cost around $52m a year.

statement: Strengthen the Emissions Trading Scheme and include agriculture
why: This party says that as the climate changes, NZ must be ready to realise once-in-a-generation opportunities. The focus should be on preventing further climate heating, adapting to climate disruption and pushing for greater global efforts to handle climate change.
how: This party would strengthen the Emissions Trading Scheme by adding a mechanism for agricultural emissions and excluding new exotic forestry. It would also ensure the Climate Change Commission sets budgets.

statement: Give councils more tools to invest in infrastructure
why: This party says local authorities have been forced to rely almost entirely on property rates to service ageing infrastructure under growing demand. New tools are needed to help them maintain these assets and build new ones.
how:
This party would ensure councils had access to more tools such as congestion charges, value capture and accommodation levies and user-pays charges to help fund infrastructure. Funds would also be available through housing funds, climate resilience funds and council-specific loans.  A 30 percent cap on the Uniform Annual General Charge would also be repealed. 
Council spending would be overseen by an expanded Infrastructure Commission.
Other sources of funding could include a Local Government Regeneration Fund, a new NZ Infrastructure Fund and a full-scale Ratepayer Assistance Scheme. All three

statement: Introduce a universal income for citizens of up to $370 a week
why: This party says the current tax system is outdated and does not address the cost-of-living crisis, unaffordable housing, or the increasing pressure of the superannuation system.  By taxing land, redistributing the revenue and raising retirement savings, household incomes could rise for 70% of New Zealanders, and another 20% would see no change.
how: This party would gradually introduce a universal citizen's income of up to $370 a week for almost all adults. This would replace most benefits, with top-up support available for retirees, parents and others. The Citizen’s Income would lift incomes but is not enough to live on. This retains the incentive to work and reduces barriers for beneficiaries wanting to earn more. The Citizens Income would be funded by a 1.75 percent annual tax on urban land values and 0.5 percent on rural land. Tax brackets would also be simplified to 28 percent, 34 percent and 39 percent.

statement: Introduce a 10-year plan to strengthen the health system
why: This party says that our health system is under immense pressure because it changes whenever governments change, sacrificing long-term progress. Success in health would be more equitable access to healthcare, a less pressured workforce and fewer people getting sick.
how: This party would seek a 10-year cross-party plan that would allow time to develop the workforce needed and to invest in infrastructure and systems. This would include a lift in health funding from the current 7.4% of GDP to 9% over the next ten years, with a greater focus on primary, community and preventative care.

statement: Give the Commerce Commission greater powers and more market support to small businesses
why: This party says consumers are paying too much because of a lack of market competition in sectors such as the supermarkets and banking. It says small business also need more business support to be competitive and keep up with technology.
how: This party would give the Commerce Commission greater powers to investigate, intervene and force structural separation of anti-competitive businesses across the economy. It would also boost R&D tax credits for small businesses and offer budgeting help. It would also ensure fairness for small businesses in the ACC and retail payment systems. This is part of a wider innovation plan which would cost an additional $1.33bn but create $4 billion revenue annually.

statement: Increase NZ's marine reserves to 30 percent of our ocean territory, and protect coastal habitats
why: This party says the seas are hitting their ecological and economic limits. Fish species are being depleted under the current quota management system, and critical habitats are unprotected. Just 0.5 percent of NZ’s extensive ocean territory is protected as a marine reserve.
how:
This party would increase NZ's marine reserves to 30% of its ocean territory by 2035 and replace the Marine Reserves Act 1971. The party also aims to deliver at least 10,000 hectares of restored coastal habitat.  It would also establish integrated ocean governance through a reinstated Ocean Secretariat.
These moves fit within a wider ocean policy. The short-term cost is expected to be no more than $100m a year, some of which would be recovered from the commercial fishing industry.

statement: Invest in sustainable ocean industries beyond fishing
why: This party says that our seas are hitting their ecological and economic limits. Fish stocks are depleted, critical habitats are unprotected and just 0.5 percent of NZ’s extensive ocean territory is protected as marine reserve. A strong "blue economy" requires investment and different management.
how: This party would invest in sustainable aquaculture, marine research and tourism initiatives, with the aim of creating $500m per year in additional “blue economy” revenue. The party's wider ocean policy also addresses fisheries management, expanding NZ's marine reserves and protecting coastal habitats. The short-term cost of these policies is expected to be no more than $100m a year, some of which would be recovered from the commercial fishing industry.

statement: Permanently ban seabed mining in NZ waters
why: This party says that the seas are hitting their ecological and economic limits. Fish species are being depleted under the current quota management system, and critical habitats are unprotected. Just 0.5 percent of NZ’s extensive ocean territory is protected as a marine reserve.
how: This party would permanently ban seabed mining in New Zealand waters as part of a broader set of coastal and marine protection measures. It would also establish integrated ocean governance through a reinstated Ocean Secretariat. The party's wider ocean policy also addresses fisheries management, sustainable aquaculture, marine research and marine tourism. The short-term cost of the oceans policy is expected to be no more than $100m a year, with some of this cost recovered from the commercial fishing industry.

statement: Include te Tiriti and Aotearoa history in education
why: This party says the responsibility of the Crown as a Treaty partner should be treated seriously, including the protection of taonga and redress of historical wrong.
how: This party would ensure Aotearoa history, including Te Tiriti, is part of the education system and support the growth of te reo teachers.

statement: Repeal legislation around customary marine title
why: This party says the responsibility of the Crown as a Treaty partner should be treated seriously, including the protection of taonga and redress of historical wrong. It argues Māori authority over marine environments is both a Te Tiriti obligation and an opportunity to restore healthier relationships with the ocean. Many iwi and hapū are already leading the way in innovative marine management.
how: This party would repeal the the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Act passed last year, which tightens the criteria for recognition of Māori marine customary rights. This is part of a wider marine policy which includes modernising legislation, recognising Māori customary management tools and including Māori as full partners in marine protection planning processes.

statement: Rewrite gene technology regulations
why: This party says that there is broad agreement across science, industry, and government that the current gene technology framework is no longer fit for purpose. However, the current bill was developed without proper public consultation, leaving critical questions around trade, liability and environmental risk. The bill includes no clear statement obligating the regulator to protect people and the environment and no full regulatory impact statement. Left as it is, the party says the bill could create one of the most liberal gene technology regimes in the world.
how: This party would not support the Gene Technology Bill in its current form, but believes it is possible to get the regulation right. It favours full industry and public consultation and backs a modern framework, based on independent expert assessment, case-by-case evaluation and accountability. It calls for a national conversation on gene technology.

statement: Forgive student loan interest for returning Kiwis
why: This party says our economy needs new ideas and science, technology and innovation are traditional sources for fresh thinking. The country needs young talented Kiwis who are currently offshore to bring their experience and skills back to help drive the economy.
how: This party would roll back the student loan interest of returning Kiwis on up to 3 years spent overseas. This would apply to both newly graduates and those currently overseas. The rollback would be applied at the end of their loan repayment, and conditional on being resident in New Zealand when the loan is repaid. This policy would cost an estimated $95m.

statement: Revamp zoning to reduce house prices
why: This party says that house prices in NZ are too high - on average, 7.3 times the median wage, when 3 times is considered affordable. There's also still a shortage of 80,000 houses. This party says the solution is unpopular: NZ has to build more and house prices have to drop.
how:
This party would simplify zoning, creting a smaller, consistent set of zones for productive farmland, civic spaces and heritage buildings. Medium density housing, mixed-used and extensions to public and retail spaces would be encouraged, and the party would streamline the processes for building tiny homes, sleepouts and extensions. 
These measures, along with a 1.75% tax on land values and more support for the construction sector, would help increase house supply, bring down house prices, and make landbanking less attractive.

statement: Boost court and rehabilitation funding to reduce reoffending
why: This party says that our prison system should be doing a better job of providing rehabilitation and other solutions that reduce the chances of reoffending.
how: This party would introduce a suite of measures including increased funding for the courts and probation services, to get remand prisoner numbers down. It would expand mental health programmes for prisoners dealing with past family violence. It would raise the age of the youth court jurisdiction, in line with developmental science, and expand drug and mental health court pilot programmes. It would take a health-led response to drug issues, including decriminalising drug possession but not supply.

statement: Decriminalise drug possession, but not supply
why: This party says that NZ's prison system should be doing a better job of providing rehabilitation and other solutions that reduce the chances of reoffending.
how: This party would It would de-criminalise drug possession (but not supply), and shift to a health-led response to drug issues.

statement: Create a 10-year education plan
why: This party says that New Zealand's education system is capable of excellence, but it has since become politicised and student results have fallen. Schools need more funding, and teachers face high workloads, poor pay and workforce planning issues. A plan is needed where curriculum and assessment design is not set by politicians, and students are better prepared to learn in new ways.
how: This party would create a 10-year cross-party education plan. It would include an independent council to oversee curriculum and assessment design, including a review of the government’s replacement of NCEA with NZCE/NZACE. It would also promote the purposeful use of technology and expand access to te reo Māori learning. The costs would be spread over 10 years, and many parts of the plan would not require extra funding.

statement: Allocate more support and staffing to early childhood education
why: This party says that New Zealand's education system is capable of excellence, but has become politicised and student performance has fallen. There is a need for more independent and longer-term planning, starting with early education which is over-stretched and under-resourced.
how: This party would introduce a 10-year education plan with cross-party support. The plan would include modernising early childhood education, by providing ensuring better staff-to-child ratios, better spaces and more core funding for community-owned services like playcentres, kōhanga reo, and kindergartens. It would also encourage the inclusion of early childhood-trained teachers in primary schools, to ease the transition for children. The cost would be spread over the 10 years of the plan and in many cases, would require no direct increase in funding.

statement: Introduce a 20-year resource and research plan for the tertiary sector
why: This party says that New Zealand's education system is capable of excellence, but has become politicised and student results have fallen. It is calling for more resourcing, more independence and longer-term planning, including better connections between vocational and academic learning.
how:
This party would push for a 20-year Skills and Learning Accord which would smooth the pathway between vocational and academic learning. This plan would aim for sustainable funding, coherent strategy and investment in research capabilities for universities, wānanga, and polytechs. 
The cost would be spread and in many cases, would require no direct increase in funding.

statement: Increase conservation funding
why: This party says that biodiversity in New Zealand is at risk. Nature needs a strong stance from the government to invest in an economy that is good for nature rather than damaging to it. Economic models should not ignore the health of the planet.
how: This party would increase conservation and biosecurity funding, with particular focus on wetlands, native reforestation and other biodiversity-rich projects.

statement: Restore adult education programmes
why: This party says that New Zealand's education system is capable of excellence, but it has become politicised and student performance has fallen. The education system needs to prepare students better for a more complex world and foster lifelong learning for adults.
how: This party would restore adult and community education. This is part of its push for cross-party agreement on a 10-year plan for the wider education sector. This long-term plan would focus on stability for students, support for teachers and modernising learning for the future.

statement: Lift health funding to 9 percent of GDP
why: This party says that our health system is under immense pressure because it changes whenever governments change, sacrificing long-term progress. People are finding it difficult to access care and the medical profession needs stability. Filling the gaps in primary care, Māori wellbeing, workforce, mental health, and elective treatment would cost at about $1.3b a year, or an additional 1.5 per cent of annual GDP.
how: This party would lift health funding from the current 7.4 per cent to 9 percent of GDP over the next 10 years. This would work in tandem with a 10-year cross-party health plan to provide certainty. Funding for GPs and other primary care providers would also be increased to help catch illness early or even prevent it. This would rise gradually from 5.7 to 10 percent of Health NZ's spending. By setting health funding as a share of GDP, it will grow consistently with the economy, rather than having to be found each Budget.

statement: Make housing more affordable with targeted construction support
why: This party says that New Zealand has a shortage of 80,000 homes and an affordability problem. Increasing the housing supply will help lower house prices; this means supporting the construction sector to overcome its lumpy pipeline and still build with quality.
how:
This party would back reputable affordable housing developments by underwriting to smooth out the 'boom-bust' cycle. It would also support offsite builders who take on apprentices. Housing quality would be encouraged with low-cost loans, and by refunding GST collected during construction to councils for environmentally high standard builds. 
These moves would be in tandem with zoning changes and a 1.75 percent urban land tax, which together would lower house prices and discourage land banking.

statement: Raise up to $60b to finance infrastructure
why: This party says that NZ's government debt is around 50 percent, about half of the average of the other OECD countries. It believes NZ has room to borrow carefully for assets that repay us over lifetimes. It adds that deferred maintenance is borrowing from our children.
how: This party would raise up to $60b over ten years through a new Infrastructure Fund, with interest costs under 1 percent of GDP. It would borrow at Crown rates instead of costly private finance, and issue bonds that KiwiSaver funds can invest in. It will also back councils with grants, not just loans, plus new funding tools so those who benefit contribute and ratepayers don't carry the load.

statement: Offer incentives to businesses to buy electric vehicles
why: This party says encouraging businesses to buy electric vehicles will reduce their ongoing fuel costs and make them more resilient to volatile prices. As businesses are big buyers of new vehicles, this would also increase the pool of EVs in the secondhand market.
how:
This party would allow accelerated depreciation and fringe benefit tax exemptions for business electric vehicles worth up to $50,000 (or $75,000 for utes and vans).
The fringe benefit tax exemption is expected to cost $31m a year, growing to $155m as uptake increases. 
The impact of accelerated depreciation will start at about $95m a year, but much of it will be recovered as depreciation timing unwinds. Both will be funded from ringfenced dividends from state gentailers.

statement: Bring in tougher rules around tobacco, vaping, alcohol, and unhealthy food
why: This party says that tobacco, alcohol and unhealthy food account for roughly a quarter of all the healthy years New Zealanders lose to death and disability. Prevention receives a small fraction of health spending relative to the share of health loss these risks cause.
how:
This party would work to reduce the harm from tobacco, as well as alcohol and unhealthy food, as part of a 10-year health plan. This would include a renewed Smoke-free New Zealand programme, with fewer places selling tobacco, and mandated de-nicotinisation of smoked tobacco. 
Quit programmes and regulated alternatives for adult smokers would be better funded, and there would be stronger protections against youth access to vapes.

statement: Rebuild the school lunch programme
why: This party says that unhealthy food account for roughly a quarter of all the healthy years New Zealanders lose to death and disability. Prevention receives a small fraction of health spending relative to the share of health loss these risks cause.
how: This party would roll out several measures to encourage healthier eating, including restoring the original lunches in schools programme. Nutrition would be an overall health priority. It would extend the nutritional standards used in hospitals to other sectors like aged care, prisons and schools. A national nutritional study would also be commissioned to better inform policymakers. The party's 10-year health plan will lift health funding to 9% of GDP, with a greater focus on prevention and primary care.

statement: Limit the lobbying power of the tobacco, alcohol and unhealthy food industries
why: This party says that tobacco, alcohol and unhealthy food companies have an undue influence over the policies that regulate them. These three sectors account for roughly a quarter of all the healthy years New Zealanders lose to death and disability. This party believes more focus needs to go on harm prevention in the health sector.
how: This party would introduce rules for lobbying and donations, which would make it tougher for industries that profit from illness. This includes a mandatory public register of lobbyists and a cooling-off period before ministers and senior officials could take industry roles in sectors they regulated.

statement: Use the money received from stakes in gentailers to fund renewable energy
why: This party says that New Zealand has solar, wind, hydro and geothermal resources but continues to rely too heavily on fossil fuels. It says increasing renewable energy and promoting the electrification household and industry electrification would have many benefits. The current electricity system is unfair; renewable energy generation has been underfunded and created expensive power bills for individuals and businesses. The government has a majority stake in several major power companies and is incentivised to keep prices high.
how: This party would add 30 gigawatts of renewable energy to the grid by 2050. This ambitious target will require building just over 556 megawatts of electricity generation to the country every year. The government currently receives approximately $500m from stakes in the electricity gentailers each year. This money would be ringfenced for investment in generation so that there is no incentive to maintain high prices. Electricity distributors would be consolidated and all electricity regulation would fall under one regulator. This party estimates that this policy would cost 500 m.

statement: Ensure NZ's emissions goals align with the Paris Agreement
why: This party says that greenhouse gas emissions targets and budgets hold the government accountable and give households, businesses and investors certainty. It believes NZ's domestic budgets, international commitments and policies must form one coherent pathway when it comes to emissions.
how: This party would restore the link between NZ's national emissions budgets with our Nationally Determined Contribution and the Paris Agreement's goal of limiting global warming to 1.5°C above pre‑industrial levels. It would also record the cost as a liability on the Crown balance sheet, and would implement the Climate Change Commission's advice on amendments to the 2050 emissions targets, which include international aviation and shipping emissions.

statement: Build a $5bn fund to support climate resilience, including $500m for nature-based solutions
why: This party says that preparing for climate change means doing our part to prevent further heating and adapting to climate disruption. This includes valuing nature as critical climate resilient infrastructure.
how: This party would create a $5bn climate resilience fund for climate adaptation, including $500m for nature-based solutions which reduce emissions and increase climate change resilience. This would include support for local government in managing flood resilience and heat stress. More widely, this party aims to help all sectors with adaptation and emissions reduction.

statement: Restore pay equity deals for care and support workers
why: This party says that recent law changes cancelled many active pay equity claims. This included disability care and support workers, and experts warn this will make it harder to hire and keep workers, cause staff shortages, and lower the quality of care.
how: This party would re-instate rules from the Equal Pay Amendment Act 2020 to ensure care and support workers get fairer pay and recognise their skills, helping to create a stable, long-lasting care workforce.

statement: Improved respite and carer support for the disabled
why: This party says accessibility and care is a growing issue. One in six Kiwis have a disability and if ageing-related access issues are factored in, 1 in 4 Kiwis will have accessibility needs in their lifetimes. Everyone should be able to participate in society with dignity and make the most of opportunities. However, the current Disability Support Services Bill did not properly consult with those it affects, and fails to give paid and unpaid carers the support they deserve.
how: This party would look to improve disability policy, including good care plans for disabled adults as their family carers age. It would back pay equity for care and support workers. It would also seek more support for unpaid carers, with improved respite care and more flexibility to balance their employment and unpaid caring roles.

statement: Oppose disabled people being paid less than minimum wage
why: This party says that many disabled people lose benefit income if they work and some are even legally paid less than the minimum wage. One in six Kiwis are disabled and when ageing-related access issues are factored in, one in four Kiwis will face access issues in their lifetimes. So access to care and income are key issues for those with disabilities.
how: This party would work to end rules that allow disabled people to be paid less than the minimum wage. It would improve support for employers to recruit and retain disabled workers. This party argues its Citizens’ Income and Disability Allowance would ensure disabled people would not lose income support for doing paid work.

statement: Ensure better connections between government systems and those with a disability
why: This party says people with long-term disabilities often find themselves endlessly repeating their story or having to prove their disability to authorities. Or they may fall through the cracks if their health, education, ACC and disability support systems are not strongly connected.
how: This party would back a "Tell Us Once" system, which would mean those with long-term disability support needs would not have to repeat their story or have tests over and over. Privacy would be protected and they would have control over how their information was shared. They would be supported to navigate the various government agencies that are connected to their case.

statement: Provide more support for the arts through a citizens income and innovation funding
why: This party says that a stronger arts ecosystem creates jobs and wellbeing, builds healthier communities and helps define national identity. NZ sits in the bottom ten OECD countries for public arts investment. The barriers for artists are less about a lack of arts funding and more about unpredictable income, and changing a mindset that the arts are a key part of the economy, rather than an optional extra.
how: This party would address the precarity of an artist's income firstly with its universal citizen’s income policy, which would enable artists to take a financial gamble on their career. Tax reforms would help over irregular income and free up charitable giving by repealing the cap on charitable donations. This party would more broadly support the arts through other policies such as an AI framework and revamp of the polytech sector, which would address copyright exploitation and recognise the arts in innovation funding.

statement: Five 'bottom lines' for supporting any government: Commerce Commission break-up powers, lobbying and donation reform, a 10-year health plan, ending bottom trawling, and Paris/Climate Commission commitments
why: Opportunity says no party can achieve its whole platform under MMP, so it names five non-negotiable policies any governing partner must accept.
how: (1) empower the Commerce Commission to investigate, intervene and force structural separation; (2) a mandatory lobbyist register and code of conduct and a per-donor cap with donations from registered voters only; (3) a 10-year cross-party health plan; (4) an immediate end to bottom trawling in the most damaged inshore areas such as the Hauraki Gulf, then a staged phase-out; (5) recommit to Paris obligations and protect the Climate Change Commission. It adds that honouring Te Tiriti is an approach it will bring to negotiations.

statement: Realign income tax to three rates: 28% up to $50,000, 34% to $200,000 and 39% above
why: Part of the Tax Reset, which Opportunity says simplifies tax and removes secondary tax rates.
how: New brackets alongside the Citizen's Income, Land Value Tax and KiwiSaver 2.0.

statement: Replace Working for Families and most benefits with tax-free Child Support Incomes and fixed top-ups
why: Opportunity says the benefit system traps people in poverty with effective marginal tax rates of up to 90%.
how: Per-child payments starting at $18,250 for a first child in the first year and falling to $7,750 for ages 4–18, plus a $9,500 sole-parent allowance, a $6,000 disability allowance, superannuitant top-ups and regional Housing Support Income payments.

statement: Phase in the Tax Reset over about a decade, starting with 18–29-year-olds and a 0.5% urban-only land tax
why: Opportunity says changes of this scale must be introduced carefully to avoid inflation and disruption.
how: Two years of planning first; Citizen's Income rolled out in age tranches of about 25% of the population; Land Value Tax starting at 0.5% on urban land and rising to 1.75%/0.5% rural by year 6; KiwiSaver 2.0 contributions rising 1% a year over six years.

statement: Allow only registered voters to donate to parties, cut the disclosure threshold to $1,000 and cap spending across the whole electoral cycle
why: Opportunity says it wants to 'sever the link' between donations and political influence.
how: Ban donations from companies, trusts and other entities and from non-voters; require audited annual party statements; apply advertising spending limits over the full three-year cycle with quarterly Electoral Commission summaries.

statement: Impose a one-year cooling-off period before ministers, senior staff and officials can become lobbyists
how: Part of its lobbying regulation, alongside a statutory code of conduct, a ban on contingency fees and foreign-lobbying disclosure.

statement: Strengthen the Official Information Act, MPs' pecuniary-interest rules and whistleblower protections, and create an independent policy costing unit
why: Opportunity says good rules mean little without institutions that enforce them.
how: Narrower OIA withholding grounds, lower pecuniary-interest thresholds, broader whistleblower coverage, a better-funded Electoral Commission and a costing unit available to all registered parties.

statement: Require Opportunity MPs to rent from unrelated parties rather than use allowances on property they own, and seek a full review of MP entitlements
why: Opportunity says public money should not build MPs' private property wealth or flow back to parties or donors.
how: Its MPs would only claim actual, reasonable accommodation costs paid to an unrelated third party and would not lease property linked to the MP, party or major donors; it would seek a review of allowances including those for former MPs and spouses.

statement: Require AI data centres to fund their own clean energy, pay full grid-connection costs and report energy and water use
why: Part of Digital Future, which Opportunity says sets guardrails to protect people, data and the environment.

statement: Require New Zealanders' critical data to be hosted onshore and favour local and open-source suppliers in government tech purchasing
how: Also: a public register of government technology projects, recognition of Māori Data Sovereignty Principles in public-sector AI procurement, more cyber-security funding and a review of rights in an AI world (algorithmic bias, copyright).

statement: Introduce a 25% tax credit for small businesses adopting new technology and a cross-party national AI framework
how: A tax credit to help SMEs adopt cutting-edge tools and a national framework on data rights, IP and investment 'shaped by the New Zealand public directly'.

statement: Double government funding for start-up incubators, accelerators, deep-tech programmes and Young Enterprise
how: As stated in the Breakthrough Economy policy.

statement: Agree a population policy for stable long-term immigration
why: Opportunity says immigration brings skills and capital but has not been matched by infrastructure and planning.
